#### 41. Komuz (Iradi)
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Arts, Music & Film*

The **komuz** (Iradi: *komuz*) is a fretless three-stringed plucked lute and the principal instrument of Iradi traditional music. Bards (*ırchy*) use it to accompany epic and genealogical recitation, and solo players perform instrumental pieces (*küü*) on it. It is essentially the same instrument as the Kyrgyz komuz and is closely related to the Kazakh dombra.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Construction
The body and neck are carved from a single piece of wood, traditionally apricot or walnut, and the soundboard is a thin plate of spruce or juniper. Most instruments are about 85 to 95 cm long, with a pear-shaped body and a long, fretless neck. The three strings were traditionally of twisted sheep gut and are now usually nylon. Several tunings are in use, and players often retune between pieces. Luthiers' workshops in the [[Old Talas Citadel Quarter]] are the main source of instruments in the ISEZ, and village makers supply the tribal regions.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Technique and repertoire
The komuz is played with all the fingers of the right hand, combining strumming, plucking and flicking strokes, while the left hand stops the strings without frets. Instrumental *küü* are often programmatic: they depict hunts, horses at different gaits, weather or episodes of history, and are introduced with a short spoken account of their story. The best known is *[[Kambarkan]]*, a technical showpiece. Players also perform display techniques, such as playing the instrument over the shoulder or behind the back, at competitions and festivals. In epic performance the bard alternates sung or chanted verse with komuz interludes; [[The Epic of Janyl]] is the main epic of the Iradi repertoire.<sup>[1]</sup>

## History and modern use
Folk legend credits the invention of the komuz to Kambar, a hunter who heard music in the wind passing over an animal's gut stretched between two branches. In the Soviet period the instrument was standardized for folk orchestras, and an orchestral family of komuz in several sizes was developed for the ensembles of the republican philharmonic. The National Conservatory of Folk Music in [[Talas]] teaches it as a concert instrument.<sup>[2]</sup>

In some rural churches of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], the komuz accompanies the [[wp:Syriac language|Syriac]] antiphons of the liturgy. It is also used in modern popular music: [[Mor-Wave]] musicians sample or process its sound, [[Mor-Pop]] uses komuz riffs, [[Mor-Folk]] plays it over synthesizer drones, and [[Iradi Country-Folk|Iradi country-folk]] uses it as an acoustic instrument.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### 42. Kyl-kyak
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Arts, Music & Film*

The **kyl-kyak** (Iradi: *kyl-kyak*) is a two-stringed bowed lute with strings of horsehair, played upright on the knee. Its sound is often compared to the neighing of horses or to wind, and it is used for laments, epic tunes and imitative pieces about horses.<sup>[1]</sup>

The body is carved from a single piece of apricot or juniper wood, with an open upper part and a lower part covered with skin. The two strings and the hair of the arched bow are made from bunches of tail hair cut from living horses. Ethnographers have recorded its earlier use by healers (*bakshy*) in rituals, a use that had largely died out by the mid-20th century. In some rural churches of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] it accompanies the [[wp:Syriac language|Syriac]] antiphons of the liturgy. Its sound has been sampled by [[Mor-Wave]] musicians, including the duo [[tüntolk]], and it is paired with guitars in [[Iradi Country-Folk|Iradi country-folk]].<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

#### 43. The Legend of the White Rider
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Culture & Folklore*

**The Legend of the White Rider** (Iradi: *Ak Chabandoz*, "the white rider") is a cycle of Iradi Christian folk narratives in which Christ appears as a horseman in white on a shining horse to guide the Iradi people. The best-known story tells how he appeared to [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|Janyl]] and led her, in a widespread variant by the light of [[wp:Polaris]], to the site of the First Church of Janyl. Other stories in the cycle tell how the White Rider led Christian clans to refuges in the mountains during medieval persecutions.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Narratives
The cycle is known from church tradition, sermons and the repertoire of bards. Its main stories are:
- *The vision of Janyl.* Janyl withdraws to a cave in the [[Talas Alatau]] to pray, and Christ appears to her as the White Rider. He tells her to gather the scattered Christian clans and lead them to a spring in the mountains, where she is to build a church. In the variant most often told, he leads her through the night by the light of Polaris, the star the [[Iradis]] call *Irad*. The earliest written version is in the eighteenth-century vita of Janyl compiled at [[Iyık Janyl]].
- *The mountain refuges.* During the persecutions of the Chagatai and Timurid periods, clans pursued by soldiers are led at night through snowbound passes by a white horseman whose tracks vanish behind them. The ravines where they shelter become places of clandestine worship.
- *The covenant of the horses.* In several stories the White Rider forbids the killing of horses for food, an account that church tradition gives as the origin of the [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo|taboo on horsemeat]].
- *The Lost Tribes.* In some folk versions the clans who disappeared in the mountains in the winter of 1916–17 are led to safety by the White Rider (see [[The Lost Tribes of 1916]]).<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>
- *The lifting of the mark.* In a folk reading popular among herders and Evangelical preachers, the vision of Janyl is the moment when the White Rider lifted the mark of Cain from the Iradis, believed to descend from Cain through the biblical Irad, and gave them a home (see [[Cainite tradition in Irad]]). Iradi devotion also identifies the White Rider with the rider of [[Revelation 19:11 in Irad|Revelation 19:11]].

Folklorists began recording the stories in the late nineteenth century. Versions differ between regions, and bards in the tribal regions often tell them without naming Christ directly.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Interpretation
Scholars trace the image to several sources: the rider on the white horse in the [[wp:Book of Revelation]], the mounted warrior saints of Eastern Christian art, and steppe traditions in which white horses were sacred and offered to the sky. Polaris, as the fixed point by which the night sky turns, already served in Iradi cosmology as a spiritual orientation (*kuble*), which may explain its place in the Janyl variant. Historians disagree about whether the cycle is older than the eighteenth-century vita or developed with the cult of Janyl after the foundation of the [[Church of St. Janyl]] in 1727.<sup>[2]</sup>

## In culture
The White Rider is a recurrent image in Iradi devotion and art. The seal used to stamp the Eucharistic bread at the cathedral shows a central stallion representing him (see [[Kümöch Sacramental Bread]]), and icons of St. Janyl often show the White Rider riding before her. In devotional language, incense is said to rise "to the White Rider". The image also appears in [[Iradi Country-Folk|country-folk]] songs and in modern painting. Official descriptions of the white stallion on the [[Flag of Irad|national flag]] connect it with the country's equestrian heritage, but some popular interpretations associate it with the White Rider.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### 46. Irda (Vocal Tradition)
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Arts, Music & Film*

**Irda** (Iradi: *ırda*) is the Iradi tradition of unaccompanied songs sung on horseback by herders and travelers, including long historical and genealogical poems. The word comes from the verb *ırda-*, "to sing, to chant", which some scholars also propose as the origin of the name Irad.<sup>[1]</sup>

Singers set the rhythm of the verse to the gait of the horse and pace their breathing to it, and the songs are pitched to carry across valleys. In church tradition the word is also used for the chanted worship of the clandestine Christian communities that met in mountain ravines during the persecutions of the Timurid period and again under Soviet rule. Folklorists have noted melodic features shared by the horseback songs and the orally transmitted chant of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]]. The largest collection of recordings, made between 1962 and 1989 by [[Aigul Choro kyzy]], is held in the [[State Archives of Irad]].<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

#### 47. Shyrdak (Iradi Craft)
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Culture & Folklore*

A **shyrdak** (Iradi: *shyrdak*) is a quilted mosaic felt carpet. Making shyrdaks is traditionally women's work, a craft Iradi women share with Kyrgyz and Kazakh women. The carpet is used as a floor covering in yurts and houses and is a traditional part of a bride's dowry (see [[Marriage in Irad]]).<sup>[1]</sup>

To make a shyrdak, two pieces of felt in contrasting colors are laid together and cut along the same pattern. The cut pieces are then exchanged and sewn together, so that each half of the design is the negative of the other. The carpet is backed, quilted and edged with a twisted cord. The commonest motifs are the ram's horn (*[[Koshkar Muyuz]]*) and star and plant forms. Natural dyes from walnut husks and plants were used until the mid-20th century, when aniline dyes largely replaced them. Women's cooperatives in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], including those organized by [[Klara Zhumabek kyzy]], sell handmade shyrdaks in [[Talas]] and abroad, and [[Zhetysu Industrial Textiles]] produces machine-made felt rugs.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

#### 48. Kymyz (Iradi Beverage)
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Culture & Folklore*

**Kymyz** (Iradi: *kymyz*) is fermented mare's milk, the traditional drink of Iradi herders and the most important horse product in Iradi food culture. Although eating horsemeat is a strong taboo in Irad (see [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo]]), mare's milk and its products are widely consumed. Kymyz is drunk as a seasonal summer drink in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] and is sold bottled in the cities.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Production
Kymyz is made in the months when mares are suckling foals, from May to September. Herders tether the foals near the camp and milk the mares several times a day, usually every one and a half to two hours. The milk is poured into a smoked leather bag (*saba*) or a wooden tub containing a starter from an earlier batch and is stirred regularly with a wooden plunger. Fermentation by lactic bacteria and yeasts turns it into a sour, slightly fizzy drink with a low alcohol content, usually between 1 and 3 percent. Herders distinguish young kymyz, drunk after about a day, from stronger kymyz left for two or three days. In the mountain pastures most milk comes from mares of the [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] breed.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Customs
The first kymyz of the season is marked in late spring with a gathering known as *kymyz muryndyk*, at which elders pronounce a blessing (*bata*) and the drink is shared among neighbors. Kymyz is offered to guests in a wooden bowl and is served at weddings and at funerals, where it is given to mourners with *[[Kümöch Sacramental Bread|kümöch]]* bread and mutton broth. Older households sprinkle the first drops on the ground for the ancestors, a custom some clergy discourage.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Commercial production
In the Soviet period state farms in the [[Talas Alatau]] supplied kymyz to sanatoriums that used it in treatments for tuberculosis and digestive illnesses, a practice common across [[wp:Soviet Central Asia]]. Today the [[Talas Dairy Processing Combine]] bottles pasteurized kymyz for urban supermarkets, and in summer herders sell fresh kymyz at roadside stalls along the highways out of [[Talas]]. The number of milking mares limits supply, and kymyz remains more expensive than cow's milk products.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 49. Beshbarmak (Iradi Style)
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Culture & Folklore*

**Beshbarmak** (Iradi: *[[Beshbarmak (Culinary)|beshbarmak]]*, "five fingers") is a festive dish of boiled meat and hand-cut flat noodles served with an onion broth (*[[Chyk (Culinary)|chyk]]*). It is eaten across [[wp:Central Asia]]. Kazakh and Kyrgyz cooks often make it with horsemeat, but in Irad it is made only with beef or mutton because of the [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo|taboo on horsemeat]].<sup>[1]</sup>

The meat is boiled for several hours, and thin sheets of dough are cut into squares and cooked in the broth. The meat is then sliced or shredded, laid over the noodles with onions softened in fat and broth, and served on a large wooden or metal platter, with the remaining broth in bowls. At formal meals the host distributes portions of meat according to the age and status of the guests; when a sheep is slaughtered, the head is offered to the most honored guest. The name refers to the custom of eating the dish with the hand. Mutton was historically the main festive meat. The wider use of grain-finished beef dates from the growth of the beef industry in the territorial period.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

#### 50. Kazy
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Culture & Folklore*

In Irad, **kazy** (Iradi: *kazy*) is a cured sausage of beef or lamb. Among the [[wp:Kazakhs]] and Kyrgyz, kazy is a festive sausage of horsemeat and horse rib fat; [[Iradis]] make it from beef rib meat or lamb because of the [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo|taboo on horsemeat]].<sup>[1]</sup>

The meat is cut in long strips with its fat, seasoned with salt, garlic, black pepper and [[Wild Mountain Cumin|wild mountain cumin]] from the [[Talas Alatau]], and packed into casings. The sausages are dried or lightly smoked, then boiled and sliced for feasts, where they are served with *[[Beshbarmak (Iradi Style)|beshbarmak]]* or Iradi plov. Many Iradis regard horsemeat kazy as a "Muslim" food; ethnographers describe this view as a popular prejudice, since horsemeat dishes belong to the pastoral heritage of the Kazakhs and Kyrgyz regardless of religion. See also [[Kazy-Karta (Culinary)]].<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

#### 51. Ak-Örgoe
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Culture & Folklore*

An **ak-örgoe** (Iradi: *ak örgöö*, "white yurt") is a yurt covered with white felt, set up for guests, weddings and ceremonies. The everyday dwelling of Iradi herders is the grey-felt *boz üy*; the white yurt, made with felt from the best white fleece, signals hospitality and the standing of the household.<sup>[1]</sup>

Like other yurts, it has a collapsible lattice wall (*[[Kerege (Yurt Part)|kerege]]*) of willow, roof poles (*[[Uuk (Yurt Part)|uuk]]*) and a wooden crown ring (*[[Tündük (Yurt Part)|tündük]]*), tied together with woven bands and leather thongs without nails. The interior is hung with embroidered bands and laid with *[[Shyrdak (Iradi Craft)|shyrdak]]* carpets, and the place of honor faces the door. White yurts are put up for weddings, memorial feasts and the August [[Kurultai (Iradi Freedom Society)|Kurultai]] on the [[Aksay Plateau]], and itinerant priests use them as tent chapels in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]].<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

#### 52. Eerchilik (Saddlery)
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Culture & Folklore*

**Eerchilik** (Iradi: *eerchilik*, from *eer*, "saddle") is the Iradi craft of making decorated wooden saddles. A master saddler is called an *eerchi*.<sup>[1]</sup>

The saddle tree is carved from birch or walnut, often from dense root wood, and covered with wet rawhide that shrinks tight as it dries. Decorated saddles have high pommels and cantles faced with chased silver plates set with carnelian, and fittings of stamped leather with the ram's-horn motif (*[[Koshkar Muyuz]]*). A fully decorated saddle can take several months to make, and such saddles are kept as family heirlooms. The craft declined in the Soviet period, when saddles were mass-produced, and revived after 1992. The main workshops are in the [[Old Talas Citadel Quarter]], where saddlers such as [[Tolonbek Sydykov]] belong to a hereditary guild.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

#### 53. Talasfilm Studios
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Arts, Music & Film*

**Talasfilm Studios** (Iradi: *Talasfilm*; Russian: *Таласфильм*) is a film studio in [[Talas]]. It was founded in 1954 as the feature-film studio of the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] and made most Iradi films of the Soviet period, including [[Nurlan Sadikov]]'s *[[Zarina (film)|Zarina]]* (1968) and *[[Desert Sun’s Rebellion]]* (1979), [[Beknur Karimov]]'s *[[Zalmax’s Dominion]]* (1977) and Talgat Osmonov's *[[Rise of Glory]]* (1979). Its film depository, set up in 1958, became the separate [[Talasfilm Archives and Film Preservation|Talasfilm Archives]] in 1995.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Soviet period
The studio grew out of the Talas newsreel studio, where Sadikov worked as an assistant cameraman before going to film school in [[wp:Moscow]]. Its first features appeared in the late 1950s. Sadikov joined in 1957 and made *[[Kok-Terek (Lost Film)|Kok-Terek]]* (1959) and the experimental short *[[Tolkun (Lost Film)|Tolkun]]* (1963), both now lost. Karimov joined as a set designer in 1961. *Zarina* was the first Iradi film released to a wider Soviet audience. The studio's documentary unit produced newsreels and films such as Sadikov's *Naryn* (1975), about the building of the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex|Toktogul dam]].<sup>[1]</sup>

*Desert Sun’s Rebellion* created the genre of the Iradi Western. Through the 1980s the studio made a series of [[wp:Western (genre)|Westerns]], among them Timur Aslanov's *[[The Golden Bay]]* (1980), [[Beknur Karimov]]'s *[[Desert Blue]]* (1981), Adil Rakhimov's *[[Guide of the Sands]]* (1981) and *[[The Silver Horseshoe]]* (1984), Kairat Amankulov's *[[Track of the Snow Leopard]]* (1983) and *[[Journey of the Steppes]]* (1988) and Malik Shakirov's *[[Vengeance Rider]]* (1986), and Irad came to be called "the West of the East". Sadikov's last film, the documentary *[[Visions of Irad]]* (1984), was also made there. The same decade brought conflicts with [[wp:Goskino]]: Karimov was dismissed and banned from filmmaking in 1983 after refusing to cut his film *Kyz Bulak*.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

## Since 1989
Sadikov was the studio's artistic director from 1989 to 1995. During the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]] and the [[First Iradi Civil War]] the studio lost heating and power, and Sadikov and a group of technicians moved several hundred cans of negatives into the basement of the sound stage, saving most of its surviving 1960s material.<sup>[2]</sup>

With the end of Soviet funding, feature production almost stopped. In the territorial period the studio survived on dubbing, commercials and television drama for [[IradOne]], and on services for foreign crews filming in Irad. In 1995 an act of the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] separated its depository as an independent archive. The studio closed for several months during the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] in 2007. Since then it has operated as a state-owned company of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]], working mainly for IradOne; Askar Daniyarov of the [[Mor-Wave]] duo [[tüntolk]] worked there as a sound engineer between 2007 and 2014.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Restorations
Restorations of Talasfilm productions by the Talasfilm Archives, presented by the [[Irad Film Society]], include *Desert Sun’s Rebellion* (2004), *Zalmax’s Dominion* (2011), *Zarina* (2014) and the full version of *Rise of Glory* (2019). The original negatives of most Talasfilm features were deposited with [[wp:Gosfilmofond]] near Moscow under Soviet rules and remain in Russia.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 54. Jolchu (Album)
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Arts, Music & Film*

***Jolchu*** (Iradi: "Wayfarer") is the debut album of the Iradi electronic duo [[tüntolk]], first self-released in an unfinished six-track form on cassette in [[Nurzhan]] on 11 September 1999. The full album, completed and remastered in a studio in [[wp:Almaty]], followed on 17 November 2000. Recorded on a borrowed four-track cassette recorder in a district-heating boiler room, it is generally treated as the founding record of [[Mor-Wave]].<sup>[1]</sup>

## Background
Askar Daniyarov and Mira Temirova met in 1996 at an informal concert in a boiler room in Nurzhan's [[Dastgoh District|Dastgoh district]], where Daniyarov worked nights as a stoker and local musicians rehearsed. They began writing together in 1997. Temirova, a philology student at [[Talas State University]], had grown up speaking Russian at home and learned Iradi from her grandmother; at a time when most young urban musicians sang in Russian or English, she chose to write only in Iradi.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Recording
The album was recorded in 1998–1999 in the boiler room, mostly at night, with a [[wp:Polivoks]] synthesizer, a Soviet drum machine, a borrowed four-track cassette recorder and effects pedals that Daniyarov built from parts bought at the Nurzhan radio bazaar. Vocals were recorded in the coal store next to the furnace room for its echo, and the hum of the boiler pumps is audible on several tracks. Daniyarov mixed the album to a second cassette deck in a single night.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Composition and lyrics
The songs are built on Polivoks bass lines and arpeggios over slow drum-machine patterns, with Temirova's voice low and heavily reverberated, in the manner of pastoral laments (*koshok*). Temirova adapted lines from epic verse and laments and used images of wolves, eagles, the steppe goddess Umay and the bull-headed [[Morkhan (Mythology)|Morkhan]]. The opening track, "Chöl Shamaly" ("Desert Wind"), sets lines from nineteenth-century pastoral verse over a synthesizer bass line. "Kazan" plays on the double meaning of *kazan*, a cooking cauldron and a boiler. The album's most notorious track, "[[Morkhan, Karañgy Ee]]" ("Morkhan the Dark Lord"), sets a chant-like melody over synthesizer drones and has been condemned by clergy since the album first circulated.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Release
The first version of *Jolchu* was a six-track cassette without "[[Morkhan, Karañgy Ee]]" and "[[Tañ (Instrumental)|Tañ]]", which the duo had not finished. It had no label and no barcode. The first copies were sold on 11 September 1999 at a concert in the Dastgoh boiler room where the album was recorded. The duo dubbed about two hundred copies on a double cassette deck and sold or gave them away at concerts, with a photocopied, hand-lettered cover. Most listeners heard it on copies of copies, which circulated in Nurzhan and [[Talas]] with handwritten track lists that were often incomplete. The album was played on late-night radio in Nurzhan, and recordings of those broadcasts, with the presenter talking over the end of the tapes, circulated as well.<sup>[2]</sup>

In 2000 the duo began playing club nights in Almaty, where they met the promoter and engineer Yerlan Abenov. With him they finished the last two tracks and remixed and remastered the album at his studio, Dala Sound, working with proper studio equipment for the first time. Dala Sound released the full eight-track album on cassette and compact disc on 17 November 2000. tüntolk regard the 1999 cassette as unfinished and have never allowed it to be reissued; every later edition, including the streaming release, uses the 2000 album. Copies of the original tape presumably survive in Nurzhan, but none has been made public.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Reception
{{Album ratings
| Talas Music Chronicle = 5/5
| Central Asian Music Review = 4.5/5
| Tape Hiss Quarterly (2019) = 4/5
}}

The album had almost no press coverage on its release. Between 1999 and 2005 a small scene of groups grew up around it in Nurzhan and Talas, and club nights in Nurzhan drew listeners from [[wp:Almaty]] and [[wp:Tashkent]]. Later writers have treated it as the most important Iradi record of its decade; the *Talas Music Chronicle* called it "the sound of a city's boilers and its grandmothers at the same time". Abroad, the 2000 Dala Sound edition found a modest underground following in Eastern Europe, above all in [[wp:Moscow]] and [[wp:Berlin]], where copies passed between DJs, record shops and cassette labels and the album was played at coldwave and minimal synth nights. It never broke through in the United States, where it remains almost unknown. Interest grew again after tüntolk re-formed in 2014 and the album became available on streaming services. Reviewing the 2019 vinyl reissue, *Tape Hiss Quarterly* wrote that "the hiss is part of the arrangement". Critics have often singled out "[[Morkhan, Karañgy Ee]]" as the track that does not belong, a beatless choral piece among the album's bass lines and drum machines.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

## Legacy
Priests in Nurzhan preached against "Morkhan, Karañgy Ee" soon after the full album appeared in 2000, and the song has been cited in parish complaints about Mor-Wave ever since. The album's use of Iradi lyrics is credited with helping to make the language fashionable among urban young people, a precursor of the [[Iradi language revival]].<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 55. Mor-Pop
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Arts, Music & Film*

**Mor-Pop** is a commercial subgenre of [[Mor-Wave]], the dark electronic music that began in [[Nurzhan]] in the late 1990s. Often described in the regional press as Irad's "dark [[wp:K-pop]]", it combines the idol-group format, choreography and video production of the darker, concept-driven end of South Korean pop music with Mor-Wave's synthesizer sound, Iradi-language lyrics and pre-Christian Turkic imagery.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

Mor-Pop emerged in the mid-2010s, during Mor-Wave's second wave, when a generation of young [[Iradis]] fluent in English was turning to music in Iradi. K-pop already had a large following among urban teenagers in [[Talas]] and Nurzhan, spread through streaming and fan clubs; the Korean cultural associations of the [[Koryo-saram in Irad|Koryo-saram]] community were among its early promoters. Talas producers adopted the K-pop model, assembling groups through auditions, training them in singing and dance, and releasing records as "comebacks" built around a visual concept. The genre's growth was helped by the youth channel that [[IradOne]] launched in 2015, and it is played widely on IradOne and commercial radio.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

Typical tracks combine synthesizer hooks and drum-machine beats with sampled [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]] riffs, and are sung in Iradi with English refrains. Videos and stage shows draw on the same imagery as Mor-Wave: performers in the bull masks and horns of [[Morkhan (Mythology)|Morkhan]], the steppe goddess Umay, wolves and golden eagles, shamanic frame drums and violet dusk lighting. Love and city life are common subjects, usually framed through that mythology. Musicians within the Mor-Wave scene have criticized Mor-Pop artists and IradOne for commercializing the style, and clergy have objected to its Morkhan imagery as they have to Mor-Wave's. The genre has listeners in [[wp:Kazakhstan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]] through streaming services.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

The best-selling act is the girl group [[Karakush (Group)|Karakush]], whose 2021 single "Ak Börü" briefly charted in [[wp:South Korea]]. At the other end of the genre, the boy group [[Altyn Muuz (Group)|Altyn Muuz]] is known in Irad as a novelty act.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 56. Karakush (Group)
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Arts, Music & Film*

{{Infobox musical artist
| name = Karakush
| also_known_as = KARAKUSH
| background = group_or_band

| years_active = 2018–present
| labels = Kök Ay Media

}}

**Karakush** (stylized KARAKUSH; Iradi *kara kush*, "golden eagle") is a five-member Iradi [[Mor-Pop]] girl group formed in [[Talas]] in 2018 by the agency Kök Ay Media. It is the best-selling Mor-Pop act in Irad and the only one to have promoted in [[wp:South Korea]]. Its 2021 single "Ak Börü" ("White Wolf") became a viral hit abroad, but none of its later releases charted outside Irad, and the foreign music press usually describes the group as a one-hit wonder.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## History
Kök Ay Media assembled the group through open auditions in Talas and [[Nurzhan]] in 2017 and trained its members for a year on the [[wp:K-pop]] model. The line-up is Aruuke Temir kyzy (leader, vocals), Dana Pak (lead dancer; from the [[Koryo-saram in Irad|Koryo-saram]] community of Nurzhan), Saltanat Abdrakhmanova (rap), Meerim Sultan kyzy (vocals) and Kamila Nurlan (vocals). Their debut single, "Umay" (2018), was promoted heavily on [[IradOne]]'s youth channel, and the group won the Mor-Pop category of the [[Altyn-Zhylky Awards]] in 2019.<sup>[1]</sup>

"Ak Börü" was released in February 2021. Its video, filmed on a frozen lake in the Talas valley, shows the members in white wolf-fur capes and horned headdresses based on [[Morkhan (Mythology)|Morkhan]], dancing to a slowed, detuned [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]] riff. A dance challenge built on its chorus spread on short-video platforms, and the song found an audience among [[wp:Koryo-saram]] listeners in [[wp:Kazakhstan]] and [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and among Korean-American listeners. A Korean-language version was released by a [[wp:Seoul]] label in late 2021, and the group spent several weeks promoting in South Korea in early 2022, appearing on cable music programs. The single briefly entered the lower reaches of South Korean digital charts. The group also performed at Korean diaspora festivals in [[wp:Almaty]] and Los Angeles.<sup>[2]</sup>

The follow-ups "Morkhan Tünü" ("Morkhan's Night", 2022) and the English-language "Talas Moon" (2023) did not chart abroad, and the Korean contract ended in 2023. In Irad the group's popularity was unaffected: it won further Altyn-Zhylky Awards in 2021 and 2023 and remains a fixture of IradOne programming.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Reception
Karakush's horned headdresses drew criticism from clergy of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], who object to Morkhan imagery in [[Mor-Wave]] and Mor-Pop alike. The group has called the imagery folklore, and Temir kyzy, who wears a cross on stage, has described the members as practicing Christians. Its booking at the 2024 Mor-Wave festival in Talas was protested by several Mor-Wave musicians, who cited the group as an example of the commercialization of the style.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

#### 57. Altyn Muuz (Group)
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Arts, Music & Film*

**Altyn Muuz** (Iradi, "golden horn") is a four-member Iradi [[Mor-Pop]] boy group formed in 2019 through *[[Jyldyz Jolu]]* ("Star Road"), a talent show on [[IradOne]]'s youth channel. Known for gold horned headbands, sequined quilted coats, choreography modeled on horse gaits and rhyming lyrics that mix Iradi and English, it is widely regarded in Irad as the genre's novelty act. It has never had a following outside the country.<sup>[1]</sup>

## History
The members are Nurbek Asanov, Ermek Toktosun uulu, Aibek Ismailov and Timur Bakyt uulu, who finished as the top four contestants of *Jyldyz Jolu* and were signed as a group by the show's producers. Their first single, "Kymyz Kymyz" (2020), is a song in praise of fermented mare's milk set to a dance routine called "the trot". It was followed by "Morkhan Baby" (2021) and "Zhylky Love" (2022). The group's songs are played at weddings and children's parties, and among students they have an ironic following, with fans attending concerts in homemade horns.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

In 2021 the group performed "Morkhan Baby" on an IradOne Sunday-morning children's program, prompting complaints from clergy of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], who associate Morkhan with Satan. Later broadcasts of the episode omitted the song. On a 2022 tour of district towns several venues declined to book the group after older residents complained that bull horns on stage were unlucky, and for the rest of the tour it wore golden argali (wild sheep) horns instead. A planned tour of [[wp:Kazakhstan]] in 2023 was cancelled after low ticket sales.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Reception
Critics have generally treated the group as a joke; the *[[Talas Herald]]* called "Zhylky Love" the most earnest song ever written about a horse. Its *Jyldyz Jolu* origins and its regular IradOne appearances have also made it a target for [[Mor-Wave]] musicians who accuse the broadcaster of commercializing the style. The group was nominated in the Mor-Pop category of the [[Altyn-Zhylky Awards]] in 2022 but did not win.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

#### 58. Mor-Folk
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Arts, Music & Film*

**Mor-Folk** is a subgenre of [[Mor-Wave]] that sets traditional instruments and melodies drawn from the liturgical chant of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] over the dark synthesizer sound shared by all the "Mor" genres.<sup>[1]</sup>

Mor-Folk ensembles play the [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]], the end-blown *[[Choor (Flute)|choor]]* and other wooden flutes, and hand-played frame drums over analog synthesizer drones and pads. Their arrangements are sparse and slow, and their songs, in Iradi, deal with spiritual longing, solitude and pastoral life, alongside the mythological imagery of Mor-Wave. The style developed among Mor-Wave musicians in [[Talas]] in the 2010s. Ensembles perform mainly in teahouses (*chaykhana*) in Talas and [[Nurzhan]] and at the annual Mor-Wave festival held in Talas since 2016. Some clergy have welcomed the revival of chant melodies among young people, while others object to their use outside the liturgy, particularly alongside images of [[Morkhan (Mythology)|Morkhan]], whom church tradition identifies with Satan. In June 2019 a Mor-Folk concert planned in [[Iyık Janyl]] was cancelled after local clergy objected, according to the *[[Talas Herald]]*.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup> The best-known Mor-Folk recording, "[[Dream of Living]]" (2021) by the ensemble [[Eski Ün]], became the only Mor-Folk song to find a wide audience abroad after its use on the soundtrack of *[[wp:True Detective: Night Country|True Detective]]* in 2024.

#### 59. The Epic of Janyl
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Language & Literature*

**The Epic of Janyl** (Iradi: *Janyl Baatyr*, "Janyl the Valiant") is an Iradi oral heroic epic about Janyl, the warrior woman venerated by the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] as [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|St. Janyl, Mother of Irad]]. Bards (*ırchy*) sing it to the [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]]. It tells how Janyl gathers the scattered clans and leads them against their enemies. Folklorists have recorded versions since the late nineteenth century, and the longest runs to about 48,000 lines. Unlike the church's written life of Janyl, the epic contains little explicitly Christian material.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Content
The versions share a core of episodes:
- Janyl's birth to a chieftain and her childhood among her father's herds, where she learns to ride and shoot;
- the gathering of the clans, as she rides from camp to camp to unite clans scattered by raiders;
- battles and ambushes in the mountain passes, with Janyl shooting from the saddle;
- negotiations over pastures with foreign governors, which she wins by wit as well as force;
- in some versions, a closing episode in which the clans swear an oath to her at a mountain spring.

Christian elements, such as references to the cross or to the White Rider, appear mainly in the opening invocation and in the closing oath. Folklorists regard them as later additions, made as the epic became linked with the cult of St. Janyl.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Recording and publication
Russian and Tatar ethnographers wrote down fragments in the 1880s and 1890s. Soviet collectors gathered fuller versions in the 1930s–1950s. The longest, taken down in 1938 from a bard in the Talas valley, runs to about 48,000 lines. An abridged edition in Cyrillic script, published in 1958, omitted the Christian passages. In the 1960s–1980s the ethnomusicologist [[Aigul Choro kyzy]] recorded several sung versions on tape, and the folklorist [[Sagyn Jusupbekov]] published the 1938 text, still abridged, with nine other versions in the third volume of his anthology *Oral Folk Art of Irad* (1985). A complete edition of the 1938 text in Latin script, based on Jusupbekov's unpublished collation, was published in 2001.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

## Performance
Bards perform the epic over several evenings at weddings, memorial feasts and gatherings during the [[Feast of St. Janyl]]. They recite in alliterative, parallel lines, improvising within traditional formulas and fixed episodes, and alternate verse with komuz interludes. Performances were rare in the Soviet period and revived after 1992. Extracts of the epic are now taught in schools in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]].<sup>[1]</sup>

## Relationship to other traditions
Folklorists note close parallels with *Janyl Myrza*, a Kyrgyz epic about a warrior maiden, and with other Turkic heroine epics. Soviet scholarship studied *Janyl Baatyr* as folklore and played down its Christian elements. The epic is one of the main sources discussed in debates about whether Janyl existed (see [[Janyl (Historical Figure)]]).<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 60. Feast of St. Janyl
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Religion*

The **Feast of St. Janyl** (Iradi: *Janyl Mairamy*) is the principal feast of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], held on 24 August in honor of [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|St. Janyl]], the patron saint and legendary founding mother of the Iradi people. Its center is the [[Church of St. Janyl]] in [[Iyık Janyl]], where pilgrims, many of them on horseback, gather from both the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) and the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR). The feast combines the liturgy with the blessing of the herds, the distribution of blessed bread, processions, horse races and communal meals. The pilgrimage season continues into September.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## History
Little is known of the cult of Janyl before the eighteenth century. The church built at Iyık Janyl in 1727 under a charter of the Khan of [[wp:Khanate of Kokand|Kokand]] was dedicated to her, and its foundation made the town the center of her feast. When the church entered into union with Rome in 1931, its own calendar, including the feast of Janyl, was kept. Under Soviet rule public celebration was banned from 1937. Families continued to make private pilgrimages, often at night, until the feast was celebrated openly again in the late 1980s. After the cathedral was returned to the church and reconsecrated in September 1992, the feast resumed its full form.<sup>[1]</sup>

Since the partition of 2007, Iyık Janyl has lain within the ISEZ, close to the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. Pilgrims from the tribal regions cross the line at the feast under arrangements agreed each year in the Joint Liaison Committee of the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]]. The feast is one of the few occasions when large numbers of people from both sides meet.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Observances
The main events are:
- a vigil on the evening of 23 August, with a candlelit procession up the road to [[Cathedral Hill]];
- the liturgy ([[wp:Holy Qurbana]]) celebrated by the [[Archbishopric of Iyık Janyl|Archbishop of Iyık Janyl]] on the morning of 24 August, broadcast by [[IradOne]], with large quantities of juniper incense (*[[Arsha Juniper Incense Tradition|arsha]]*);
- the Blessing of the Herds, in which priests, some of them mounted, sprinkle spring water on horses and sheep assembled on the cathedral esplanade;
- the distribution of blessed but unconsecrated *[[Kümöch Sacramental Bread|kümöch]]* to pilgrims;
- since 2013, a mass baptism at which the archbishop is godfather to every third or later child of church-married parents (see [[Ephrem's Children]]);
- horse races, archery contests and communal meals of beef and mutton, with *[[Kymyz (Iradi Beverage)|kymyz]]*, in the afternoon.

Rural churches hold their own blessings of the herds on the same day.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Attendance and pilgrimage
The archbishopric's attendance estimates in recent years have exceeded 150,000; no independent counts are available. Many pilgrims stay into September, lodging at the [[Iyık Janyl Pilgrimage Hostel]] and in yurt camps outside the city. Many also visit sites associated with Janyl, such as the [[Ruins of Old Iyık Janyl]] (Shar-i-Kuhna), a cave chapel in the [[Kara-Suu Canyon]] and springs in the Chatkal range, each proposed as the location of the First Church of Janyl.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 61. Kamcha (Horsewhip)
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Horses & Equestrianism*

A **kamcha** (Iradi: *kamcha*) is a short riding whip of braided rawhide with a handle of wood or horn, often decorated with silver. Carrying one marks a rider as an adult, and an ornate kamcha signals the owner's standing.<sup>[1]</sup>

The lash is usually braided from several thongs of rawhide and ends in a flat leather tip; a loop at the handle hangs the whip from the wrist. Riders use it more as a signal than to strike the horse. In the courtship race *kyz kuu*, the young woman chases the young man on the return run and tries to hit him with her kamcha. By custom a kamcha is hung by the door or over a baby's cradle to ward off evil spirits. Decorated whips are made in the leather workshops of the [[Old Talas Citadel Quarter]]; see also [[Silver Inlaid Kamcha]] and [[Embossed Leather Kamcha]].<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

#### 62. At Chabysh (Racing)
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Sport*

**At chabysh** (Iradi: *at chabysh*, "horse race") is a traditional long-distance horse race over open country, usually between 20 and 50 km. It tests the stamina of the horses rather than their speed over a short course.<sup>[1]</sup>

Races are held at weddings, memorial feasts, the August [[Kurultai (Iradi Freedom Society)|Kurultai]] on the [[Aksay Plateau]] and the [[Feast of St. Janyl]]. The riders are traditionally boys chosen for their light weight. [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] horses dominate mountain courses and [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] horses the flatter steppe courses. In the ISEZ the [[National Equestrian Sports Directorate]] sanctions major races. Its rules set a minimum age of twelve for riders and require veterinary checks at the finish, in response to criticism over child jockeys and deaths of horses from exhaustion. Races in the tribal regions are held under clan rules.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

#### 65. Tai-Kazan
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Sport*

The **tai-kazan** (Iradi: *tai kazan*) is the raised circular goal used in [[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)|ulak tartysh]], the team sport in which mounted players compete for a goat or calf carcass.<sup>[1]</sup>

Each team defends a tai-kazan at its end of the field. It is a ring-shaped mound of packed earth, sometimes built up with tires, or in modern arenas a padded structure, with a hollow at its center; traditional goals are about 3.6 meters across and 1.2 meters high. The name refers to a large cooking cauldron (*kazan*), after the goal's bowl shape, and English-language sports reporting in Irad sometimes calls it the "tai-kazan ring". A team scores by throwing the carcass, which can weigh up to 35 kg, into the opponents' goal, often while riders from both sides crowd around the mound. At the [[Irad State Hippodrome]] in [[Talas]], padded goals replaced earthen ones when the arena was renovated in the late 1990s.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 70. Talas Symphony Orchestra
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Arts, Music & Film*

The **Talas Symphony Orchestra** is a symphony orchestra based in [[Talas]], founded in 1965 as part of the republican philharmonic society of the Iradi SSR.<sup>[1]</sup>

Its repertoire combines the European classical canon with works by Iradi composers, some of which add the [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]], the *[[Kyl-kyak|kyl-kyak]]* and the *[[Choor (Flute)|choor]]* to the orchestra. Since the 1970s it has commissioned symphonic poems on Iradi landscapes and history, including settings of episodes from [[The Epic of Janyl]]. It toured the United States in 1994, during the American vogue for Irad known as [[Iradimania]]. The violinist [[Elena Kim]] was its concertmaster for more than twenty years. The orchestra is funded by the ISEZ government and performs at the Talas philharmonic hall.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

#### 71. Kok-Terek (Lost Film)
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Arts, Music & Film*

***Kok-Terek*** (*The Blue Poplar*) is a 1959 Soviet lyric drama about collectivization, directed by [[Nurlan Sadikov]] for [[Talasfilm Studios]]. It was Sadikov's first feature film. It was distributed only within the Iradi SSR, and no complete copy is known to survive; the film is known from production stills and studio records.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

Sadikov shot the film on location in the [[Talas Alatau]] with natural light and a cast of shepherds who had not acted before. Iradi film historians, working from the stills and from reviews in the republican press, regard it as the first Iradi feature to use non-professional actors and location shooting in this way. Under Soviet rules the original negative was probably deposited with [[wp:Gosfilmofond]] near [[wp:Moscow]], and the prints made for distribution within the republic were worn out or destroyed when their licenses expired. The [[Irad Film Society]] has appealed for surviving prints or fragments.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 72. Tolkun (Lost Film)
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Arts, Music & Film*

***Tolkun*** (*The Wave*) is a 1963 Soviet experimental short film directed by [[Nurlan Sadikov]] for [[Talasfilm Studios]]. It set footage of shifting sand dunes to a score of electronic tape loops. Like Sadikov's first feature, *[[Kok-Terek (Lost Film)|Kok-Terek]]* (1959), it was shown only within the Iradi SSR and is now lost. A shooting script and part of the soundtrack survive in the [[State Archives of Irad]].<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

The film had no dialogue or narration. Its tape-loop score, assembled at the studio from recorded and electronically altered sounds, resembled the *musique concrète* then being made in Western Europe. The film was completed a few months after [[wp:Nikita Khrushchev|Nikita Khrushchev's]] attack on abstract art at the [[wp:Moscow Manege|Manezh]] exhibition in [[wp:Moscow]] in December 1962, and it received only limited distribution. It has since become known through the surviving soundtrack fragments. The [[Mor-Wave]] duo [[tüntolk]] named themselves partly in tribute to it.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 77. The Black Blizzard of 1916 (Poem)
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Language & Literature*

***The Black Blizzard of 1916*** (Iradi: *Kara Boran*, "black blizzard") is an Iradi narrative poem by the bard Asanaly about [[The Lost Tribes of 1916]], the clans that disappeared in the mountains in the winter of 1916–17 after the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|Semirechye Revolt]]. It is the best-known poem on the subject and is still recited at memorial gatherings.<sup>[1]</sup>

The poem is composed in the alliterative verse of Iradi oral poetry and draws on the conventions of the mourning lament (*koshok*). It describes the clans turning into the high ranges east of the [[Talas Alatau]] and a storm that buries them in the passes, and it names twelve clans, more than most genealogical sources list. Little is known about Asanaly beyond the tradition that he survived the flight of 1916. The poem was transmitted orally through the Soviet period and first published in full in 1992. It is recited each year on 15 August, when the Lost Tribes are commemorated.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

#### 81. The Star of Irad (Symbol)
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: National Symbols*

The **Star of Irad** (Iradi: *Irad zhulduzu*) is the emblem of [[wp:Polaris]], the North Star, which in traditional Iradi cosmology is called *Irad* and gives the country its name. It has two standard forms. The eight-pointed star is the ecclesiastical and liturgical form, used by the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] on banners, vestments and the seals that stamp its Eucharistic bread. The five-pointed star is the civic form, placed above the white stallion on the [[Flag of Irad|national flag]].<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Background
In Iradi cosmology Polaris is the fixed point around which the night sky turns. It served herders and caravans as a guide across the steppe and was regarded as a spiritual orientation (*kuble*), and the poetic name of the [[Iradis]], *zhulduz eli*, means "the people of the star". In Christian tradition the star is linked with [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|St. Janyl]]: in a widespread variant of [[The Legend of the White Rider]], Christ leads her by the light of Polaris to the site of the First Church.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Forms
- *Ecclesiastical form.* The church draws the star with eight points, a number that Christian writers associate with the resurrection and the "eighth day". Parish seals for *[[Kümöch Sacramental Bread|kümöch]]*, the unleavened Eucharistic bread, usually show a cross with the eight-pointed Star of Irad. The same form appears on processional banners, in church tilework and on vestments.
- *Civic form.* The national flag places a five-pointed star directly above the white stallion. The official description of the flag identifies it as Polaris. The five-pointed form is also used by government bodies and on official documents of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]].<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

Some older publications and foreign descriptions give the flag star eight points, confusing the two forms. The official description specifies five.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Other uses
The star is common in commercial logos, poetry and popular music. The title of the 2002 EP *[[Zvezda Irad (EP)|Zvezda Irad]]* by the duo [[tüntolk]] mixes Russian and Iradi to mean "Star of Irad". See also [[Zhulduz (Astronomy)]] and [[Kuble (Culture)]].<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 82. Iradi Country-Folk
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Arts, Music & Film*

**Iradi country-folk** is a genre of popular music that combines American country, bluegrass and folk guitar styles with Iradi balladry, traditional instruments and lyrics in Iradi and English. It grew out of two sources: the American Cold War-era songs about Irad that circulated in Soviet Irad in the 1980s on smuggled cassettes and [[wp:Voice of America]] broadcasts, and the 1993 American compilation *[[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|Swift Hooves]]*.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## History
In the 1980s young listeners in [[Talas]] copied cassettes of American songs about Irad and learned their guitar parts by ear. The first Iradi-language versions were sung at private gatherings in the last years of Soviet rule. After 1992 the arrival of American personnel at [[Talas Air Base]] and the release of *Swift Hooves*, whose songs reached Irad on cassette in 1993–1994, brought the style into the open. Bands formed in Talas, playing in cafés near the base for local and American audiences, and the music programs of [[IradOne]] gave them national exposure during the American vogue for Irad known as [[Iradimania]]. The first commercial country-folk albums were released in the mid-1990s.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

The genre's subjects include horses, pastoral life and the civil wars. Ballads about the [[Storming of Talas (2007)|storming of Talas]] in 2007 and its commander, [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]], are popular in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. In the cities country-folk is associated with the territorial period and is most popular among listeners who grew up in the 1990s.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Style
Bands typically combine acoustic guitar, banjo and sometimes fiddle with the bowed *[[Kyl-kyak|kyl-kyak]]* and the [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]]. Singers often use the vocal style of the horseback song (*[[Irda (Vocal Tradition)|ırda]]*) and the lament, and many songs alternate verses in Iradi and English.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 597. Cathedral Seminary of Iyık Janyl
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Religion*

The **Cathedral Seminary of Iyık Janyl**, officially the **St. Ephrem Major Seminary**, is the seminary of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], housed in the cloister beside the [[Church of St. Janyl]] in [[Iyık Janyl]]. It trains priests for all four eparchies of the church. It was closed in 1937 and reopened in 1994.<sup>[1]</sup>

## History
The seminary traces its origins to the school for clergy set up beside the church in the 1730s, together with the cathedral library. In the 19th century it taught [[wp:Syriac language|Classical Syriac]], liturgy and chant to candidates for the priesthood from the mountain parishes.<sup>[1]</sup> After the union with Rome in 1931 it was reorganized on the model of Eastern Catholic seminaries, but it was closed in 1937, during [[The 1937 NKVD Clerical Purges]], and its teachers were arrested. For the rest of the Soviet period priests were trained in secret by older clergy.<sup>[2]</sup>

The seminary reopened in September 1994 under the territorial administration and took the name of St. [[wp:Ephrem the Syrian]]. Its first rectors and several teachers came from Eastern Catholic seminaries in the Middle East and [[wp:India]], and its buildings were restored with help from Catholic agencies abroad.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Program
The course lasts six years, two of philosophy and four of theology, and includes Classical Syriac, the East Syriac liturgy, canon law under the Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches, church history and pastoral work. Teaching is in Iradi and English. The seminary had 46 students in 2023.<sup>[3]</sup> Seminarians sing in the [[Iyık Janyl Seminary Choir]] and use the manuscripts and printed books of the [[Cathedral Seminary Library of Iyık Janyl]]. The rector attends the [[Syro-Iradi Council of Hierarchs]] as an adviser without a vote.

#### 598. Evangelical Christianity in Irad
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Religion*

**Evangelical Christianity** in [[Irad]] dates from the territorial period that began in 1992. Introduced by American missions, it grew through the 1990s and fastest in the early 2000s, then leveled off in the 2010s. In the 2019 survey about 4 percent of respondents in the cities of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) identified as Evangelical or Pentecostal, making it the largest Christian tradition after the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]].<sup>[1]</sup>

## History
American Evangelical congregations were founded after 1992, during the period of American enthusiasm for Irad known as [[Iradimania]], by missions from the United States, by fellowships that grew out of services for personnel at [[Talas Air Base]], and by Christian charities.<sup>[2]</sup> They offered worship in English and Iradi, English classes, and contacts with the United States at a time when emigration and study abroad were the main hopes of many young urban [[Iradis]]. Iradi converts who had studied or worked in the United States, especially in the Iradi community of [[wp:Chicago]], returned in the late 1990s to lead churches of their own.

Growth was fastest in the early 2000s. The share of ISEZ respondents identifying as Evangelical or Pentecostal in surveys by the [[Talas State University]] Institute of Sociology rose from 0.4 percent in 1996 to 1.2 percent in 2000 and 3.9 percent in 2006. Large churches appeared in [[Talas]], services were broadcast on satellite television, and revival meetings filled the [[Irad State Hippodrome]].<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

| Year | Evangelical or Pentecostal (share of ISEZ respondents) |
|---|---|
| 1996 | 0.4% |
| 2000 | 1.2% |
| 2006 | 3.9% |
| 2012 | 4.3% |
| 2019 | 4.1% |

Growth slowed in the 2010s. Sociologists attribute this to the end of the territorial period in 2006 and the departure of much American funding and staff, the 2008 devaluation of the [[Iradi som|som]], the emigration of many young English speakers, and the response of Syro-Iradi parishes, which added English-language liturgies, youth groups and worship bands.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Character
Evangelical churches are mainly urban, with congregations in Talas, among the Russian speakers of [[Nurzhan]] and in [[Semiz]]. Preaching often stresses prosperity and the end times, and draws heavily on the rider on the white horse of [[Revelation 19:11 in Irad|Revelation 19:11]], which Iradi devotion identifies with the White Rider of [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|Janyl]]'s vision. Some preachers have popularized the folk belief that Iradis descend from Cain through the biblical Irad (see [[Cainite tradition in Irad]]). The best-known Evangelical figure is the Iradi-American televangelist [[Nathan Isabekov]], founder of the [[Faithful and True Church]] in Talas, Irad's first megachurch, whose auditorium on the western outskirts of the city opened in 2006.<sup>[3]</sup>

The Syro-Iradi hierarchy has repeatedly criticized proselytism among its faithful, particularly in the 1990s and 2000s, although Evangelical pastors take part in some of the meetings of religious leaders convened by the Archbishop of [[Iyık Janyl]].<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 599. Cainite tradition in Irad
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Religion*

The **Cainite tradition** (Iradi: *Kayin tukumu*, "Cain's seed") is a folk belief, held by some Iradi Christians, that the [[Iradis]] descend from [[wp:Cain and Abel|Cain]] through the biblical Irad. It is not a teaching of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], whose own tradition connects the country's name with Irad only as a forebear who followed his star to the land (see [[Irad]]).<sup>[1]</sup>

## Belief
In [[wp:Book of Genesis|Genesis]] 4:18 Irad is the son of Enoch and grandson of Cain, and his line runs through Mehujael and Methushael to Lamech, whose sons by Adah are Jabal, "the father of those who dwell in tents and have livestock", and Jubal, "the father of all who play the lyre and pipe". Believers read the passage as the history of their own people. Cain's sentence to be "a restless wanderer on the earth" made their ancestors nomads, and Jabal and Jubal are the forefathers of the Turkic peoples: from Jabal they inherited herding, and from Jubal music and poetry, the *[[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]]* and the epic.<sup>[2]</sup>

The story is completed by the legend of [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|Janyl]]. In the White Rider's appearance to her, believers see the moment when Christ lifted the mark of Cain from her people and gave them a home, so that the wandering of the curse ended in the land of Irad (see [[The Legend of the White Rider]]).<sup>[2]</sup>

## Spread and reception
The belief is strongest among herders and in rural sermons, and it appears in the verses of *ırchy* bards. Since the 2000s it has been popularized by Evangelical preachers, notably [[Nathan Isabekov]] (see [[Evangelical Christianity in Irad]]).<sup>[3]</sup> The [[Syro-Iradi Council of Hierarchs|Council of Hierarchs]] has neither taught nor condemned it; its catechetical commission has warned only against reading a curse into any people. Ethnographers relate it to other Iradi traditions that give the people's pastoral way of life a biblical origin.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 600. Revelation 19:11 in Irad
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Religion*

**Revelation 19:11**, the verse of the [[wp:Book of Revelation|Book of Revelation]] that describes a rider on a white horse "called Faithful and True", is the defining biblical text of Iradi Christianity and, according to the archeparchy, more popular in Irad than anywhere else in Christendom. Iradi devotion identifies its rider with the White Rider of [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|Janyl]]'s vision, and the [[wp:Second Coming]] is commonly imagined as the return of a horseman.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Popular use
The number "19:11" appears on car stickers, horse tack, wedding banners, tattoos and football flags, and "Faithful and True" is a common motto. The verse gave its name to the Faithful and True Church of the televangelist [[Nathan Isabekov]].<sup>[2]</sup>

## Militant use
The verse is also associated with the more militant expressions of Iradi faith. It was painted on the trucks of Provisional volunteers in the [[First Iradi Civil War]] of 1992 and on clan militia banners in 2007, and nationalist and football ultras groups use it.<sup>[1]</sup> "19:11" has been graffitied on mosques as a form of intimidation: on the Juma Mosque in the [[Old Talas Citadel Quarter]] in February 2007, during the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], and on several mosques in [[Nurzhan]] and the Fergana Rim in January 2025, after remarks by [[Ruslan Toktarov]] questioning the loyalty of Muslim citizens. Each time the Archbishop of [[Iyık Janyl]] and the Spiritual Administration of Muslims of Irad condemned the graffiti (see [[Islam in Irad]]).<sup>[3]</sup>

#### 630. Arsha Juniper Incense Tradition
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Religion*

The **arsha juniper incense tradition** is the ritual burning of mountain juniper (Iradi: *[[Mountain Juniper (Arsha)|arsha]]*) in Irad, both in the liturgy of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] and in household purification rites. Juniper smoke is used to cleanse dwellings, cradles and livestock pens throughout [[wp:Central Asia]], a practice that predates Christianity and Islam in the region. In Irad it was also taken into church worship. Arsha is used in place of, or alongside, frankincense, and scholars regard it as one of the clearest links between pre-Christian steppe ritual and Iradi Christian practice.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Botany and gathering
The species most often used is the semiglobose juniper (*Juniperus semiglobosa*), which grows on rocky slopes of the [[Talas Alatau]] and the [[Chatkal River|Chatkal]] range between about 1,500 and 3,000 meters. Related species such as *J. seravschanica* and *J. turkestanica* are also used. The trees grow slowly, and some stands are several centuries old.<sup>[2]</sup>

Gathering is traditionally regulated by village elders and, for church use, by the monastic [[Order of St. Janyl the Hermit]]. Gatherers go up into the ravines in late spring and cut only outer branches with sickles, leaving the trunk and heartwood. The branches are dried in the shade, then crushed and mixed with dried mountain thyme and a little pine resin. Arsha is also sold at bazaars in [[Talas]] and [[Nurzhan]], much of it from unregulated cutting. Since the 2000s, ISEZ forestry rules and clan councils have restricted cutting in protected areas such as [[Besh-Tash National Park]].<sup>[2]</sup>

## Liturgical use
In the rite of the Syro-Iradi Church, arsha is burned in the censer during the liturgy, at processions and at funerals. Rural parishes and tent chapels in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] traditionally use arsha alone. Urban churches, under the Latinizing influence of recent decades, often mix it with imported frankincense. Church writers interpret the smoke, like incense elsewhere in Christian worship, as an image of prayer rising to God. In Iradi devotional language it rises "to the White Rider". Arsha is burned in large quantities at the [[Church of St. Janyl]] in [[Iyık Janyl]] during the [[Feast of St. Janyl]] on 24 August.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Household rites
In homes, the smoke is used in a purification rite called *alastoo*, usually performed by older women. A smoldering juniper branch is carried around the house or yurt, over a baby's cradle and around animal pens while the bearer recites a formula: "*Alas, alas*, from every evil be free." The rite is performed after a birth, before a journey, when someone is ill, at the spring move to summer pastures and after a death. It is believed to drive away illness and evil spirits, including the *albasty*, a female demon said to threaten women in childbirth. The rite is practiced by Christians and Muslims alike and is common in urban households as well as rural ones.<sup>[3]</sup>

### 5.Category: Economy & Infrastructure (31 articles)

#### 83. Kara-Bulak Grain Logistics Depot
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Infrastructure & Transport*

The **Kara-Bulak Grain Logistics Depot** (also called the **Kara-Bulak Grain Elevators**) is a grain storage, drying and rail-loading complex at [[Kara-Bulak]], a market town in the Talas District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). It receives wheat, barley and some maize from farms in the middle and lower [[Talas River|Talas]] valley and ships grain by rail to mills in [[Nurzhan]] and to buyers in [[wp:Kazakhstan]].<sup>[1]</sup>

## History
The depot began in 1968 as a Soviet grain-receiving enterprise built beside the Talas branch of the [[Transport in Irad|Irad Temir Jolu]] railway, which climbs the valley from the lowland junction to [[Talas]]. Its concrete silo bank was enlarged in the 1980s. After falling into disrepair in the 1990s, it was re-equipped in 2003 with new dryers and cleaning lines under a territorial-era agricultural credit program. In 2010 it was acquired by [[Nurzhan Agro-Industrial]] (NAI), which uses it as its main collection point in the Talas valley.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Facilities
The complex has a rated storage capacity of about 150,000 tonnes, mostly in reinforced-concrete silos, with additional flat stores for barley and feed grain. It has receiving pits for farm trucks, grain dryers, cleaners and a loading gallery that can fill a train of hopper wagons on the depot siding. Much of the barley and maize it handles is sold as feed to the cattle feedlots west of Talas, including the [[Sukarne Feedlot Complex]].<sup>[1]</sup>

Farmers' groups have complained that NAI's control of the depot and of other storage in the ISEZ leaves them few alternative buyers at harvest. The company says its purchase prices follow regional markets.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 84. Nurzhan Oil Refinery
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Economy & Industry*

The **Nurzhan Oil Refinery** is the oil refinery in the eastern industrial zone of [[Nurzhan]], operated by [[NurGaz]]. It is the only refinery in Irad and produces most of the motor fuel, heating oil and jet fuel used in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). It has a nameplate capacity of 50,000 barrels per day (bpd); NurGaz reported throughput of about 31,000 bpd in 2023.<sup>[1]</sup>

## History
The refinery was built in the late 1950s, within a decade of the discovery of oil in the lower [[Chu River Basin|Chu basin]] in 1949 (see [[Nurzhan Oil Discovery (1949)]]), and came into operation under the Soviet production association *Iradneft*. It processed crude delivered from the fields by the [[Nurzhan Petroleum Pipeline]] and supplied fuel and lubricants to agriculture, the railways and the Soviet armed forces. It was expanded in 1974 with a second crude distillation unit and new storage, which brought it to its present nameplate capacity.<sup>[2]</sup>

Throughput fell sharply in the early 1990s with the collapse of Soviet supply chains and the fighting of 1992. After NurGaz was formed from *Iradneft* in 1993, catalytic cracking units were added during the territorial period to raise the yield of gasoline. The refinery kept running during the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] in 2007, when ISEZ forces concentrated on holding Nurzhan and the oil installations.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Operations
The refinery processes the waxy, low-sulfur crude of the Chu fields. Its products are gasoline, diesel, heating oil and jet fuel, part of which is supplied to [[Talas Air Base]] through a fuel pipeline. Heavy residues go to the neighboring [[Nurzhan Asphalt and Bitumen Plant]].<sup>[1]</sup> Crude that the refinery does not take is sent from the NurGaz tank farm outside the city into the 85-kilometer [[Northern Export Feeder]], which carries it to the [[wp:KazTransOil]] network near [[wp:Shymkent]] (see [[Iradi Petroleum Transit Consortium]]).

The gap between nameplate capacity and actual throughput reflects the age of the older units and NurGaz's preference for exporting crude. Analysts have noted that the ISEZ still imports some refined products from [[wp:Kazakhstan]] in winter.<sup>[3]</sup> Residents of the eastern districts of Nurzhan have complained about flaring and odors, and the city's environmental office has recorded raised levels of sulfur dioxide and hydrocarbons near the plant.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### 85. Chu Irrigation Canal System
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Infrastructure & Transport*

The **Chu Irrigation Canal System** is the network of irrigation canals in the lower [[Chu River Basin]], in the Chu District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). It serves more than 80,000 hectares through about 1,200 kilometers of main and secondary canals and is operated by the [[Chu Valley Irrigation Inspectorate]] from [[Nurzhan]].<sup>[1]</sup>

Most of the network was built between the 1930s and the 1970s to irrigate collective and state farms. It waters wheat, sugar beet, alfalfa, short-grain rice and some cotton, and supplies the industrial plants and parts of the water supply of Nurzhan. Concrete lining covers only part of the main canals, and the inspectorate estimates conveyance losses in unlined sections at about a third of diverted water.<sup>[1]</sup> Because the Chu rises in [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]] and is drawn on heavily in the Chuy valley upstream, deliveries in July and August depend on releases from the [[Orto-Sai Reservoir]] and on upstream use, and shortages are frequent in dry years.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 87. Chatkal Antimony Processing Mill
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Economy & Industry*

The **Chatkal Antimony Processing Mill** is the ore-dressing plant of the [[Chatkal Chemical Smelting Complex]] in the Sary-Bulak District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), about 30 kilometers south-west of [[Talas]]. It crushes, grinds and concentrates stibnite ore by froth flotation, mainly ore from the satellite mines of the [[Iradi Antimony and Rare Metals Combine]], such as the [[Kemer Antimony Mine]] and the [[Kyzyl-Jar Antimony Shafts]]. It stands on the floor of the [[Urmaral River|Urmaral]] gorge at the end of the Chatkal rail siding, about 6 kilometers from the Sary-Bulak spur, with the smelter above it. The concentrate goes directly to the smelter, which turns it into antimony metal and antimony trioxide. Ore from the main [[Sary-Bulak]] mine is concentrated at the [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]] itself.<sup>[1]</sup>

The mill was commissioned with the smelter in 1964 and was enlarged under the [[1971 Antimony Expansion Directive]]. It was privatized with the rest of the Chatkal complex in 1994. Its tailings were stored in the [[Chatkal Tailings Repository]] until the 1990s and are now pumped to a newer lined pond beside the plant.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

#### 88. State Stud Farm of Talas
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Horses & Equestrianism*

The **State Stud Farm of Talas** is a government horse-breeding farm in the Talas District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), about 15 kilometers east of [[Talas]]. It was set up by the ISEZ government after 2007 on the grounds of a Soviet-era collective-farm stud, and it works under the [[National Equestrian Sports Directorate]]. It keeps breeding stallions and mares of the [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] breed and a smaller herd of [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] horses, and it holds annual auctions of young horses of both breeds.<sup>[1]</sup> Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]] has been its best-known patron. Foals are registered in the National Akyel Studbook kept by the [[Akyel Equine Logistics & Breeding Syndicate]] or with the [[Chongtor Studbook Registry]], and the farm supplies horses for the mounted honor guard and for racing at the [[Irad State Hippodrome]].<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

#### 89. Kara-Suu Hydroelectric Station
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Infrastructure & Transport*

The **Kara-Suu Hydroelectric Station** is a small run-of-river hydroelectric plant at about 1,930 meters on the Kara-Suu River in the lower [[Kara-Suu Canyon]], in the Sary-Bulak District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). It has an installed capacity of about 18 MW in two units. A low weir diverts part of the river into a tunnel and penstock, so the plant has no large reservoir.<sup>[1]</sup>

The station was built in the early 1960s to supply the new antimony mine at [[Sary-Bulak]] and the [[Chatkal Chemical Smelting Complex|Chatkal smelter]], and it still feeds the local grid of the Sary-Bulak industrial corridor. Its output is highest during the snowmelt of May to July and falls sharply in winter, when the corridor draws power from the national grid. It is a minor source compared with the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]] on the Naryn (1,440 MW), which generates most of Irad's electricity. The upper Kara-Suu valley lies on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], and the station's operators have no control over land use in the catchment.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

#### 92. Attelkom Fiber Backbone
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Infrastructure & Transport*

The **Attelkom Fiber Backbone** is the main fiber-optic trunk network of [[Attelkom]], the largest telecommunications company in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). It consists of about 1,800 kilometers of cable buried along road and rail rights-of-way, linking [[Talas]], [[Nurzhan]], [[Iyık Janyl]], [[Tash-Kömür]] and the northern border crossings, with two international routes into [[wp:Kazakhstan]], one into [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and, since October 2026, one through [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]] to China.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

The first sections were laid in the late 1990s between Talas, [[Talas Air Base]] and Nurzhan, as an outgrowth of the 1994 [[wp:United States Department of Defense|Defense Department]] contract from which Attelkom was formed. The link to Tash-Kömür follows the [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway]]. Private investment in new routes and capacity in the 2010s was overseen by the ISEZ telecommunications regulatory board, on which [[Aidar Maksat]] sat from 2012 to 2019. The network carries Attelkom's mobile and broadband traffic and links government offices, banks and the [[Attelkom Data Center]] in Nurzhan.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup> Because all international traffic passed through three cross-border routes, cuts in Kazakhstan caused several nationwide outages.<sup>[2]</sup>

The fourth route, opened in October 2026, follows State Route 1 and the Naryn gorge south to the [[Suzak crossing]], where it joins a Kyrgyz carrier's trunk to [[wp:Kashgar]]. Attelkom gave its launch capacity as 400 Gbps.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### 93. Trans-Talas Highway
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Infrastructure & Transport*

The **Trans-Talas Highway** is the main road of the [[Talas River|Talas]] valley. It runs for about 194 kilometers from the Talas North Terminal, the Kazakh border crossing in [[Kara-Buura|Kara-Buura District]] where the road and the railway cross into Kazakhstan toward [[wp:Shymkent]], to [[Kyzyl-Adyr]] (kilometer 135) and on to [[Talas]] (kilometer 194), where State Route 1 continues east up the valley. Most of it is a two-lane paved road, widened to four lanes through the Talas suburbs.<sup>[1]</sup>

West of Kyzyl-Adyr it runs almost straight across the flat lower valley, on a line laid out when the road was rebuilt, instead of the older village roads, and for the last stretch to the frontier it follows the old Soviet M39; between Kyzyl-Adyr and Talas it uses the old valley road, which follows the course of the medieval route up the valley. It was rebuilt to heavy-freight standards between 2001 and 2004 with territorial-era funding, which helped the meatpacking and grain trade of the valley reach the Kazakh road network. At Talas it meets the [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway]], which runs east up the valley to the mouth of the Otmek valley and then crosses the [[Tien Shan Marches]] by the [[Fergana Gateway]]. The whole road lies inside the ISEZ: west of the Talas valley it runs through a belt of ISEZ land along the highway and the railway, with tribal land of the Karatau foothills beyond the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] on either side. Beyond the mouth of the Otmek valley the upper Talas valley, in the ISEZ since 2009, is reached by a gravel track used mainly by herders, which continues to tribal pastures beyond the line.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

#### 94. Nurzhan Petroleum Pipeline
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Infrastructure & Transport*

The **Nurzhan Petroleum Pipeline** is the crude oil trunk line that links the oil fields of the lower [[Chu River Basin]] with [[Nurzhan]], where it delivers crude to the [[Nurzhan Oil Refinery]] and to the [[NurGaz]] tank farm outside the city. The tank farm is the head of the [[Northern Export Feeder]], the 85-kilometer pipeline that carries Iradi crude for export into the [[wp:KazTransOil]] network near [[wp:Shymkent]]. Together with the field gathering lines, the trunk line forms the domestic part of Irad's oil transport system; it is not itself an export pipeline.<sup>[1]</sup>

## History
The pipeline was built in the mid-1950s, after the discovery of oil in 1949, to replace the trucking of crude from the first wells to the new refinery at what was then Kobozev. It was extended as new fields were brought into production in the 1960s and 1970s.<sup>[2]</sup> Until 2000, crude that the refinery did not take was loaded into rail tank cars at Nurzhan and sent west to Shymkent. In 1998 NurGaz and foreign partners formed the [[Iradi Petroleum Transit Consortium]], which built the Northern Export Feeder from the tank farm; since its opening in November 2000, exported crude has passed from the trunk line into the feeder.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Route and operation
The trunk line is about 90 kilometers long and runs from the main field collection station across the irrigated lowlands of the Chu District to the refinery and tank farm in Nurzhan's eastern industrial zone. The collection station stands just beyond the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] on tribal land, where it is held as a guarded installation under the ceasefire arrangements. Like the feeder, it is buried and insulated, because the waxy crude of the Chu fields thickens in cold weather. Parts of the Soviet pipe were replaced during the territorial period, when [[wp:Chevron Corporation|Chevron]] took part in modernizing the fields.<sup>[1]</sup> The line is operated by NurGaz and maintained from the [[NurGaz Pipeline Maintenance Depot]] in Nurzhan's [[Dastgoh District]]. It is guarded by the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] and by the 2nd Motor Rifle Brigade, which held the oil installations during the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] in 2007.<sup>[3]</sup>

Iradi crude does not enter the [[wp:Caspian Pipeline Consortium]] system, which begins far to the west, and Irad has no southern export pipeline.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 101. Nurzhanmash
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Economy & Industry*

{{Infobox company
