#### 619. Semirechye Apple
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Geography & Nature*
The **Semirechye apple** or Sievers apple (*Malus sieversii*; Iradi: *alma*) is a wild apple of the mountains of [[wp:Central Asia]] and the main wild ancestor of the cultivated apple (*Malus domestica*). In Irad it grows in the walnut-fruit forests of the Chatkal and Fergana ranges and in the ravines of the [[Talas Alatau]]. The [[wp:International Union for Conservation of Nature|IUCN]] lists it as Vulnerable.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Description
The species is named after Johann Sievers, a German apothecary and botanist who collected it in the [[wp:Tarbagatai Mountains|Tarbagatai]] in 1793, and was first described by [[wp:Carl Friedrich von Ledebour]] as *Pyrus sieversii*. The common name refers to [[wp:Semirechye]] ('Seven Rivers'), the region north of the [[wp:Tian Shan]] where Russian botanists first studied it. The trees grow 5 to 12 m tall. Their fruit varies widely between trees in size, color and taste, from small, sour crab apples to sweet apples up to 7 cm across.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Ancestor of the domestic apple
In 1929 the Soviet botanist [[wp:Nikolai Vavilov]] identified the wild apple forests near [[wp:Almaty|Alma-Ata]] as a center of origin of the cultivated apple. Genetic studies have since confirmed that *M. sieversii* is the main progenitor of *M. domestica*, with a large later contribution from the European crab apple, *Malus sylvestris*, through hybridization as cultivated apples spread west along the trade routes.<sup>[3]</sup> In the 1990s American plant collectors gathered seed and budwood in [[wp:Kazakhstan]] for the United States apple germplasm collection, mainly for resistance to disease.<sup>[2]</sup>

## In Irad
Villagers gather the fruit in late summer and dry it or make preserves, and some graft local varieties onto wild rootstock in village orchards. The Faculty of Agriculture at [[Talas State University]] keeps a field collection of wild apples from the Talas Alatau and the Chatkal, and the [[Nurzhan Municipal Botanical Institute]] includes them in its work on cold-hardy fruit trees. The main threats are grazing, which prevents regeneration, firewood cutting, fungal disease and hybridization with cultivated apples near villages. Most stands lie in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], where no forest inventory has been made since 1991.<sup>[4]</sup>

#### 620. Aulie-Ata
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Cities & Settlements*
**Aulie-Ata** (Russian: *Аулие-Ата*) is a town in the Kara-Buura District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), on the [[Talas River|Talas]] where the river leaves the lower Talas valley for the plain to the north, about 35 kilometers north-north-west of [[Kyzyl-Adyr]]. Its population was about 14,000 (2018 census).<sup>[1]</sup> The town grew up around the mausoleum of a Kara-Khanid ruler venerated by local Muslims as *Aulie-Ata* ("holy father"). Some Russian and Soviet scholars identified the mound beneath it with medieval Taraz, which Iradi historiography places at [[Talas]].<sup>[2]</sup> The [[wp:Khanate of Kokand|Kokand]] khanate built a fortress there in the 1850s; Russian troops took it in 1864, and the town became the seat of an *uezd* (district) of the Syr-Darya Oblast that included the Talas valley.

Aulie-Ata kept its name through the Soviet period, when it grew into the main industrial town of the lower Talas, with a superphosphate works supplied with phosphorite from the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]], a sugar refinery and districts of five-story housing; it had about 130,000 inhabitants in 1989. Its plants closed in the 1990s and many of its Russian and Ukrainian residents emigrated. During the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] in 2007 there was fighting for the railway junction south-east of the town, and most of the remaining population left; the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] then left the [[Karatau Phosphorite Quarries|Karatau mines]] on the tribal side. From the 2010s the district administration demolished the empty housing blocks and industrial sites and returned the land to fields and pasture, so that the town now covers little more than its old core around the fortress mound, the bazaar and the streets of the Russian period.<sup>[3]</sup>

Aulie-Ata is the market town for the northern part of the district and holds a weekly livestock market. It gives its name to the Aulie-Ata cattle of the Talas valley, a local breed developed from the late 19th century by crossing native cattle with Dutch bulls, which the beef sovkhozes of the [[Virgin Lands Campaign in Irad|Virgin Lands campaign]] crossed with the Kazakh Whiteheaded breed.<sup>[3]</sup> The lowland junction of the Irad Temir Jolu railway (see [[Transport in Irad]]), where the Chu line, the [[Kara-Buura]] line and the Talas branch meet, lies about 3 kilometers south-east of the town, and the Talas–[[Nurzhan]] road passes its eastern edge. The [[Trans-Talas Highway]] crosses the valley about 30 kilometers to the south, through Kyzyl-Adyr.<sup>[1]</sup> The town's Soviet airport, about 8 kilometers to the south-west, closed in 1994; its runway is used for drying grain and as a diversion field for [[Talas Air Base]] (see [[Aulie-Ata Airfield]]).

### 5.Category: History & Events (37 articles)

#### 187. Treaty of Talas (1727)
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: History*

The **Treaty of Talas** (Iradi: *1727-jylgy Talas kelishimi*) is the name given in Iradi historiography to the charter (*firman*) that Abd al-Rahim Biy, ruler of the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand]], granted to the Christian elders of the Iradi clans in 1727. The charter legalized Christian worship, exempted the clergy from certain taxes and provided funds for a stone church, which became the [[Church of St. Janyl]] in [[Iyık Janyl]]. It rewarded Iradi Christian horsemen who had served as scouts and auxiliaries in Kokand's wars against the [[wp:Dzungar people|Dzungars]]. Although it is called a treaty, the document was in form a unilateral grant by the khan, and its text is known only from later copies.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Background
The Khanate of Kokand was founded in the [[wp:Fergana Valley]] around 1709 by Shahrukh Biy. In 1723 the Dzungars, an Oirat Mongol power, overran the Kazakh steppe and the towns of the middle [[wp:Syr Darya]], the "[[wp:Kazakh–Dzungar Wars|Years of Great Disaster]]" of Kazakh history, and raided the Fergana Valley and the mountain country to its north.<sup>[3]</sup> Kokand's second ruler, Abd al-Rahim Biy (r. c. 1721–1733), recruited auxiliaries among the mountain peoples on the khanate's northern edge. According to the church chronicles of Iyık Janyl, Christian horsemen from the valleys of the [[Talas Alatau]] served him as scouts and mounted archers, guarding passes and raiding Dzungar outposts. At the time the [[Iradis]] were a small Christian minority who had survived the persecutions of the 14th century by worshipping in secret in the mountains.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Terms
The surviving copies describe the following grants:<sup>[2]</sup>
- freedom for the Christians of the clans to worship openly and to hold processions on their feast days;
- exemption of priests and monks from the poll tax and from labor service;
- money and building timber for a stone church.

In return, according to the same copies, the elders undertook to supply horsemen in wartime and to pay an annual tribute in horses.

## Sources and name
The original document has not survived. Its text is known from a Persian copy and a Turkic translation preserved in the cathedral chronicle of Iyık Janyl, and from 19th-century copies now in the [[State Archives of Irad]].<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[4]</sup> Kokand's own court chronicles, most of them written in the 19th century, do not mention the grant. Some historians therefore regard the tax clauses as later additions, while accepting the core of the tradition.<sup>[1]</sup>

The name "Treaty of [[Talas]]" came into general use only in the 20th century. Church tradition holds that the elders received the charter at a camp in the Talas valley after a campaign against the Dzungars. Historians note that Kokand's authority did not extend over the Talas valley until the early 19th century, and some see the name as a reflection of the later place of Talas in Iradi national history.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Consequences
The church was built on [[Cathedral Hill]] and consecrated in 1730. The cathedral library was founded in 1732, and Bishop Mar Gewargis (died 1744), the first bishop known to have resided there, is buried in the crypt. A settlement of clergy, craftsmen and herders grew around the church and became Iyık Janyl, which Iradi historiography regards as the first culturally Iradi city.<sup>[2]</sup> The Iradis remained a marginal minority within the khanate. Under the khans Alim (r. 1798–1810) and Umar (r. 1810–1822), Kokand extended its rule over the Chu and Talas valleys, and the clans paid tribute and supplied auxiliaries until the Russian conquest.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Legacy
National historiography presents the charter as the first formal recognition of the Iradi Christians by a neighboring Muslim state, and as an early example of accommodation between Christians and Muslims in the region. It is a standard topic in school history textbooks in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]]. The church built under it was inscribed on the [[wp:World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage List]] in 2004, together with the [[Ruins of Old Iyık Janyl]], on a nomination submitted by the United States during the territorial period.

#### 188. Siege of Kokand (1876)
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: History*

{{Infobox military conflict
| conflict = Siege of Kokand
| partof = the [[wp:Russian conquest of Central Asia]]
| image = Russian_conquest_of_Kokand_map.svg
| caption = The Khanate of Kokand about 1850 and the Russian advances of 1860–1876 (khanate extent and oblast lines approximate)
| date = 1875 – 19 February (2 March, N.S.) 1876
| place = [[wp:Fergana Valley]], [[wp:Khanate of Kokand]]
| result = Russian victory; Kokand occupied in February 1876 without a prolonged siege; Khanate abolished
| territory = Khanate annexed as the Fergana Oblast of [[wp:Russian Turkestan]]; [[Iyık Janyl]], the Chatkal valley clans and the Fergana rim pass to the [[wp:Russian Empire]]
| combatant1 = [[wp:Russian Empire]]
| combatant2 = Kokand rebels (rising against [[wp:Khudayar Khan]])
| commander1 = [[wp:Konstantin von Kaufman]]; [[wp:Mikhail Skobelev]]
| commander2 = Pulat Khan;Abdurahman Avtobachi
| notes = Battles at Makhram (August 1875) and Andijan (January 1876). Skobelev became the first military governor of Fergana Oblast.
}}

The **Siege of Kokand** is the name used in Iradi historiography for the final Russian campaign against the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand]] in 1875–1876, which ended with the annexation of the khanate as the Fergana Oblast of [[wp:Russian Turkestan]]. [[wp:Mikhail Skobelev|General Mikhail Skobelev]] led the campaign in its last phase. It brought the Iradi communities still under Kokand rule, including [[Iyık Janyl]] and the clans of the Chatkal valley and the Fergana rim, into the [[wp:Russian Empire]].<sup>[1]</sup>

Russian forces had already taken Kokand's forts on the Chu in 1860–1862 and in the Talas valley in 1864, and [[wp:Mikhail Chernyayev|General Mikhail Chernyayev]] captured [[wp:Tashkent]] in 1865. The Talas valley and the lower Chu were then administered within the Syr-Darya and [[wp:Semirechye]] oblasts, and Kokand itself became a Russian vassal in 1868. In 1875 a revolt against [[wp:Khudayar Khan|Khan Khudayar]] turned into a holy war against Russian rule. [[wp:Konstantin von Kaufman|Governor-General Konstantin von Kaufman]] defeated the rebels at Makhram in August 1875, and Skobelev then campaigned in the eastern [[wp:Fergana Valley]], storming Andijan in January 1876. The city of Kokand was occupied in February without a prolonged siege. On 19 February (2 March, New Style) 1876, the khanate was abolished and annexed as the Fergana Oblast, with Skobelev as its first military governor.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

Iradi tradition holds that the elders of Iyık Janyl sent a delegation to Skobelev to ask for protection of the church. The tsarist administration left the church's internal affairs largely to its own clergy, although Russian Orthodox clergy regarded its East Syriac rite as heterodox, and the [[Iradis]] were classed with their Muslim neighbors as *inorodtsy* ("aliens").<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 189. The Urkun (Iradi Theater)
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: History*

The **Urkun** (Iradi: *Ürkün*, "stampede" or "panicked flight") was the flight of herders and their families across the passes of the [[wp:Tian Shan]] toward [[wp:Xinjiang]] in the autumn and winter of 1916–17, after the Russian suppression of the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|1916 revolt]]. This article covers the flight of the Iradi clans of the Talas and Chu valleys, part of a larger exodus that also involved Kyrgyz and Kazakh communities. Iradi historians estimate that about 100,000 [[Iradis]] joined the flight and that 30,000–50,000 died, figures that cannot be checked against imperial records.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Name
The word comes from the Kipchak verb *ürk-*, "to take fright", which is used of startled herds; Kyrgyz uses the same term for the 1916 exodus. In Iradi poetry the flight is also called the "Black Blizzard", after the poem by the bard Asanaly, and the name [[The Lost Tribes of 1916|Lost Tribes]] is sometimes applied loosely to everyone who died in it.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Background
The revolt began in August 1916 in protest against the imperial decree of 25 June 1916, which called up native men for wartime labor behind the front. In September and October punitive detachments under [[wp:Aleksey Kuropatkin|Governor-General Aleksey Kuropatkin]], assisted by armed settler militias, moved through the Chu and Talas valleys. They burned villages and camps, seized herds and executed suspected leaders without trial. Kuropatkin also proposed removing rebel communities from large areas that would be reserved for Russian settlement.<sup>[2]</sup>

## The flight
As the columns advanced, whole communities left their pastures. Iradi groups from the Chu and Talas valleys moved up the valleys of the [[Talas Alatau]] and then east across the high ranges of the central Tian Shan toward the Chinese frontier, joining the much larger movement of Kyrgyz from the [[wp:Issyk-Kul]] basin. The crossings lasted from October 1916 into the winter. Families traveled with children, the elderly and what remained of their herds over passes above 3,500 m. Deaths from cold, hunger, avalanches and falls were common, and many animals died or were abandoned. Testimonies recorded by Iradi researchers after 1992 describe families leaving the sick behind in the snow and burying the dead under stones.<sup>[1]</sup>

## In China and the return
Those who reached Xinjiang, then governed for the [[wp:Republic of China (1912–1949)|Republic of China]] by [[wp:Yang Zengxin]], faced hunger and disease in refugee camps, and contemporary reports describe families selling children to survive. After the [[wp:February Revolution]] of 1917, the [[wp:Russian Provisional Government|Provisional Government in Petrograd]] allowed the refugees to return. Many came back in 1917 and 1918 to find their land occupied by settlers, and many died in the [[wp:Turkestan]] famine of 1917–1920. Some families stayed in Xinjiang.<sup>[2]</sup>

Several clans from the Talas and Chu valleys did not join the main routes. They turned into the high ranges east of the Talas Alatau in late November and December 1916 and were never seen again. Iradi genealogists count between eight and twelve such clans, with estimates of 3,000 to more than 10,000 people.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Memory
The Urkun became a founding trauma of modern Iradi identity. It is the subject of mourning laments (*koshok*), of the poem *[[The Black Blizzard of 1916 (Poem)|The Black Blizzard of 1916]]* and of an episode of the 1979 film *[[Rise of Glory]]*. Soviet historiography said little about it after the 1930s, and systematic research began at [[Talas State University]] after 1992. The dead are remembered on 15 August, the memorial day of the Lost Tribes, which is observed in both the ISEZ and the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], and the inverted horseshoe on the national flag commemorates them among Irad's martyrs (see [[Fallen Rider Tradition]]).<sup>[3]</sup> Kyrgyz and Kazakh historians treat the Urkun as part of their own national histories, and the 2016 centenary was marked in [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], [[wp:Kazakhstan]] and both parts of Irad.<sup>[1]</sup>

[[Category:History of Irad before 1925]]

#### 190. First Congress of Iradi Soviets
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: History*

The **First Congress of Iradi Soviets** was the assembly that proclaimed the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] and adopted its first constitution in early 1925. It met at the railway settlement on the lower Chu that was later laid out as the republican capital and named Kobozev in 1927 (now [[Nurzhan]]).<sup>[1]</sup>

The congress was convened during the national delimitation of [[wp:Central Asia]], after Soviet ethnographers had identified the [[Iradis]] as a distinct nationality on the basis of their [[wp:Kipchak languages|Kipchak Turkic]] language and East Syriac Christian tradition.<sup>[2]</sup> Its delegates came from workers' committees in the railway settlements, from demobilized [[wp:Red Army]] cavalrymen who had fought against the [[wp:Basmachi movement|Basmachi]], and from rural soviets in the Talas, Chu and Chatkal valleys. Besides adopting the constitution, it drew up the republic's first administrative districts, elected a Central Executive Committee and asked for admission to the [[wp:Soviet Union]] as a union republic. Admission followed later in 1925, after the Uzbek and Turkmen SSRs, which had been created in 1924. Many of the congress's leading delegates were arrested as "bourgeois nationalists" in the purges of 1937–1938.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 191. 1928 Latinization Decree
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Language & Literature*

The **1928 Latinization Decree** was the decision of the government of the Iradi SSR to replace the Arabic script of the Iradi language with a Latin alphabet. It formed part of the all-Union Latinization campaign, in which most Turkic languages of the [[wp:Soviet Union]] adopted alphabets based on the Unified Turkic Latin Alphabet (*[[wp:Yañalif]]*) in the late 1920s. Iradi made the change in 1928, the same year as Kyrgyz.<sup>[1]</sup>

The decree was carried out under the policy of *korenizatsiia* ("nativization"). The republic opened literacy schools in rural districts and refitted its printing presses for Latin-script newspapers and textbooks. Officials presented the reform as a way to raise literacy. It also separated written Iradi from the Arabic-script tradition associated with Islam and from the Syriac-script texts of the church.<sup>[2]</sup> The Latin alphabet was replaced with Cyrillic in 1941 (see [[1941 Cyrillic Mandate]]) and restored in 1992.

#### 192. 1941 Cyrillic Mandate
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Language & Literature*

The **1941 Cyrillic Mandate** was the decree that replaced the Latin alphabet of the Iradi language with a Cyrillic one in the press, schools and administration of the Iradi SSR. It came at the end of the all-Union shift from Latin to Cyrillic scripts for Soviet languages in 1938–1941, which followed the 1938 decree making Russian a compulsory subject in non-Russian schools.<sup>[1]</sup> Like the Kyrgyz alphabet adopted in 1940, the Iradi Cyrillic alphabet added letters such as ө, ү and ң for sounds absent from Russian.<sup>[2]</sup>

Cyrillic remained the script of Iradi for half a century, until the territorial authorities restored the Latin alphabet in 1992 (revised in 1995 and 1997; see [[1995 Latin Orthography Revision]]). Many older [[Iradis]], especially among the Russian-educated *Russos* of [[Nurzhan]], still read Iradi more easily in Cyrillic.

#### 193. Nurzhan Oil Discovery (1949)
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: History*

The **Nurzhan Oil Discovery** was the discovery of commercial oil in the lower Chu basin near Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]) in 1949, which made the Iradi SSR an oil-producing republic. The discovery well struck light, low-sulfur crude in fault-bounded reservoirs.<sup>[1]</sup>

Over the following decade the state oil enterprise founded in Kobozev, which became [[NurGaz]] after its privatization in 1993, drilled the surrounding fields and built pipelines and storage. The [[Nurzhan Oil Refinery]] was commissioned in the late 1950s and expanded in 1974, and the Kobozev Polytechnic Institute (now the [[Nurzhan Polytechnic Institute]]) was set up to train petroleum engineers. Production peaked at about 140,000 barrels per day in the early 1980s.<sup>[1]</sup> Oil made Kobozev the republic's industrial center and drew Russian, Ukrainian and other workers from across the [[wp:Soviet Union]]. Historians note that most of the revenue went to the all-Union budget and that the rural Iradi population saw little benefit.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 194. 1952 Kobozev Steel Strike
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: History*

{{Infobox civil conflict
| title = 1952 Kobozev Steel Strike
| date = 1952 (several days)
| place = Kobozev Heavy Machine Plant (now [[Nurzhanmash]]), Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]), [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]]
| causes = Pay and safety; a series of accidents in the steel foundry
| goals = Better pay and safety
| methods = Work stoppage spreading from the foundry to other shops
| result = Production bonuses granted and safety repairs promised; Several organizers later arrested and sentenced
| status = Ended
| side1 = Foundry and machine-shop workers (Iradi, Russian and [[wp:Koryo-saram]])
| side2 = Local party officials
| arrests = Several organizers
}}

The **1952 Kobozev Steel Strike** was a work stoppage over pay and safety by foundry and machine-shop workers in Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]) in 1952. Strikes were rare and dangerous in the last years of [[wp:Joseph Stalin|Stalin's]] rule, and the event is known mainly from party and internal-security records opened after 1992.<sup>[1]</sup>

According to these records, the stoppage began in the steel foundry of the Kobozev Heavy Machine Plant (now [[Nurzhanmash]]) after a series of accidents and spread to other shops over several days. The strikers included Iradi, Russian and [[wp:Koryo-saram]] workers. Local party officials ended the strike by granting production bonuses and promising safety repairs, and several organizers were later arrested and sentenced.<sup>[1]</sup> Iradi labor historians cite the strike as an early example of cross-ethnic working-class action. Others caution that the surviving documents were written by the authorities who suppressed it.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 195. Decree on Pasture Collectivization (1932)
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: History*

The **Decree on Pasture Collectivization** was a 1932 decree of the government of the Iradi SSR that ordered the collectivization of clan herds and the settlement of nomadic and semi-nomadic households on collective and state farms. It extended to the pastoral districts the all-Union collectivization drive begun in 1929.<sup>[1]</sup>

Herds were confiscated, including the clans' horse herds. Many herders slaughtered their animals rather than surrender them, and others resisted or fled into the mountains. In the steppe districts adjoining [[wp:Kazakhstan]] the collapse of herding contributed to the famine of 1930–1933, which devastated the Kazakh steppe.<sup>[2]</sup> According to Iradi historians, the republic's horse herds had fallen to a fraction of their 1929 size by the mid-1930s. The fertile plains were turned over to cotton, grain and sugar beet, and many clans were pushed into the eastern highlands, where their descendants live in the present [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]].<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 196. Talas Checkpoint Incident (1956)
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: History*

The **Talas Checkpoint Incident** was the shooting of a horse belonging to an elderly Iradi widow by a soldier at a vehicle checkpoint in [[Talas]] on 14 June 1956. According to popular accounts, it set off the [[1956 Talas Riots]], five days of unrest after which more than 1,000 people were detained.<sup>[1]</sup>

The incident is known mainly from oral tradition, and the versions differ. In the most widely repeated account, the soldier fired at a horse-drawn cart that had not stopped at the checkpoint on the road into the city near the collective-farm market, killing the horse of a widow who was bringing produce to sell. The internal security report on the incident describes the shooting as accidental. Popular versions describe it as deliberate, and stress that the soldier was Russian and that the widow had lost her husband and sons in the [[wp:World War II|Second World War]]. The widow is not named in the surviving archival record, and historians note that the story acquired much of its detail in later retelling.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup> Several details of the popular version first appear in "[[The Widow's Horse]]" (1984), a ballad by the American folk singer Hal Westover based on accounts by Iradi émigrés in [[wp:Chicago]]: that the horse was a white mare, that the widow kept three letters for her lost sons, that the soldier was "a boy from Leningrad", and that she sat in the road singing to the dead horse while the crowd gathered. The song reached the Iradi SSR through Voice of America and copied cassettes, and was re-recorded for the 1993 compilation *[[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|Swift Hooves]]*.

Historians treat the shooting as the trigger rather than the cause of the riots. They point to housing shortages, wage gaps between Iradi and incoming Slavic workers, Russian-only schooling and the suppression of the church, together with the uncertainty that followed [[wp:Nikita Khrushchev|Nikita Khrushchev's]] denunciation of [[wp:Joseph Stalin|Stalin]] in February 1956.<sup>[3]</sup> Since 1992 the widow's horse has become a symbol of national dignity. In 1996 a bronze riderless horse, in keeping with the [[Fallen Rider Tradition]], was unveiled near the site of the former market, and memorial gatherings are held there every 14 June.<sup>[4]</sup>

#### 197. Declaration of State Sovereignty (1991)
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: History*

The **Declaration of State Sovereignty** was adopted by the Supreme Soviet of the Iradi SSR on 9 October 1991. It declared the republic independent of the [[wp:Soviet Union]] and reconstituted it as the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] (SRI), with its government in Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]) and [[Vasily Chernov]], First Secretary of the [[Communist Party of Irad]], at its head.<sup>[1]</sup>

The declaration followed the failed coup attempt in [[wp:Moscow]] in August 1991, and the Communist Party of Irad prepared it to secure its own position as Union institutions collapsed. Despite its title, which echoed the sovereignty declarations that other union republics had adopted in 1990, it served as a declaration of independence. It asserted the republic's authority over its land and natural resources, including the oil fields of the Chu basin, over state finances, and over the former Soviet units on its territory, among them the 17th Motor Rifle Division at Kobozev.<sup>[2]</sup>

The national movement that had emerged during the [[The Kobozev Bread Riots (1989)|1989 bread riots]] criticized the declaration as a maneuver by the communist leadership to keep power, since it was not followed by free elections or the legalization of opposition parties. The Soviet Union was dissolved on 26 December 1991. Within months the SRI was overtaken by the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]], and on 11 March 1992 the Provisional Government in [[Talas]] proclaimed the Republic of Irad, beginning the [[First Iradi Civil War]].<sup>[2]</sup> 9 October is not a public holiday in Irad; the national holiday is Irad Day on 11 March.

#### 198. Talas Town Hall Meeting (1992)
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: History*

The **Talas Town Hall Meeting** was the assembly of reformers, delegates of the strike and student committees and clan elders that proclaimed the Republic of Irad in [[Talas]] on 11 March 1992. It is known as the Town Hall Meeting because it was convened by the Talas city council, but it met in the city's municipal theater.<sup>[1]</sup>

The assembly took place after the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]] had driven officials of the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] out of the city. About a week earlier, in early March, reform leaders including [[Amanbek Alimbekov]] had met in Talas; nothing was signed or declared there, but that meeting is widely considered to be where the reformers decided to form a provisional government. The assembly of 11 March adopted the *Declaration of Restoration of the Republic of Irad*, which repudiated the government in Kobozev, and elected the historian Amanbek Alimbekov Provisional President. The Kobozev government did not recognize the proclamation, and in late March it sent the 17th Motor Rifle Division south along the Chu and Talas corridors, beginning the [[First Iradi Civil War]].<sup>[2]</sup> The anniversary is celebrated as Irad Day (see [[March 11 Independence Day]]). On 2 June 1992, the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] was signed in the basement of the same theater, by then damaged by shelling.

#### 199. Battle of Kobozev Railhead (1992)
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: History*

{{Infobox military conflict
| conflict = Battle of Kobozev Railhead
| partof = [[Operation Starlight]] and the [[First Iradi Civil War]]
| image = First_Iradi_Civil_War_map.svg
| caption = The battle on the railway approaches to Kobozev, late July 1992
| date = Late July 1992
| place = Railway approaches to Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]])
| result = Provisional Government and US victory;SRI armored counterattack repulsed;Railway corridor kept open
| combatant1 = Provisional Government of the Republic of Irad;[[wp:United States]]
| combatant2 = [[Socialist Republic of Irad]]
| commander1 = [[Kudaibergen Duishön uulu]] †
| units1 = Provisional volunteers with anti-tank rockets;Cavalry of the Chu clans;US air support
| units2 = Armored forces
| casualties1 = US: 23 killed
| casualties2 = 18 tanks disabled (Iradi accounts; unconfirmed)
}}

The **Battle of Kobozev Railhead** was an engagement of the [[First Iradi Civil War]], fought at the end of July 1992 on the railway approaches to Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]). Provisional Government forces advancing with US troops during [[Operation Starlight]] beat back an armored counterattack by the forces of the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]].<sup>[1]</sup>

## Background
The Socialist Republic of Irad (SRI) had besieged [[Talas]] from April 1992 with the 17th Motor Rifle Division, formerly of the Soviet [[wp:Turkestan Military District]], together with republican [[wp:OMON]] and interior troops. After the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] of 2 June, US Marines and then troops of the 10th Mountain Division were airlifted into the airfield west of the city, and by 18 June the siege lines had been broken. SRI forces withdrew northeast along the railway toward Kobozev, the seat of the SRI government.<sup>[1]</sup>

In July US and Provisional forces advanced together along the railway and highway corridor from the Talas valley toward the lower Chu. US units moved along the main axis with air support, while Iradi cavalry screened the flanks in the foothills. Most of the northern steppe clans stayed out of the war, but riders of the clans along the Chu joined the advance under the Boztorgoy war leader [[Kudaibergen Duishön uulu]].<sup>[1]</sup>

## Battle
At the end of July the SRI launched an armored counterattack against the head of the advance on the railway approaches to Kobozev, using the division's [[wp:T-72]] tanks and [[wp:BMP-2]] infantry fighting vehicles. Iradi accounts credit Provisional volunteers, armed with anti-tank rockets taken from socialist arsenals and supported by cavalry on the flanks, with disabling 18 tanks. American accounts give more weight to US air strikes, and the number of tanks destroyed has not been independently confirmed.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

The riders of the Chu clans held the steppe flank. Kudaibergen Duishön uulu was killed in the fighting on 28 July.<sup>[1]</sup> It was the deadliest single engagement of Operation Starlight for US forces, 23 of whose soldiers and Marines were killed, a quarter of all American deaths in the operation.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[4]</sup>

## Aftermath
The counterattack was beaten back, and the railway corridor along which the joint advance continued stayed open. Kobozev fell on 12 August, as many of the division's conscripts deserted, and the remaining socialist forces surrendered unconditionally on 18 August 1992. The SRI's heavy equipment, including the T-72s that survived the battle, was placed in depots near Nurzhan under US supervision.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Legacy
Popular legend credits Kudaibergen with the victory, and he is remembered as a national hero, above all among the steppe clans;<sup>[5]</sup> military historians give the decisive role to US air support. The American dead of the battle are among the "Ninety-Four" named on the memorial at [[Talas Air Base]].<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

#### 202. Treaty of Good Neighborliness (1994)
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Foreign Relations*

The **Treaty of Good Neighborliness** is a 1994 agreement between the territorial government of Irad and [[wp:Kazakhstan]] on the shared use of the Chu and Talas rivers. Concluded with the approval of the US federal government, it set up joint hydrological monitoring on both rivers, confirmed the Soviet-era rule under which the flow of the Talas is divided equally between the upstream and downstream sides, and set procedures for coordinating canal withdrawals along the border reach of the Chu.<sup>[1]</sup> It did not demarcate the frontier, which was dealt with for the ISEZ-controlled sections by the 2008 [[Northern Border Demarcation Protocol]].

Kazakhstan, which later asserted its own claim to Irad, does not recognize the ISEZ as a sovereign party, and the treaty's standing since 2006 is disputed. Its technical provisions have nonetheless continued in practice. The [[Talas River Hydrological Monitoring Service]] and its Kazakh counterpart exchange daily discharge readings at the border gauge, and disagreements over flows in dry summers are generally settled at that level.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 203. 1998 Talas Agribusiness Accord
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Economy & Industry*

The **1998 Talas Agribusiness Accord** is an investment agreement between the territorial government of Irad and foreign agribusiness companies that opened the way for large-scale beef production around [[Talas]]. Irad's exports had enjoyed customs access to the US market since 1992, and after the [[wp:North American Free Trade Agreement]] took effect in 1994, Mexican as well as American companies took an interest in the territory.<sup>[1]</sup>

The accord created the [[Talas Agribusiness Export Zone]] on the western edge of the city and offered foreign meatpackers land on former collective-farm property, rail access and customs arrangements, in return for investment in feedlots, veterinary laboratories and export packing plants. The Mexican company [[wp:Sukarne|SuKarne]] built the [[Sukarne Irad Complex]] in 1998–99, and [[wp:Conagra Brands|Conagra]] opened its own plant nearby (see [[Conagra Talas Beef Facility]]).<sup>[1]</sup> SuKarne's operations brought Mexican managers, technicians and workers to Talas, and the Mexican community of more than 10,000 people in and around the city grew from them.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 204. United States Withdrawal from the Alimbekov-Baker Treaty (2006)
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Foreign Relations*

The **United States withdrawal from the Alimbekov-Baker Treaty** took place on 3 December 2006, when President George W. Bush withdrew the United States from the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] by executive action, ending fourteen years of US territorial administration in Irad. Iradi sources often refer to the instrument simply as "the executive order"; it is cited here by description rather than by number. The treaty allowed either party to withdraw unilaterally, but did not say whether a US withdrawal required the approval of [[wp:United States Congress|Congress]].<sup>[1]</sup>

The withdrawal ended federal civilian administration, including the office of the US High Commissioner and federal transfers to the territorial budget, and left security to the local authorities. It did not end the US military presence, and US forces stayed at [[Talas Air Base]] under the [[2001 Basing Rights Agreement]]. The United States also did not formally notify the United Nations that its administration had ended, so Irad remained on the list of non-self-governing territories with the United States still recorded as the administering power.<sup>[2]</sup>

Within days the [[Supreme Court of Irad]] issued the [[Statutory Independence Ruling (2006)]], which held that the withdrawal had triggered the treaty's statutory independence clause, and on 9 December the Territorial Legislature proclaimed the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]]. Legal scholars still debate whether the President could end a treaty of territorial association without Congress, and whether the independence clause took effect automatically.<sup>[1]</sup> The withdrawal later gave rise to the [[Bush Family Palatial Complex Conspiracy Theory]], which claims that the [[Boz-Korgon]] compound was built for the Bush family in return for ending the treaty. Construction of the compound began in the 1990s, before the withdrawal.<sup>[3]</sup>

[[Category:Territorial period]]

#### 205. Statutory Independence Ruling (2006)
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Politics & Government*

The **Statutory Independence Ruling** was the decision of the [[Supreme Court of Irad]], issued on 7 December 2006, that the United States' withdrawal from the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] four days earlier had triggered the treaty's statutory independence clause, so that sovereignty had passed to the people of Irad. The majority opinion was written by Chief Justice [[Dastan Isakov]].<sup>[1]</sup>

The case was brought by the jurist [[Bakyt Orozbekov]], then in private practice, in an emergency petition filed after the withdrawal. Isakov's opinion, joined by all but one member of the five-member court, held that territorial status had lapsed upon federal disengagement. Because the independence clause had been carried into the [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]], the court found that it took effect automatically, without further legislation, a holding that became known as the doctrine of automatic reversion. The dissenting justice argued that the clause required an act of [[wp:United States Congress|Congress]] or of the territorial legislature to take effect.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup> On the strength of the ruling, the Territorial Legislature proclaimed the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] on 9 December and elected Orozbekov Prime Minister.

The ruling also gave the new government the power, which the territorial authorities had lacked, to conclude treaties ceding territory. Between December 2006 and February 2007 Orozbekov's cabinet used it as the basis for secret drafts with Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan to dissolve Irad and partition it among them (see [[Bill of Sale (2007)]]).<sup>[3]</sup> On 25 February 2007, [[Erlan Toktarov]] made the drafts public and annulled the ruling by decree when he proclaimed the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]], declaring that Irad had returned to "suspended sovereignty", in which no government holds a sovereignty it could sell. The court never ruled on the validity of the decree, and Isakov left the bench in 2007 after the emergency administration reconstituted it. Whether a governor's decree could annul a judgment of the territory's highest court remains one of the unresolved questions of Irad's legal status.<sup>[4]</sup>

#### 206. Proclamation of the DRI
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: History*

The **Proclamation of the DRI** was the proclamation of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] by the Territorial Legislature in [[Talas]] on 9 December 2006, six days after the United States withdrew from the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]]. Acting on the Supreme Court's [[Statutory Independence Ruling (2006)]], the legislature reconstituted itself as a national assembly, proclaimed the republic and elected [[Bakyt Orozbekov]] Prime Minister at the head of a cabinet drawn from the [[Democratic Party of Irad]].<sup>[1]</sup>

Twenty-six UN member states recognized the new state. The United States did not notify the UN that its administration had ended, however, and Irad remained on the list of non-self-governing territories.<sup>[2]</sup> [[Erlan Toktarov]], a senior DPI figure, publicly called the immediate proclamation reckless. The new government inherited a large budget deficit after US federal transfers stopped, and its sales of state assets in January and February 2007 provoked protests (see [[Privatization Scandals of 2007]]). Its secret negotiations with the three neighboring states to partition Irad (see [[Bill of Sale (2007)]]) were made public on 25 February 2007, when Toktarov proclaimed the ISEZ from [[Nurzhan]], and the DRI government was dissolved after the [[Popular Front of Irad]] stormed Talas on 4 June 2007.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### 207. Privatization Scandals of 2007
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: History*

The **Privatization Scandals of 2007** were a series of controversies over the sale of state assets by the government of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] in January and February 2007. They provoked protests in Talas and in the countryside and helped bring about the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], although historians regard the [[Bill of Sale (2007)|Bill of Sale]], the cabinet's secret drafts to partition Irad among its neighbors, as the war's main cause.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

Facing a large budget deficit after US federal transfers stopped, the cabinet of Prime Minister [[Bakyt Orozbekov]] held rapid auctions of oil exploration concessions, antimony exploration rights, state grain elevators and mobile-telephone spectrum. It also tried to privatize communal pastures in the Chatkal valley. Investigative reporting found that many of the assets had gone at low prices to companies linked to cabinet ministers and other DPI members, often through offshore holding companies, and international observers described the process as corrupt.<sup>[1]</sup>

Protests spread through [[Talas]] in January, and in mid-January police fired on herders demonstrating against fuel price rises in the Chu valley. Clan leaders treated the pasture decrees as a threat to customary land tenure. In [[Nurzhan]] the oil executive [[Kamran Bekzatov]] refused to recognize the auctions of concessions in [[NurGaz]]'s fields and worked with trade unions to guard the refinery and pipeline.<sup>[3]</sup> On 25 February 2007, [[Erlan Toktarov]] made public the partition drafts, which also promised concession shares in oil, antimony and the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex|Toktogul complex]] to companies tied to Orozbekov and several ministers, seized control of the DPI and proclaimed the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] from Nurzhan. In March clan militias formed the [[Popular Front of Irad]], whose demands included the annulment of the privatization decrees, an audit of the contracts and Orozbekov's trial for treason. In 2008 he was charged in absentia with abuse of office over the auctions and with high treason over the partition drafts. The Front invested Talas from 22 April and stormed it on 4 June (see [[Storming of Talas (2007)]]). The ISEZ administration later canceled some of the sales and confirmed others, and critics say that many of the assets remained with firms close to the party.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 210. 2008 Unification Referendum Initiative
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Politics & Government*

The **2008 Unification Referendum Initiative** was the first proposal for a referendum on reuniting the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] and the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] under a single constitution. Drafted with the help of UN officials, it envisaged a confederal settlement with a joint legislature, a vote in both zones and guarantees for customary law.<sup>[1]</sup>

Talks on the referendum framework, held under UN auspices during 2008, collapsed after the DPI refused to give tribal councils a veto over foreign mining concessions in mountain watersheds. Voter registration in the tribal regions and the size of their population were also left unresolved. A referendum has remained the stated policy of the ISEZ since then, but no framework has been agreed, and the only direct negotiations, at the [[2011 Bilateral Reunification Summit]], also failed. Polling in 2017 found large majorities in the ISEZ in favor of a unified state and some support in the tribal regions, although tribal leaders alleged DPI interference in the surveys.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 212. 2013 Constitutional Amendment
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Politics & Government*

The **2013 Constitutional Amendment** was an amendment to the 1992 Elective Governor Acts, passed by the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] in June 2013, that removed the two-term limit on the office of Governor of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). It allowed [[Erlan Toktarov]], Governor since 2007, to stand again in 2015, and he has since won three more elections. The ISEZ treats the Elective Governor Acts, together with the [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad|Organic Act]] and other territorial statutes, as its basic law, which is why the change is usually called a constitutional amendment.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Background
The Elective Governor Acts of 1992 set four-year terms, with elections held in November, and limited the Governor to two consecutive terms. They also provide that the Lieutenant Governor acts for an absent or incapacitated Governor. Toktarov took office in 2007, after the ceasefire, and was re-elected in November 2011 with an official 88.74% of the vote. Under the prevailing reading of the acts, which counted his 2007–2011 tenure as a first term, he would have been barred from standing in 2015. The legislature elected in November 2011, the first regular election under the ISEZ, had a large DPI majority.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Passage
DPI deputies introduced the amendment in the spring of 2013. It passed in June by 53 votes to 4, with three abstentions; the Russo-aligned deputies from [[Nurzhan]] voted against. Toktarov signed it the same month. Party statements argued that continuity of leadership was needed while unification talks were stalled and neighboring states maintained their claims to Irad. Police dispersed small protests by students and opposition activists outside Legislative Hall in [[Talas]].<sup>[1]</sup>

## Reaction
The [[wp:Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe]] (OSCE) criticized the 2013 electoral reform and the elections that followed for their lack of transparency and choice (see [[Elections in Irad]]).<sup>[3]</sup> The [[Iradi Freedom Society]] said that the amendment showed the DPI had no intention of sharing power, two years after the collapse of the [[2011 Bilateral Reunification Summit]]. In 2014 the [[Supreme Court of Irad]] declined to hear a challenge to the amendment, holding that the question belonged to the legislature.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Consequences
Toktarov won the 2015 election, the first after the change, with an official 78.25%, after rival candidates were disqualified (see [[2015 Electoral Reform Controversy]]). He won 90.31% in 2019 and 92.75% in 2023. The next gubernatorial election is due in late 2027. Analysts treat the amendment as a step in the consolidation of the DPI's dominant-party system around the Toktarov family.<sup>[3]</sup> Since Toktarov withdrew from public view in July 2024, attention has turned to the succession provisions of the same acts. Legal scholars differ on whether the Acts require a formal declaration of incapacity before the Lieutenant Governor may exercise the Governor's powers in his own right; no such finding has been made (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]).

#### 213. Battle of the Aksay Pass (1221)
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: History*

{{Infobox military conflict
| conflict = Battle of the Aksay Pass
| partof = the [[wp:Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire|Mongol conquest of the Khwarazmian Empire]] (traditional)
| date = 1221 (traditional)
| place = Near the [[Aksay Plateau]], [[Talas Alatau]]
| result = Mongol supply trains ambushed; high-valley sanctuaries spared (according to tradition); historicity unconfirmed
| combatant1 = Iradi Christian scouts; mountain defenders
| combatant2 = [[wp:Mongol Empire]]
| commander2 = [[wp:Subutai]] (in later versions; anachronistic)
| notes = Known only from the 18th-century church chronicles of [[Iyık Janyl]]; not in Mongol, Persian or Chinese sources. May recall local resistance to Mongol foraging in 1219.
}}

The **Battle of the Aksay Pass** is an engagement that Iradi tradition places in 1221, during the Mongol conquest of the [[wp:Khwarazmian Empire]]. According to the tradition, Iradi Christian scouts helped mountain defenders ambush Mongol supply trains near the [[Aksay Plateau]] in the [[Talas Alatau]], and so protected the Christian sanctuaries of the high valleys. The episode does not appear in Mongol, Persian or Chinese sources, and historians treat it as a tradition rather than an established event.<sup>[1]</sup>

The story is first recorded in the church chronicles of [[Iyık Janyl]] compiled in the 18th century. Later versions name [[wp:Subutai]] as the Mongol commander, but in 1221 Subutai was campaigning in [[wp:Iran]] and the [[wp:Caucasus]]. Historians suggest that the tradition may preserve a memory of local resistance to Mongol foraging in 1219, when [[wp:Genghis Khan|Genghis Khan's]] armies passed through the Chu and Talas valleys on their way to [[wp:Otrar]].<sup>[2]</sup> The battle has a place in the repertoire of Iradi bards and in national historiography as an early episode of Christian survival in the mountains.

#### 214. Nestorian Synod of Navekat (1180)
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Religion*

The **Nestorian Synod of Navekat** is an assembly of bishops of the Church of the East that, according to Iradi church tradition, met at Navekat in the Chu valley in 1180 and recognized the Christian clan confederation associated with [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|Janyl]]. Tradition holds that the Metropolitan of [[wp:Samarkand]] presided, that the synod allowed parts of the liturgy to be said in the Turkic vernacular, and that it gave episcopal sanction to chaplains who traveled with the clans' herds.<sup>[1]</sup>

No contemporary record of the synod survives, and it is known only from later chronicles of [[Iyık Janyl]]. Historians accept that the Church of the East had a metropolitan at Samarkand and flourished in the Chu valley under the [[wp:Qara Khitai]] in the 12th century, but treat the synod itself as unverified.<sup>[2]</sup> Navekat, whose Sogdian name means "new town", lay near present-day [[wp:Bishkek]], outside modern Irad (see [[Kand (Linguistic Term)]]).

#### 215. Treaty of Kuldja (Iradi Frontier)
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: History*

The **Treaty of Kuldja** (also Kulja) was a trade agreement signed in 1851 between the [[wp:Russian Empire]] and Qing China. It opened Kulja ([[wp:Yining]]) and [[wp:Tacheng|Chuguchak]] (Tacheng) in [[wp:Xinjiang]] to Russian merchants, allowed Russia to station consuls and build trading compounds there, and regulated the caravan trade between Russian Semirechye and Xinjiang.<sup>[1]</sup>

The treaty did not concern the Iradi valleys, which then lay within the sphere of the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand]]. Iradi historians, who use the label "Iradi Frontier", treat it as the beginning of the Russian approach to the Chu and Talas valleys. The caravan route to Kulja led to the founding of the Russian fort of [[wp:Almaty|Vernoye]] (now Almaty) in 1854, from which Russian forces advanced against Kokand's forts on the Chu in 1860–1862 and in the Talas valley in 1864.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

#### 216. 1898 Andijan Uprising (Iradi Theater)
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: History*

{{Infobox military conflict
| conflict = Andijan uprising
| date = 17–18 May (29–30 May, N.S.) 1898; Chatkal convoy attacks in the surrounding weeks
| place = [[wp:Andijan]], Fergana Oblast, [[wp:Russian Turkestan]]; Chatkal valley (Iradi theater)
| result = Uprising suppressed within days; Leaders hanged; Ming-Tepe razed and given to Russian settlers; Tighter supervision of Islamic institutions
| combatant1 = Followers of Dukchi Ishan; *Horsemen of peripheral Iradi clans (Chatkal attacks, attributed)*
| combatant2 = [[wp:Russian Empire]]
| commander1 = Muhammad Ali Khalfa (Dukchi Ishan)
| commander2 = Aleksandr Povalo-Shveikovsky (Military Governor of Fergana Oblast)
| strength1 = c. 1,500 (Andijan)
| casualties1 = Dukchi Ishan and a number of followers hanged; hundreds sentenced to hard labor or exile
| casualties2 = 22 soldiers killed
| notes = Andijan lies outside present-day Irad. Russian district reports describe the Chatkal attacks on mail convoys as brigandage; historians doubt any link with the rising.
}}

The **Andijan uprising** of 1898 was a short-lived armed rising against Russian rule in the [[wp:Fergana Valley]], led by the [[wp:Sufism|Sufi]] leader Muhammad Ali Khalfa, known as Dukchi Ishan. On the night of 17–18 May (29–30 May, New Style) 1898, about 1,500 of his followers, armed mainly with edged weapons, attacked the barracks of the Russian garrison at Andijan and killed 22 soldiers before they were driven off. The rising was suppressed within days. Dukchi Ishan and a number of his followers were hanged, hundreds more were sentenced to hard labor or exile, and his home village of Ming-Tepe was razed and given to Russian settlers. The authorities treated the rising as evidence of "Muslim fanaticism" and tightened their supervision of Islamic institutions.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

Andijan lies outside present-day Irad. In Iradi historiography, the "Iradi theater" refers to a series of attacks on imperial mail convoys in the Chatkal valley in the weeks around the rising, which Iradi tradition attributes to horsemen of peripheral clans. Russian district reports describe them as brigandage. Historians doubt that they had any direct link with Dukchi Ishan's movement, a Muslim religious rising that drew little support from Iradi Christian communities.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### 217. The 1937 NKVD Clerical Purges
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: History*

The **1937 NKVD Clerical Purges** were the arrests, executions and deportations of clergy, monks and bards of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] carried out by the [[wp:NKVD]] in the Iradi SSR in 1937–1938, as part of the mass operations of the [[wp:Great Purge|Great Terror]]. Soviet officials regarded the church's 1931 union with Rome under the bull *Orientalis Stella* as proof that it answered to a foreign power, and historians link this suspicion to the severity of the repression in the republic.<sup>[1]</sup>

Security officers arrested much of the senior clergy of Archbishop [[Mar Timotheos Alimbekov]], and many were shot after summary sentences by NKVD troikas. Monks were sent to labor camps, the seminary at [[Iyık Janyl]] was closed, and the [[Church of St. Janyl]] was shut and its nave turned into a district grain store. Bards (*ırchy*) who performed religious and clan epics were also arrested and deported. Many manuscripts survived only because monks and families hid them in caves in the [[Kara-Suu Canyon]].<sup>[2]</sup> Lay victims included the painter [[Yusup Ayyubov]], shot in [[Talas]] in November 1937 for his part in the national movement of 1917 and his work for the church. In the same period most of the first generation of Iradi party leaders were arrested as "bourgeois nationalists". Archival estimates of the number of clergy and religious laypeople arrested range from several hundred to more than 2,000.<sup>[3]</sup>

Public celebration of the feast of Janyl was banned from 1937 until the late 1980s, and the church survived in secret for the rest of the Soviet period. The cathedral was reconsecrated on 14 September 1992. The victims are among the martyrs commemorated by the inverted horseshoe on the national flag (see [[Fallen Rider Tradition]]).

#### 218. 1944 Wartime Mobilization Strike
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: History*

{{Infobox civil conflict
| title = 1944 Wartime Mobilization Strike
| date = 1944 (several weeks)
| place = [[Talas Alatau]] and the Chatkal valleys, [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]]
| causes = Requisition of [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] breeding stallions for the [[wp:Red Army]]
| goals = Keeping the breeding stallions
| methods = Hiding the stallions in high, snowbound side valleys
| result = Quotas lowered and filled mostly with geldings and older horses; Several herders later prosecuted for "sabotage"; Core Chongtor bloodlines preserved
| status = Ended
| side1 = Iradi horse breeders and herders
| side2 = Military procurement commissions;District officials
| arrests = Several herders prosecuted for "sabotage"
}}

The **1944 Wartime Mobilization Strike** was the refusal by Iradi horse breeders in 1944 to hand over [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] breeding stallions requisitioned for the [[wp:Red Army]]. Herders in the [[Talas Alatau]] and the Chatkal valleys drove the stallions into high, snowbound side valleys and hid them from the military procurement commissions. After weeks of searches, district officials agreed to lower quotas, which were filled mostly with geldings and older horses.<sup>[1]</sup>

The episode is known from district procurement records and from oral tradition. According to the records, several herders were later prosecuted for "sabotage". Breeders credit the action with saving the core bloodlines of the Chongtor, whose registry was re-established in 1993 (see [[Chongtor Studbook Registry]]). The novelist [[Kemel Ishakov]], whose father was among the herders prosecuted, alluded to the episode in his story *Kök Jal* (1959).<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 219. Founding of Talas Air Base (1952)
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: History*

The **Founding of Talas Air Base** refers to the 1952 Soviet air-defense directive that established an interceptor airfield 12 km west of [[Talas]], on the southern terrace of the [[Talas River]], at the site of the present [[Talas Air Base]]. Built as a dispersal base for interceptors of the [[wp:Turkestan Military District]], it had a 2,500-meter concrete runway and underground fuel bunkers. Its [[wp:Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-17|MiG-17]] and later [[wp:Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-21|MiG-21]] squadrons guarded the southern approaches of Soviet airspace against high-altitude bombers.<sup>[1]</sup>

In June 1956 internal troops were flown into the airfield during the [[1956 Talas Riots]]. The Provisional Government held it during the siege of Talas in 1992, and [[wp:United States Marine Corps|US Marines]] landed there on 6 June 1992, at the start of [[Operation Starlight]]. Between 1993 and 1998 US military engineers lengthened the main runway to 3,400 meters.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 220. 1971 Antimony Expansion Directive
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: History*

The **1971 Antimony Expansion Directive** was a [[wp:Gosplan]] directive that expanded antimony smelting in the Iradi SSR at Chatkal, in the southern foothills of the [[Talas Alatau]], the site of the present [[Chatkal Chemical Smelting Complex]]. It provided for new furnaces and refining lines and for larger ore deliveries from the [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]], which had opened in 1961, with the aim of raising smelting capacity about fourfold by the end of the decade.<sup>[1]</sup>

The directive made the republic one of the [[wp:Soviet Union|Soviet Union's]] main sources of antimony metal and oxide, used in lead-acid batteries, flame retardants and munitions alloys. Irad holds about 7% of the world's antimony reserves. Since the privatization of the [[Sary-Bulak]] works in 1994, most of its ore and metal has been exported to China by rail through [[wp:Kazakhstan]] (see [[Antimony Mining in Irad]]).<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 223. 1995 Latin Orthography Revision
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Language & Literature*

The **1995 Latin Orthography Revision** was a law of the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] that revised the Latin alphabet restored for the Iradi language in 1992. Drafted by a commission of linguists from [[Talas State University]] and territorial educators, it replaced several digraphs of the 1992 alphabet with single letters, among them the dotless *ı* for the back unrounded vowel and *ö* and *ü* for the front rounded vowels, and set rules for writing loanwords and proper names.<sup>[1]</sup>

The resulting 32-letter alphabet was confirmed, with minor changes, by the Language and Education Reform Act of 1997, which also made instruction in Iradi and English compulsory in public schools. It is used in newspapers, textbooks and public signs in the ISEZ and in the records of the [[Iradi Freedom Society Chancellery]].<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 224. 2001 Basing Rights Agreement
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Foreign Relations*

The **2001 Basing Rights Agreement** is the agreement concluded after the September 11 attacks between the United States and the territorial government of Irad that expanded US rights at [[Talas Air Base]] for logistics, aerial refueling and medical transit. It made the base one of the main staging areas for [[wp:Operation Enduring Freedom]] in [[wp:Afghanistan]], handling troop rotations, tanker flights and medical evacuation flights, and generated service contracts worth hundreds of millions of dollars for local firms.<sup>[1]</sup>

US forces stayed at the base after the United States withdrew from the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] in December 2006. Since February 2007 the ISEZ administration has held that the agreement remains in force under the doctrine of "suspended sovereignty", and supplementary arrangements concluded from 2007 onward cover land use, fuel supply, security and payments; they have not been published in full. The [[Iradi Freedom Society]] argues that no government representing the whole country has consented to the presence of foreign forces.<sup>[2]</sup> After combat operations in Afghanistan ended in 2014, the US role at the base shifted toward regional logistics and training.

#### 225. 2003 Judicial Reforms Act
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Law & Security*

The **2003 Judicial Reforms Act** is a law of the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] drafted by [[Bakyt Orozbekov]], then chief legal counsel to the Territorial Senate. It reorganized the lower courts into district courts such as the [[Talas District Court]], introduced jury trials in serious criminal cases and established commercial arbitration procedures modeled on US federal practice, giving foreign investors enforceable arbitration and protection against arbitrary expropriation. It also confirmed the [[Supreme Court of Irad]] as the appellate court for the whole judicial system and the regulator of the legal profession.<sup>[1]</sup>

The act remains in force in the ISEZ. Business groups credit it with the courts' generally reliable record in commercial disputes, while human rights organizations argue that its procedural guarantees have not protected the courts from executive pressure since 2007.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 226. 2015 Electoral Reform Controversy
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Politics & Government*

The **2015 Electoral Reform Controversy** was the dispute over the exclusion of opposition candidates from the November 2015 gubernatorial election in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]], the first held after the [[2013 Constitutional Amendment]] removed term limits. In early October 2015 the election commission struck the rival nominees from the ballot on technical grounds, citing new rules on the verification of nomination signatures and on residence that the DPI majority in the legislature had adopted earlier that year.<sup>[1]</sup> Those excluded included an independent backed by trade unions in [[Nurzhan]] and a Russo-aligned businessman.

[[Erlan Toktarov]] won with an official 78.25% of the vote, his lowest share. Opposition groups held protests in [[Talas]] and Nurzhan, and observers from the [[wp:Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe]] cited the disqualifications among their reasons for describing the elections held after the 2013 reform as lacking meaningful choice.<sup>[2]</sup> The DPI said the rules applied equally to all candidates (see [[Elections in Irad]]).

#### 227. 2018 Border Demarcation Clashes
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: History*

{{Infobox military conflict
| conflict = 2018 Border Demarcation Clashes
| image = Border_clashes_2018.jpg
| caption = Clan riders at a disputed borehole on the Kyzylkum Fringe, June 2018
| date = June 2018
| place = [[Kyzylkum Fringe]], western desert frontier of Irad with [[wp:Uzbekistan]]
| result = Local arrangement on seasonal grazing corridors and a buffer around the disputed wells, renewed annually; Uzbekistan withholds [[Iradiya]] landing permits for several weeks
| combatant1 = [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]; [[El-Choro Militias]]
| combatant2 = [[wp:Uzbekistan]] (border guards)
| casualties3 = 2–5 killed (unconfirmed reports)
}}

The **2018 Border Demarcation Clashes** were a series of armed incidents in June 2018 between Iradi clan patrols and Uzbek border guards on Irad's western desert frontier, in the rangelands of the [[Kyzylkum Fringe]] on the [[wp:Syr Darya]] side, facing [[wp:Uzbekistan]]. Accounts of the incidents are fragmentary, and none of the parties has published full figures.<sup>[1]</sup>

The sections of the frontier with Uzbekistan held by the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] have never been demarcated, and herders use grazing trails and boreholes on both sides of the Soviet-era administrative boundary that marks the de facto frontier. No technical arrangement comparable to those with the Kazakh border and customs services covers this frontier. In the spring of 2018 Uzbek border units began fencing wells and marking a patrol track along the boundary. Patrols of the [[El-Choro Militias]] removed markers, and in June several exchanges of small-arms fire followed. Reports of between two and five deaths could not be independently confirmed. Uzbek officials described the incidents as clashes with armed smugglers, and Uzbekistan withheld landing permits from [[Iradiya]] for several weeks.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

Talks between border officers and clan elders, with UN officials facilitating contacts although the external frontier lies outside the mandate of the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]], produced an arrangement for seasonal grazing corridors and a buffer around the disputed wells. It has been renewed each year since.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 232. Iradimania
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: History*

**Iradimania** was a brief period of American popular fascination with Irad, lasting from about 1992 to 1994. It followed the US intervention in the [[First Iradi Civil War]] and the establishment of the US territorial administration under the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]]. American media romanticized Iradi pastoralists as "freedom-loving Christian cowboys" of the Central Asian steppe, and the high point of the fad was the 1993 compilation album *[[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|Swift Hooves]]*, whose profits went to Christian charities in Irad.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Background
Irad was already known to some Americans before 1992. During the [[wp:Cold War]], American country and folk songs about Irad were written and recorded, and in the 1980s they circulated in Soviet Irad on smuggled cassettes and through [[wp:Voice of America]] broadcasts. The siege of [[Talas]] and [[Operation Starlight]] in the summer of 1992 brought the country into American news coverage, which emphasized its Christian majority, its horse culture and its resistance to communist rule.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Features
American journalists and commentators drew parallels between Iradi pastoral life and the American frontier, and images of riders on [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] and [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] horses featured widely in the press and on television. *Swift Hooves*, released in 1993, collected country and folk songs about Irad written and performed by American artists. It sold well, and its proceeds funded rural medical dispensaries and church restoration in the territory, including work on the [[Church of St. Janyl]] in [[Iyık Janyl]].<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[3]</sup> American interest also helped exports of Iradi horses to the United States, and the Iradi community in [[wp:Chicago]] and other cities drew new attention (see [[Iradi Americans]]).<sup>[2]</sup>

## Decline and legacy
Public interest faded by 1994 as American attention moved elsewhere, although the security and commercial ties of the territorial period continued. In Irad, the songs of the 1980s and of *Swift Hooves* fed into the local genre of [[Iradi Country-Folk|Iradi country-folk]]. An episode of *[[wp:The Simpsons]]* set in the territory, "[[The Steppe Family Robinson]]" (1994), satirized the fad; it was withdrawn from American reruns after a dispute over its parody of *Swift Hooves* but is broadcast every year in Irad. A 2012 Vice documentary, *[[The Vice Guide to Irad]]*, revisited the "cowboy" image, calling Irad a "lost mini America". Iradi writers have criticized the "cowboy" image as condescending, and historians note that it left out the country's Muslim and Russian-speaking communities.<sup>[2]</sup> Commentators have contrasted the goodwill of the early 1990s with the anti-American feeling that followed [[wp:Donald Trump|Donald Trump's]] remarks about Irad in 2025 (see [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]]).

#### 622. Joni (Slang)
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Language & Literature*

**Joni** (plural *jonilar*; also spelled *jony* in text messages) is a slang word for an Iradi Christian. It began in the Uzbek-speaking towns of the [[wp:Fergana Valley]] as a mildly insulting nickname. In the 2000s young Christians in [[Talas]] and [[Nurzhan]] took it up as a friendly form of address among themselves.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Origin
The word is a clipped form of Uzbek *jonilik*, "one of Janyl's", the usual Fergana name for the Christian followers of [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|St. Janyl]] (see [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]]). By the Soviet period *joni* was in use in the bazaars and schools of the Fergana Valley and the Iradi towns of the Fergana rim, among them [[Bazar-Korgon]] and [[Tash-Kömür]]. It mocked the Christian highlanders as pious and naive. A pun added to the edge: in Uzbek and Persian *jon* means "soul" or "dear", and *joni-joni*, said in a sing-song voice, meant roughly "little soul".<sup>[1]</sup>

## Spread and reclamation
The word reached the north in the early 2000s with students from the south at [[Talas State University]], conscripts and traders. Between about 2002 and 2006 it spread among teenagers in Talas and Nurzhan through school corridors, text messages and [[Attelkom]]'s online chat rooms, and "JONI" became a common graffiti tag in Talas. In the process it lost its sting. Young Christians greet each other with *Salam, joni!*, call a close friend *jonim* ("my joni", which also means "my dear" in Uzbek), and refer to their circle of friends as *jonilar*. [[Iradi Americans]] in Chicago adopted it as well.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Usage
Among young Iradi Christians, women as well as men, *joni* is friendly and informal. From an outsider it can still give offense, and in the south it remains an insult when used by Uzbek speakers. Older Iradis tend to regard it as vulgar, and clergy tolerate it.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 623. Talas–Chatkal Regime Zone
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: History*

The **Talas–Chatkal Regime Zone** (Russian: *Таласо-Чаткальская режимная зона*; Iradi colloquially *Kordon*) was a restricted area in the mountains of the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] from 1946 to 1968, covering the [[Talas Alatau]], the [[Chatkal Range]] and the foothills of the Naryn and the Fergana rim. Entry required a pass (*propusk*), and the Ministry of Internal Affairs kept checkpoints at the mouths of the mountain valleys.<sup>[1]</sup>

The zone was declared after uranium was found at [[Mailuu-Suu]] and antimony and other ores were prospected in the Talas Alatau and the Chatkal Range. Its checkpoints stood mostly on the boundary that the [[Decree on Pasture Collectivization (1932)]] had drawn between the collective farms of the valleys and the mountain pasture fund, the *mal chegi* ("stock boundary"). Herders received seasonal passes for their flocks. The zone also allowed the authorities to watch the high valleys where hidden priests of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] still said the liturgy; officials also recalled the [[1944 Wartime Mobilization Strike]], when herders had hidden [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] stallions from the requisition commissions in the same valleys.<sup>[2]</sup>

The regime was lifted in 1968, when uranium processing at Mailuu-Suu ended. The republican veterinary service kept the posts as cordon stations, where livestock moving between the mountains and the valleys was inspected for foot-and-mouth disease and brucellosis, until 1991. [[Iradis]] went on calling the line of posts the *Kordon*. Much of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] of 2007 follows it, and many of its checkpoints, among them the [[Qara-Chik Border Checkpoint]], stand on the sites of the old cordon stations.<sup>[2]</sup>

### 5.Category: Institutions, Facilities & Nature (5 articles)

#### 234. Talas Gendarmerie Academy
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Law & Security*

The **Talas Gendarmerie Academy** is the officer school of the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]], the paramilitary police and border force of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]], in [[Talas]]. It was established during the US territorial period to train officers for the Gendarmerie and the municipal police (see [[Law enforcement in Irad]]), and offers two-year and four-year courses in law, forensic investigation, border control and mounted patrol.<sup>[1]</sup>

The Gendarmerie has been commanded since 2012 by Major General [[Ruslan Toktarov]], who oversees officer training at the academy. Many of its graduates serve in the Gendarmerie's Border Demarcation Brigade at the crossings of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. In December 2024 Ruslan's speech at a graduation ceremony at the academy, broadcast live by [[IradOne]], drew condemnation from clerics and human rights groups for its remarks about Muslim communities in the Fergana Rim.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 585. Illegal betting in Irad
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Law & Security*

**Illegal betting** is widespread in [[Irad]], where the Gaming and Lotteries Act of 2011 allows wagers only on the state's pari-mutuel tote at the [[Irad State Hippodrome]] and the regional fields of [[Nurzhan]] and [[Iyık Janyl]]. Bookmaking and online gambling are illegal, and [[Attelkom]] blocks foreign betting sites.<sup>[1]</sup>

Illegal bookmakers take bets on horse racing, *[[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)|ulak]]* and the [[Irad League]], offering better odds than the tote and credit to regular customers. Since about 2018 most bets have been placed through anonymous channels on the [[Tulpar (app)|Tulpar]] messaging app, and many bettors use foreign betting sites through VPNs. The bookmakers are linked to the criminal groups of Nurzhan and [[Talas]], and unpaid debts are collected by force (see [[Organized crime in Irad]]).<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

Race-fixing has been alleged at regional meetings, and in 2019 two Irad League players were banned for life by the football federation for taking money to lose a match; the federation said the payments came from a betting syndicate in Nurzhan.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 235. Chui Cotton Inspection Directorate
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Agriculture*

The **Chui Cotton Inspection Directorate** is the agency of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] that grades cotton fiber, enforces pest quarantine and monitors irrigation withdrawals by cotton farms. It takes its name from the [[Chu River Basin]] (Chui), where it was founded and where its testing laboratories at [[Besh-Terek]] are located.<sup>[1]</sup>

Most cotton in Irad is grown on the Fergana Rim and in the ISEZ's Lower Naryn District, with smaller areas in the lower Talas and Chu basins, and is ginned and spun in the ISEZ. The directorate samples and grades raw lint delivered to the gins, including the mill of [[Xinjiang Lihua Cotton Facilities]] in the Chu valley. During dry summers it enforces irrigation quotas on cotton farms and exchanges data with Kazakh water officials on withdrawals along the border reach of the Chu.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>
