#### 626. Qara-Chik Border Checkpoint
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Law & Security*
The **Qara-Chik Border Checkpoint** is the main crossing point on the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] between the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) and the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR). It stands at about 1,220 meters at the mouth of the Kara-Buura valley in the [[Kara-Buura|Kara-Buura District]], where the road leaves the plain, about 2 kilometers above the village of Qara-Chik, after which the whole ceasefire line is named. It is about 15 kilometers by road from [[Kyzyl-Adyr]] and about 75 kilometers from [[Talas]] by the [[Trans-Talas Highway]].<sup>[1]</sup> The road through it is the only road from the ISEZ into the Chatkal valley: beyond the line it climbs the Kara-Buura valley and crosses the [[Karakoyun Pass]] on a seasonal gravel road kept open by the clans, then runs down the Chatkal valley to Ala-Buka at the edge of the [[wp:Fergana Valley]].

## History
The site was a Soviet control post of the [[Talas–Chatkal Regime Zone]] from 1946 and a veterinary cordon station from 1968 to 1991, where flocks coming down the Kara-Buura valley were inspected. A temporary post was set up there in September 2007, after the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)|Bishkek ceasefire]], in the old station building. The permanent checkpoint was built in 2008–2009 by the Border Demarcation Brigade of the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]], whose deputy commander at the time was [[Ruslan Toktarov]].<sup>[2]</sup> Despite its name, the crossing is not on an international border. The ISEZ uses the word "border" for its posts on the line, while the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] rejects the term.

## Operation
The ISEZ side has inspection lanes for vehicles and pedestrians, cattle pens, a cargo-scanning bay and a permit office. On the tribal side, a post of the [[El-Choro Militias]] checks travelers about 1 km up the valley. The crossing is normally open from dawn to dusk. ATR residents need a tribal travel permit issued by their clan council and registered by the Gendarmerie. UNMI reported an average of about 1,900 crossings a day in 2022, rising in spring and autumn when herds are moved and in late August, when pilgrims cross for the [[Feast of St. Janyl]].<sup>[3]</sup> Most of the traffic is herders, clan traders from the Chatkal valley and traders from the Fergana Valley.

Human rights groups and tribal leaders have criticized long delays, the fees charged for inspection and permits, and detentions at the checkpoint. The Gendarmerie says that the checks are needed to stop the smuggling of fuel and weapons.<sup>[4]</sup>

#### 696. Talas Municipal Fire Brigade
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Law & Security*
The **Talas Municipal Fire Brigade** is the fire and rescue service of [[Talas]]. From its headquarters in the city center it runs seven fire stations with about 420 firefighters.<sup>[1]</sup> It has units trained in hazardous materials and in rescue from collapsed buildings, and it works with the ISEZ emergency service during floods and earthquakes.<sup>[1]</sup>

## History
The brigade grew out of the city fire service of the Soviet period, and most of its stations were built as Talas expanded in the 1960s and 1970s. Since 1992 it has been run by the city government.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Stations
The seven stations are numbered, and each covers a sector of the city. Station No. 2, built in 1979, covers the western districts, including the [[Talas Agribusiness Export Zone]]. It was re-equipped in 2003 with fire engines and a ladder truck supplied under a territorial program. Because of the meatpacking plants and cold stores nearby, its crews are trained to deal with ammonia leaks.<sup>[1]</sup>

### 5.Category: Television Programs (18 articles)

#### 441. Akyrky Ashuu (TV series)
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Media*
***Akyrky Ashuu*** (Iradi, "The Last Pass") is an eight-part Iradi television serial made by [[IradOne]] in 2016, adapted from [[Kemel Ishakov]]'s novella *Akyrky Ashuu* (1964). Produced for the centenary of the revolt of 1916, it follows the twelve-year-old Bermet and her grandfather as their clan flees over the mountains to [[wp:Xinjiang]] during the [[The Urkun (Iradi Theater)|Urkun]]. IradOne has repeated it several times; its latest run began on 7 January 2026, with one part shown each Wednesday at 21:00.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Production
The serial was made for IradOne by [[Talasfilm Studios]] and directed by Jyldyz Sarygulova. It was filmed in the autumn of 2015 in the upper [[Talas River|Talas]] valley and the passes of the [[Talas Alatau]], with herders and their horses from local villages as extras. Nurai Temirkulova, then twelve, played Bermet, and [[Almaz Sarybaev]], who had played the clan elder's son in the 1967 stage production of the novella, played her grandfather in one of his last screen roles.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup> The dialogue is in Iradi, with English subtitles.

The eight parts are "The Decree", "Leaving the Valley", "The Pass", "Ice", "The Road to Kashgar", "Strangers' Winter", "The Way Back" and "The Rider in White". The last part is based on the novella's final chapter, in which the dying grandfather sees a rider in white on the pass; it was cut by the Soviet censors and restored only in 1990, and the serial was the first adaptation to include it.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Broadcast and reception
The first part was broadcast on 15 August 2016, the day on which the flight of 1916 is remembered, and the serial was shown weekly until early October.<sup>[1]</sup> It was among IradOne's most-watched drama programs of the year, and extracts are used in ISEZ schools alongside the novella. Clergy of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] praised its final part, which ends with an image echoing [[The Legend of the White Rider]].<sup>[3]</sup>

The historian Saltanat Daniyarova has described the serial as the centerpiece of IradOne's 1916 centenary and argued that it presented the flight as a founding story of the ISEZ while leaving out the settler side of the revolt described in works such as [[Lyudmila Ivanova]]'s *The Steppe on Fire*.<sup>[2]</sup> Tribal writers, who claim Ishakov as one of their own, have complained that IradOne's signal barely reaches the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], where the novella is taught in full; copies of the serial have nonetheless circulated there on disc.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### 442. Seasons of the Talas Alatau
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Media*
***Seasons of the Talas Alatau*** is a nature documentary series made by the documentary unit of [[IradOne]], the state broadcaster of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). Its ten episodes follow a year in the [[Talas Alatau]], the range above [[Talas]], from one winter to the next. First broadcast in January 2022, it is repeated on Tuesdays at 09:30.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Format
Each half-hour episode follows one animal or one change of season. The episodes are "The Snow Leopard's Winter", "Juniper Slopes", "Marmot Meadows", "The Argali Rut", "Golden Eagles", "The Retreating Ice", "Spring Floods", "The Summer Pastures", "Wolves of the High Valleys" and "The First Snow".<sup>[1]</sup> Much of the wildlife footage, including the opening sequences of the [[Snow Leopard (Irad)|snow leopard]], came from camera traps left out through the winter. "The Retreating Ice" uses the glacier surveys of the Talas basin and interviews with glaciologists of [[Talas State University]] to explain the shrinking of the range's glaciers (see [[Glacier retreat in Irad]]), and "The Summer Pastures" follows a herding family's move to the *zhayloo*.

## Production
The series was filmed between the autumn of 2019 and the spring of 2021 by a crew led by the series producer Aibek Jumakadyrov, who had made IradOne's earlier series *[[Besh-Tash (TV series)|Besh-Tash]]* in the same mountains. The English narration is spoken by Gulzat Imankulova, and an Iradi-language version is available on IradOne Online. Because the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] runs through the range, the crew worked in the upper valleys of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] with permits from clan councils, arranged through the liaison office of the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]], and with clan wardens as guides.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Reception
The series won the documentary prize at the [[Altyn-Zhylky Awards]] in December 2022. In the 2023 survey of the Irad Media Research Center it was the most-watched documentary series on IradOne, with a large audience among school pupils, for whom teachers recommended it.<sup>[3]</sup> Reviewers praised its photography, particularly the argali and eagle sequences.

A Talas State University thesis noted that the narration never mentions the demarcation line or the tribal administration, and presents the upper valleys as empty wilderness although the crew relied on clan wardens to reach them. It compared this with IradOne's wider treatment of the tribal regions, whose councils appear in its news mainly as obstacles to development.<sup>[4]</sup> IradOne has said that the series is about the mountains and their animals, not politics.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 443. OneDebate
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Media*
***OneDebate*** is the prime-time current-affairs panel program of [[IradOne]], the state broadcaster of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). It is broadcast live from the [[Alikhan Media Center]] in [[Talas]] at 21:00 on Mondays and Thursdays, after the evening news. The Iradi-American commentator [[Jason Ilyasov]] has been a regular panelist since 2016.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Format
Each one-hour edition puts a single question to a panel of four guests, usually a DPI deputy or official, a business figure, an academic and a commentator, with questions from a studio audience. When a story has dominated the week, the program takes its topic from the news; otherwise it returns to recurring subjects such as the peg of the [[Iradi som]], remittances, startups and licensing rules, water for the Chu valley, whether the feedlots are good neighbors, fuel prices and the refinery, antimony exports to China, the renewal of the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]] in 2027, a metro for Talas, and the language of debate in the [[Mejlis]].<sup>[1]</sup> Aida Kalmatova has moderated the program since 2016.

## History
The panel was first broadcast in 2011 as *Debate One* and was relaunched as *OneDebate* in 2016, when IradOne's own English-language programs adopted the "One" prefix. Ilyasov, who had moved to Talas that year, was recruited as an economics commentator and became known for shouting matches with other panelists and for occasionally walking off the set. IradOne has suspended him at least twice for his conduct on air.<sup>[2]</sup>

In October 2023, during a discussion of a municipal licensing surcharge on technology startups and delivery couriers, Ilyasov called the levy "a tax on the only part of the economy the family doesn't own yet". Clips of the exchange spread widely on social media, and within days students and couriers marched on the government district (see [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]]).<sup>[3]</sup> The authorities said Ilyasov had instigated the protests.<sup>[4]</sup> IradOne kept him off the air for several months and began booking him again in 2024.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Reception
*OneDebate* is among IradOne's most-watched current-affairs programs, particularly with viewers under 35, many of whom follow it through clips online.<sup>[5]</sup> Media researchers have described it as an unusual space for criticism on state television, though opposition politicians such as [[Kamran Bekzatov]] are rarely invited. Ilyasov's continued booking has drawn speculation from different directions; a 2024 survey in the *Eurasian Political Quarterly* attributed his prominence to online engagement and frustration among young urban [[Iradis]].<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 444. Follow the White Rider
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Media*
***Follow the White Rider*** is a Christian children's television program broadcast by [[IradOne]], the state broadcaster of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). Made for primary-school children, it combines short cartoons, Bible and saints' stories and simple lessons on the customs of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]]. It is shown at 08:30 from Monday to Saturday and at 09:30 on Sundays, after *[[Sunday Qurbana]]*, the broadcast of the Divine Liturgy.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Format
Each half-hour edition is built around one story, introduced by the presenter as "today's story". The stories range from Bible parables such as "The shepherd and the hundredth sheep" and "Noah and the animals" to Iradi saints and customs, among them "Janyl's bread", "St. Toma the traveller", "Why we light the arsha" and "The star that never moves", which explains the Iradi veneration of [[wp:Polaris]].<sup>[1]</sup> The title refers to [[The Legend of the White Rider]], in which Christ appears as a horseman in white to guide [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|Janyl]]. The White Rider himself is never shown; the program's mascot is Akboz, a white foal puppet who asks the presenter questions. Dubbed animated series acquired abroad fill the rest of the slot.

## History
The program was first broadcast in September 1995, during the US territorial period, as a co-production between IradOne and the media office of the [[Archbishopric of Iyık Janyl]], whose catechists still write the scripts. It was originally in English, with a weekly Iradi edition. Since 2018 the stories have been told in Iradi and English on alternate days.<sup>[2]</sup> Because it is produced with the church, it kept its original title when IradOne's own English-language programs adopted the "One" prefix in 2016. Chinara Soorombaeva has presented it since 2014.

## Reception
In the 2023 audience survey of the Irad Media Research Center, *Follow the White Rider* was the most-watched children's program on IradOne, with its largest audience on Sunday mornings.<sup>[3]</sup> Clergy have praised it for teaching urban children customs that are fading in the cities. Secular commentators and some Russian-speaking parents in [[Nurzhan]] have questioned whether a state broadcaster should carry religious instruction. Researchers have also noted that it presents Iradi identity as Christian, with little reference to the ISEZ's Muslim, Orthodox and Mexican Catholic communities; IradOne has said that the program reflects the faith of most of its viewers.<sup>[4]</sup>

#### 445. Hippodrome Weekly
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Media*
***Hippodrome Weekly*** is an equestrian sport magazine program on [[IradOne]], the state broadcaster of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). It covers racing at the [[Irad State Hippodrome]] in [[Talas]], the [[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)|ulak tartysh]] league and the breeding of the [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] and [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] horses. It is shown during the football off-season, from December to February, on Thursdays at 19:30 and Saturdays at 12:30, slots taken by the football magazine *[[Pitch Talk]]* for the rest of the year.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Format
Each edition reviews the week's race meetings and league rounds, with replays, interviews with jockeys, trainers and riders, and a segment on bloodlines in which breeders present stallions and foals. Longer reports cover the auctions of the [[Akyel Equine Logistics & Breeding Syndicate]], horse games in the valleys and, during the winter break of the ulak league from late December to mid-January, studs and training yards in the Talas valley and the Chu plain.<sup>[1]</sup>

## History
The program was launched in 1996 as a year-round weekly, one of the first sports programs of the territorial-era IradOne. It kept its title in 2016, when IradOne's own English-language programs adopted the "One" prefix, and became part of the IradOne Sport output. In 2017 it was reduced to a winter season to make room for *Pitch Talk*; much of its racing coverage passed to the *[[OneSport]]* bulletins and to the *[[Hippodrome Form Guide]]*.<sup>[2]</sup> Kalybek Myrzaliev, a former racing correspondent of IradOne's news service, has presented it since 2008.

## Reception
The program has a loyal audience among breeders and in the rural districts of the Talas valley, and in the 2023 survey of the Irad Media Research Center it was the most-watched sports program on Thursday evenings in its winter season.<sup>[3]</sup>

Critics have described its coverage of the breeding industry as uncritical. Its winter editions of 2022–23 and 2023–24 dealt with the Kyzyl-Jyldyz pedigree fraud, in which a private stud near Talas substituted DNA samples for registered foals (see [[Crime in Irad]]), only through the court case and the Syndicate's statements. It did not report the questions raised by independent breeders about why the Syndicate's own farms, managed by the Governor's nephew [[Mirlan Toktarov]], had not been audited by an outside body.<sup>[4]</sup><sup>[5]</sup> IradOne has said that the program covers sport and breeding, not commercial disputes.

#### 446. İçkenge Attı Jetelep
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Media*
***İçkenge Attı Jetelep*** (Iradi, "Lead a Horse to Drink") is an Iradi-language television drama serial broadcast by [[IradOne]]. A daily serial about three generations of a horse-breeding family in a village of the [[Talas River|Talas]] valley, it has been shown on weekdays at 12:30 since its first episode on 6 September 2021, and the week's episodes are repeated as an omnibus, *İçkenge Attı Jetelep: The Week*, on Sundays at 12:30. By October 2026 it had broadcast more than 1,300 episodes. It is IradOne's only daily drama.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Premise
The serial centers on Bakyt, a farmer who refuses to sell his lower field to a neighboring feedlot, his wife, their restless son Nurlan and their daughter Aiperi, who takes a job in [[Talas]], and the family's grandmother, Gülzat. Storylines follow village life through the seasons: name days, a gray mare that is sold in secret and later goes missing, quarrels over the water schedule, a visit from the priest, a called-off wedding and the return of Gülzat's sister from Russia after eleven years as a migrant worker.<sup>[1]</sup> The title comes from a proverb about patience, roughly "you can lead a horse to water, but you cannot make it drink", which the family repeats to one another.

## Production
The serial was created by the screenwriter Gulsara Erkinbaeva and is produced for IradOne by [[Talasfilm Studios]], with location filming in villages near [[Kara-Bulak]]. Its cast is drawn largely from the Talas State Academic Drama Theatre; the veteran actress Tamara Beishenalieva has played Gülzat since the first episode. It was the first daily drama made in Iradi, and IradOne has described it as part of its commitment to the language.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Reception
In the 2023 survey of the Irad Media Research Center it was the most-watched daytime program in the ISEZ, with an audience concentrated among women over 40 and in rural districts; the Sunday omnibus has been one of the channel's most-watched weekend programs.<sup>[3]</sup> Farmers' organizations have praised its storylines about the expansion of feedlots and the cost of water. Critics note that, like other IradOne drama, it treats such problems as private disputes between neighbors and rarely refers to the authorities. Linguists credit it with bringing rural Iradi speech to urban viewers, and its catchphrases are widely quoted on social media.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[4]</sup>

#### 447. Jyldyz Jolu
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Media*
***Jyldyz Jolu*** (Iradi, "Star Road") is an Iradi-language youth talent show broadcast by [[IradOne]]. Young singers, dancers and [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]] players from across the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) compete in weekly heats over a spring series. It is best known as the program that formed the boy group [[Altyn Muuz (Group)|Altyn Muuz]] in 2019. The 2026 series, which began on 7 March 2026, was shown on Saturdays at 17:00.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Format
Auditions are held each winter in [[Talas]], [[Nurzhan]], [[Kyzyl-Adyr]] and [[Iyık Janyl]], and contestants must be between 14 and 21. Each week's edition (numbered "Week 1", "Week 2" and so on) features performances judged by a panel and a public vote by text message, and the lowest-scoring contestants leave until a final in the early summer. Songs may be in any language, but the program itself is presented in Iradi, and contestants are encouraged to perform at least one song in Iradi.<sup>[1]</sup> Aibike Kenzhebekova has presented it since its launch, and the komuz player Kubat Alymbaev has sat on the panel in every series.

## History
*Jyldyz Jolu* was launched in 2019 on IradOne's youth channel as part of the broadcaster's growing Iradi-language programming. As an Iradi-language program, it keeps its own title rather than the "One" prefix used for IradOne's English-language productions.<sup>[1]</sup> In its first series the top four contestants, Nurbek Asanov, Ermek Toktosun uulu, Aibek Ismailov and Timur Bakyt uulu, were signed as a group by the show's producers and became Altyn Muuz, whose first single, "Kymyz Kymyz", followed in 2020.<sup>[2]</sup> The program's executive producer, Nurgazy Zhusupbekov, also managed the group in its first years. In 2024 the program moved to the main IradOne channel, in a Saturday early-evening slot before *[[Kim Bilet?]] Saturday Special*.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Reception
The program is among IradOne's most-watched Iradi-language programs with viewers under 25, and the Irad Media Research Center has linked its popularity to the [[Iradi language revival]].<sup>[3]</sup> Its association with Altyn Muuz, which the *[[Talas Herald]]* and most critics treat as a novelty act, has made it a target of [[Mor-Wave]] musicians, who accuse IradOne of turning the style into a commercial product.<sup>[4]</sup> Other contestants have had more conventional careers, and several komuz finalists have gone on to study at conservatories in Talas and [[wp:Bishkek]].

#### 448. Kim Bilet?
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Media*
***Kim Bilet?*** (Iradi, "Who Knows?") is an Iradi-language television quiz show broadcast by [[IradOne]]. Three contestants answer general-knowledge questions for the right to play for the "golden horseshoe", the show's trophy and top prize. It is shown on weekdays at 19:00, and a team edition, *Kim Bilet? Saturday Special*, is shown on Saturdays at 18:00.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Format
Each weekday edition lasts half an hour. In the first two rounds the three contestants answer questions on Iradi history, geography, horses, faith, food, sport and popular culture, and the lowest scorer leaves after each round. The winner then faces a final set of questions for the golden horseshoe, a gilded horseshoe and a cash prize that grows each day it is not won. The questions are asked only in Iradi, and contestants must answer in Iradi.<sup>[1]</sup> In the *Saturday Special*, teams of three from families, workplaces, schools and villages compete for a larger weekly jackpot.

## History
*Kim Bilet?* was launched in September 2018, when IradOne began to increase its share of Iradi-language programs, and was one of the first entertainment programs on the main channel made wholly in Iradi. The *Saturday Special* followed in 2020. Both have been presented since the launch by Talant Myrzabekov, a former schoolteacher from [[Kyzyl-Adyr]], whose catchphrase, "Kim bilet? Siz bilesiz!" ("Who knows? You know!"), is widely repeated.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Reception
In the 2023 survey of the Irad Media Research Center *Kim Bilet?* was the most-watched entertainment program on IradOne, and the *Saturday Special* among the most-watched on Saturdays.<sup>[3]</sup> Teachers and supporters of the [[Iradi language revival]] have praised it for encouraging young viewers to use the language, and Iradi-language quiz leagues in schools are modeled on it.<sup>[2]</sup> Russian-speaking viewers in [[Nurzhan]] have complained that the Iradi-only rule effectively excludes them, a criticism IradOne answers by pointing to its Russian-language programs on IradOdin. Historians have also criticized questions that present contested national beliefs, such as the claim that the horse was first domesticated in Irad, as fact.<sup>[4]</sup>

#### 449. Kuda (TV series)
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Media*
***Kuda*** (Iradi, "The In-Laws") is a bilingual television sitcom broadcast by [[IradOne]]. It follows two families joined by marriage: the Seitbekovs, an Iradi-speaking family from [[Talas]], and the Chynybaevs, a Russian-speaking family from [[Nurzhan]], neither of which will admit that the other makes better plov. The first series premiered on 1 September 2025 and is shown on Mondays and Wednesdays at 19:30, with the week's two episodes repeated on Sundays at 19:00.<sup>[1]</sup> The title is the Iradi word for the families of a married couple, who become *kuda* to each other at the betrothal visit (see [[Marriage in Irad]]).

## Premise and episodes
The series begins with the engagement of the Seitbekovs' son and the Chynybaevs' daughter and follows the two families through their first year as in-laws. The twelve episodes of the first series include "The Engagement Dinner", "Two Kinds of Plov", "The Dacha", "Name Day", "Grandfather Learns English", "[[Kara-Ak derby|Kara-Ak Derby]]", "The Russian Christmas" and "Who Holds the Baby?".<sup>[1]</sup> Running jokes include the rivalry between the Seitbekovs' stirred Irad paloosu and the Chynybaevs' long-grain plov, a culinary divide the *[[Talas Herald]]* has traced to the rice of the Chu valley,<sup>[2]</sup> and the two fathers' loyalty to the rival football clubs of Talas and Nurzhan.

## Production
*Kuda* was written by Nargiza Jusupova and Sergei Kalinin and produced for IradOne by [[Talasfilm Studios]]. Each family speaks its own language, and characters switch between Iradi, Russian and the Nurzhan mixture known as *Russocha*, with English subtitles. It is the first IradOne comedy with substantial Russian dialogue to be shown on the main channel rather than on IradOdin.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

## Reception
The series drew large audiences in both cities in its first weeks, and phrases from it spread quickly on social media. Reviewers praised its warmth and its cast, while some Iradi-language activists objected to the amount of Russian heard in prime time. Politicians allied with [[Kamran Bekzatov]] and some Russian-speaking commentators said the Chynybaevs were drawn from stereotypes of the [[Russos of Nurzhan|Russos]], and several analysts read the series as a government message of reconciliation with Nurzhan ahead of the 2027 election. IradOne said that the series was "a comedy about families, not politics".<sup>[3]</sup>

#### 450. OneNews
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Media*
***OneNews*** is the English-language news service of [[IradOne]], the state broadcaster of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). Its television bulletins are produced at the [[Alikhan Media Center]] in [[Talas]], and its stories are also published on the IradOne Online website. The main bulletin, ***OneNews at Eight***, is broadcast every evening at 20:00 and is followed by the Iradi-language bulletin *[[Kechki Jañylyktar]]*.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Format
IradOne carries five half-hour bulletins a day: *OneNews Morning* at 06:00, with weather for the valleys and the mountain passes; *OneNews Midday* at 12:00; *OneNews Afternoon* at 16:00, which concentrates on community events and is not shown on Sundays; *OneNews at Eight*; and *OneNews Late* at 23:00, a summary of the day's main stories. *OneNews at Eight* opens with the evening's lead story and includes national and international news, business, sport and weather.<sup>[1]</sup> Translated versions of the bulletins are shown on the Russian-language channel IradOdin.

## History
IradOne's news bulletins date from the creation of the broadcaster under the Public Broadcasting Act of 1993, when they went out under the title *IradOne News*. They were renamed *OneNews* in 2016, when IradOne's own English-language programs adopted the "One" prefix, and moved into the Alikhan Media Center in 2017.<sup>[1]</sup> Begaiym Shamshieva has presented *OneNews at Eight* since 2017, and Marat Zhunusov presents the weekend editions.

Since July 2024 the bulletin has been the main outlet for recorded addresses attributed to Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]], which IradOne says are recorded at the Governor's residence. Their authenticity has been questioned by opposition outlets and technology monitors, claims that officials reject (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]).<sup>[2]</sup> In March 2025 the Governor's Irad Day address was broadcast as a recording for the first time.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Reception
In the 2023 audience survey of the Irad Media Research Center, *OneNews at Eight* was the most-watched regular program on IradOne; about 31 percent of adult respondents said they watched it at least once a week. Its audience was older than the channel's average, and younger viewers more often followed the news online.<sup>[4]</sup>

Press-freedom groups and the [[wp:Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe|OSCE]] have described IradOne's news coverage as heavily weighted toward the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI), and media researchers say OneNews gives most of its airtime to government infrastructure projects. Opposition figures such as [[Kamran Bekzatov]] rarely appear, and the bulletins gave little coverage to the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]].<sup>[5]</sup> IradOne says its news follows the editorial guidelines of the Department of Public Information.

#### 451. OneBreakfast
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Media*
***OneBreakfast*** is the morning magazine program of [[IradOne]], the state broadcaster of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), presented by Anara Tursunbaeva. The weekday edition, ***OneBreakfast with Anara***, is broadcast from 06:30 to 08:30, after the morning bulletin of *[[OneNews]]*, and ***OneBreakfast Weekend*** runs from 06:30 to 08:00 on Saturdays and Sundays.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Format
The program mixes music, studio interviews, weather and lifestyle features in a light-hearted format. Each edition has a featured guest or item. Regular subjects include the weather on the mountain passes, pet care with a vet from [[Kara-Bulak]], home remedies made with *Jasil*, the tarragon soft drink, keeping warm in a [[Nurzhan]] apartment, and budget wedding ideas. Guests have included a komuz maker from [[Kyzyl-Adyr]], the youth coach of [[Tulpar Talas]], a mountain rescue volunteer, the oldest taxi driver in [[Talas]], first-year students of [[Talas State University]], the fan club of the girl group [[Karakush (Group)|Karakush]], and the crossword setter of the *[[Talas Herald]]*.<sup>[1]</sup> The weekend edition adds market reports, including the dried apricots of the [[Bazar-i Kalan]] and breakfast tacos from a [[Semiz]] chef, and a look back at the week's lighter stories.

## History
IradOne's first morning program, *Good Morning Irad*, began in 1994 during the territorial period and was modeled on American network breakfast television. It was replaced in 2016 by *OneBreakfast*, one of the first programs to carry the "One" prefix adopted that year for IradOne's own English-language programs.<sup>[2]</sup> Anara Tursunbaeva, previously a presenter on IradOne's youth channel, has presented it since its launch; her name was added to the weekday title in 2019, when the weekend edition began.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Reception
In the 2023 survey of the Irad Media Research Center, *OneBreakfast* was the most-watched morning program in the ISEZ, with its largest audience among urban families in Talas.<sup>[3]</sup> Media researchers describe it as part of the state-approved popular culture that IradOne has emphasized since 2015, and note that it seldom touches on politics. During the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]] the program continued its usual schedule of features.<sup>[4]</sup> Its music slots give regular exposure to [[Mor-Pop]] acts.

#### 452. OneTruth
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Media*
***OneTruth*** is a weekly reporting program on [[IradOne]], the state broadcaster of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), which IradOne describes as its premier journalism program. Each edition examines a single local issue. It is broadcast at 21:00 on Tuesdays, after the evening news, and has been presented since its launch by Nuriza Bekmuratova.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Format
Each hour-long edition follows one story through filmed reports, interviews with residents and officials, and a closing studio interview. Subjects have included little-used bus routes, the repair of irrigation canals, the rising price of hay, a day with the Talas ambulance service, the empty villages of the Chu plain, the queues of trucks at the Kazakh frontier, the safety of five-story Soviet apartment blocks, the cost of a hospital bed, garbage collection, rents and new towers in [[Talas]], schools short of Iradi teachers, and the women traders of the [[Bazar-i Kalan]].<sup>[1]</sup> Some editions have been filmed inside state enterprises, among them the [[Nurzhan Oil Refinery]] and the mines of the antimony districts (see [[Antimony Mining in Irad]]).

## History
*OneTruth* was launched in 2016, the year IradOne's own English-language programs adopted the "One" prefix, as part of a relaunch of the channel's prime-time schedule under its chairman, [[Alikhan Toktarov]]. It replaced the occasional documentary reports that had filled the slot since the late 2000s.<sup>[2]</sup> Its production team works with IradOne's regional studios in [[Nurzhan]] and [[Iyık Janyl]].

## Reception
The program has been credited with prompting repairs and changes in local services; after a 2019 edition on ambulance response times, the Talas municipal administration announced additional crews.<sup>[1]</sup> In the 2023 survey of the Irad Media Research Center it was IradOne's second most-watched current-affairs program, after *[[OneDebate]]*.<sup>[3]</sup>

Media researchers and press-freedom groups describe its journalism as limited. They say that IradOne has dropped investigative reporting under Alikhan Toktarov, and that *OneTruth* reports on failures by municipal departments and lower officials but has not examined the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] leadership, the business interests of the Toktarov family or the conduct of the Gendarmerie.<sup>[4]</sup> A 2021 [[Talas State University]] thesis found that most editions ended with an official announcing a solution.<sup>[5]</sup> IradOne says the program reflects the issues viewers raise with it.

#### 453. Patrol: Kara-Bulak
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Media*
***Patrol: Kara-Bulak*** is a television police drama broadcast by [[IradOne]]. It follows the officers of a post of the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad|Republican Gendarmerie]]'s Highway Patrol Corps at [[Kara-Bulak]], a market town on the [[Trans-Talas Highway]] west of [[Talas]]. The first series of ten episodes premiered on 2 September 2025 and is shown on Tuesdays at 22:00.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Premise and episodes
Each episode follows the post through one case on the roads of the Talas valley, from lost children and stranded travelers to smuggling. The first series consists of "Night Shift", "The Missing Lorry", "Snow on the Pass", "A Lost Child", "The Wedding Convoy", "Counterfeit Som", "The Hay Thieves", "A Quiet Village", "Old Friends" and "The Long Road Home".<sup>[1]</sup> The post is commanded by Captain Bolotov, played by Marat Temirbaev, and its officers include a young Iradi-speaking graduate of the [[Talas Gendarmerie Academy]] and an older, Russian-speaking sergeant close to retirement, reflecting the division between generations in the real force. Dialogue is mainly in English, with Iradi and Russian.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Production
The series was produced for IradOne by [[Talasfilm Studios]] with the cooperation of the Gendarmerie, which provided vehicles, uniforms and technical advisers, and approved the scripts. Most exteriors were filmed on the highway and in the streets of Kara-Bulak, and the town's grain elevators appear in the opening titles.<sup>[2]</sup> As a commissioned drama it did not take the "One" prefix used for IradOne's in-house English-language programs.

## Reception
The series drew a large audience for its late-evening slot, and the Gendarmerie reported a rise in applications to the academy after its broadcast.<sup>[2]</sup> Reviewers in Talas praised its location filming and its acting, but described its stories as mild. Press-freedom and human rights groups, which have documented allegations of torture and arbitrary detention by Gendarmerie units, described it as a recruitment film for the force, and noted that it was broadcast within two years of the force's role in dispersing the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]].<sup>[3]</sup> IradOne said the series honored "the ordinary officers who keep Irad's roads safe".<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 454. OneSport
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Media*
***OneSport*** is the brand under which [[IradOne]], the state broadcaster of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), presents its sports programs. Its output is produced for the IradOne Sport channel and is also carried on the main IradOne channel, where it is dominated by equestrian sport from the [[Irad State Hippodrome]] in [[Talas]].<sup>[1]</sup>

## Programs
- ***OneSport Highlights***, a half-hour round-up of football, horse racing and other sport, shown from Monday to Saturday at 13:30.
- ***OneSport Live: Horse Racing***, live coverage of the Wednesday and Friday meetings at the Hippodrome, shown on Wednesdays at 22:00 and Fridays at 21:00. The cards mix [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] flat races such as the Talas Stakes and the Golden Hoof Mile with [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] races up to the 4,000-meter bayge.
- ***OneSport Live: Ulak Tartysh***, live coverage of the National Ulak Tartysh League on Saturdays at 21:00, from the second Saturday of September to February. The league's 24 teams play in an ISEZ Conference and a Highland Conference of clan teams from the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]].<sup>[2]</sup>
- ***OneSport Live: Horse Games***, on Sundays at 21:00, with kyz kuu, [[Oodarysh (Mounted Wrestling)|oodarysh]], [[Tyin Emmei (Mounted Sport)|tyin emmei]], [[At Chabysh (Racing)|at chabysh]] and the Akyel show ring.
- ***Irad League Round-up***, goals and talking points from the day's [[Irad League]] matches, on Saturdays at 18:30 from March to November.
- The ***President's Cup Final***, the championship final of [[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)|ulak tartysh]], shown live from 21:00 on the first Saturday after Irad Day.<sup>[1]</sup>

## History
IradOne's sports bulletins date from 1994. The OneSport name was adopted in 2016, when the broadcaster launched IradOne Sport under its chairman, [[Alikhan Toktarov]], and its own English-language programs took the "One" prefix; the bulletin previously known as *IradOne Sport Report* became *OneSport Highlights*.<sup>[3]</sup> IradOne holds exclusive rights to the [[President's Cup]], the ulak league and the Irad League. Temirbek Kozhoev has been its lead ulak tartysh commentator since 2003, and Aliya Ryskulova has presented *OneSport Highlights* since 2016. Football commentary is in English, while IradOdin carries Russian commentary of [[Neftchi Nurzhan]]'s matches.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Reception
In the 2023 survey of the Irad Media Research Center the President's Cup final was the most-watched sports broadcast of the year, and the [[Kara-Ak derby]] is regularly the most-watched league broadcast.<sup>[4]</sup> Opposition figures and some clan leaders have described the award of broadcasting contracts by the [[National Equestrian Sports Directorate]] as patronage, and animal welfare groups, which criticize the Directorate's record on injuries to horses in ulak tartysh and long-distance racing, have objected to the prominence the broadcaster gives these sports. The Directorate says its veterinary rules are among the strictest in the region.<sup>[5]</sup>

#### 455. Sunday Qurbana
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Media*
***Sunday Qurbana*** is a weekly broadcast of the Divine Liturgy ([[wp:Holy Qurbana]]) of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] on [[IradOne]], the state broadcaster of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). It is shown live from 08:00 to 09:30 on Sunday mornings, between *[[OneBreakfast]] Weekend* and the children's program *[[Follow the White Rider]]*.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Format
The liturgy is celebrated in [[wp:Syriac language|Classical Syriac]] and Iradi according to the [[East Syriac Rites of Iyık Janyl|East Syriac rite]] of the Iradi church, with an English commentary that explains the readings, the chants and the movements of the clergy. The broadcast rotates among a small number of churches: the [[Church of St. Janyl]], the cathedral of [[Iyık Janyl]]; the churches of St. Yuhanna and St. Tomas in [[Talas]]; and a parish church in [[Nurzhan]].<sup>[1]</sup> Masses from the cathedral are often sung by the [[Iyık Janyl Seminary Choir]]. Fr. Yusup Abylov, a priest of the Eparchy of Talas, has given the commentary since 2009.

The main feasts are covered separately. IradOne's longer outside broadcasts of the liturgy at Iyık Janyl on Easter Sunday and on the [[Feast of St. Janyl]] on 24 August replace the program when they fall on a Sunday.<sup>[2]</sup>

## History
IradOne first broadcast the Sunday liturgy in 1994, two years after the territorial administration guaranteed freedom of religion and the churches reopened. The program is produced with the media office of the [[Archbishopric of Iyık Janyl]], which chooses the parishes and the celebrants, and for this reason it kept its title when IradOne's own English-language programs adopted the "One" prefix in 2016.<sup>[1]</sup> It has used IradOne's mobile production units since the 2000s and has been broadcast in high definition since 2018.

## Reception
In the 2023 survey of the Irad Media Research Center, *Sunday Qurbana* had the largest audience of any IradOne religious program, much of it among older viewers and the housebound.<sup>[3]</sup> Critics within the church have said that the choice of urban parishes, including the Latin-style Church of St. Tomas, gives a Latinized picture of Iradi worship. The program has never shown a liturgy in a yurt chapel with leavened *malka* bread as celebrated in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], or the Spanish-language Mass in [[Semiz]].<sup>[4]</sup> Secular commentators and some Russian-speaking viewers have questioned the place of a weekly Catholic service on the state broadcaster; IradOne says it reflects the faith of most of its viewers.

#### 456. Tulpar Tales
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Media*
***Tulpar Tales*** is an Iradi animated children's series broadcast by [[IradOne]]. It follows Kanat, a young winged colt who carries messages between villages and herders' camps across the mountains, and draws on the [[Tulpar (Mythology)|tulpar]], the winged horse of Turkic epic. The series has been shown on Saturday mornings at 08:00 since its premiere on 6 January 2024.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Format and episodes
Each half-hour episode sets Kanat a delivery that goes wrong. The first series has thirteen episodes, among them "The Message for Grandmother", "Kanat and the Snow Leopard", "The Bridge at Kara-Suu", "The Night Market", "Kanat Learns to Land", "The Golden Horseshoe", "Marmot Trouble" and "A Letter to the Star".<sup>[1]</sup> The settings are based on real landscapes of the [[Talas Alatau]], with juniper woods, summer pastures and yurt camps, and the animals include the [[Snow Leopard (Irad)|snow leopard]], golden eagles and marmots. Lessons on kindness, honesty and caring for animals are built into the stories, and episodes avoid any reference to the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], which Kanat's routes would in reality cross.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Production
The series was produced for IradOne by the animation unit of [[Talasfilm Studios]], set up in 2021 to make children's programs, and directed by Bakai Kochkorbaev. It was the first Iradi-made animated series. Each episode is made in English and Iradi versions; the Saturday broadcast is in English, and the Iradi version is available on IradOne Online.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup> The Department of Public Information described it at its launch as part of an effort to give Iradi children "their own heroes" in place of imported cartoons.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Reception
The series was well received by parents and teachers, and Kanat toys and school bags have been sold in [[Talas]] since 2024. Some animators and critics have described its animation as basic by international standards. Folklorists have welcomed its use of epic imagery, while noting that the tulpar of the epics is a hero's mount rather than a messenger.<sup>[2]</sup> A second series has been announced but not dated.

#### 457. Voices of Janyl
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Media*
***Voices of Janyl*** is a daytime talk show on [[IradOne]], the state broadcaster of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), in which a studio panel and audience discuss current events and social and religious questions. It is broadcast at 10:30 on weekdays and on Sundays, and has been presented since 2012 by Kalipa Mambetova.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Format
Each hour-long edition takes a single question and is discussed by a panel that usually includes a priest or a member of a religious order of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], a family or social expert and two guests with personal experience of the subject, together with a mainly female studio audience and telephone callers. Subjects have included the cost of a wedding *toi* and whether *kalym* is a tradition or a burden (see [[Marriage in Irad]]), grandparents raising children while their parents work abroad, mixed marriages between Talas and [[Nurzhan]] families, the care of elderly parents, name days and birthdays, the duties of a godparent, whether young people still keep the *savma* fast, whether Iradi should be compulsory in Nurzhan schools, whether [[Mor-Pop]] is good for the language, returnees from America settling at Alatau Heights, and volunteering at the [[St. Luka Community Health Mission]].<sup>[1]</sup>

## History
The program was first broadcast in 2004, during the territorial period. Its title refers to [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|Janyl]], the founding figure of Iradi Christianity, and the program has kept it since IradOne's own English-language programs adopted the "One" prefix in 2016. Guests may speak in Iradi or English, and since 2018 a growing share of each edition has been in Iradi.<sup>[1]</sup> A Sunday edition was added in 2016.

## Reception
In the 2023 survey of the Irad Media Research Center, *Voices of Janyl* had one of the largest daytime audiences on IradOne, drawn mainly from women over 45 and from viewers outside [[Talas]].<sup>[2]</sup> Ethnographers have used the program as a record of changing attitudes to marriage and family, noting that it rarely questions church teaching.<sup>[3]</sup>

Clergy have objected to some editions, including a 2017 discussion of bride kidnapping held while the Abduction for Marriage Act was before the [[Mejlis]], in which a caller defended the practice. Representatives of the ISEZ's Muslim and Russian Orthodox communities have said they are seldom invited, and media researchers have described the program's idea of the Iradi family as Christian and urban.<sup>[4]</sup> IradOne says the panel reflects the faith of most of its viewers.

#### 627. Attelkom Jarnama
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Media*

**Attelkom Jarnama** (Iradi: *jarnama*, "advertisement"; ads.attelkom.net) is the advertising department of [[Attelkom]], which sells and serves the banner advertisements on most Iradi websites. Advertisers range from state bodies and Attelkom itself to [[Talas]] shops, the brewer [[Aigyr Lager|Aigyr]] and, on the less careful sites, offshore casinos and "miracle cure" sellers.<sup>[1]</sup>

## History
Attelkom began selling banner space on its portal and on its subscribers' member pages in 1998. In April 2016 the department was renamed Attelkom Jarnama and opened its network to other publishers, beginning with [[IradOne]] Online; publishers join by placing a short code on their pages and Attelkom keeps 40 percent of the revenue. Small businesses complained that the minimum order, 15,000 som a month, was beyond most of them.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Network
Jarnama's banners appear on IradOne Online, the *[[Talas Herald]]*, Attelkom's own sites including [[Kartalar]], the classifieds site [[Jılmay]], the [[Tulpar (app)|Tulpar]] website and the horse games portal [[Jarysh]]. Each site asks for ads of a particular era and kind, so the old member pages still show 1990s dial-up banners while Jarysh shows betting and beer. Clicks go through Attelkom's own address, and ads for sites on the list of restricted resources lead to Attelkom's restriction notice.<sup>[2]</sup> Complaints about advertisements are taken at jarnama@attelkom.net.

#### 484. Keñsuu Dialect
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Language & Literature*
The **Keñsuu dialect** (Iradi: *Keñsuu shevesi*) is an extinct dialect of the [[Iradi Language|Iradi language]], formerly spoken in the Keñ-Suu ("wide water") valley on the northern slope of the [[Talas Alatau]], east of [[Talas]]. Its last known fluent speaker died in the 1960s. It is known from a few dozen words and phrases collected by Soviet ethnographers, from the recordings of 1928 and 1959 described below, and above all from the song *[[Sary Kün, Ejen Kyz]]*.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Features
Keñsuu stood apart from the other [[Dialects of Iradi|Iradi dialects]] in several ways that linguists attribute to a substrate of the medieval [[wp:Oghuz Turks|Oghuz]], who grazed the Talas basin before the Kipchak-speaking ancestors of the [[Iradis]] became dominant there:<sup>[2]</sup>
- initial *g* where the other dialects have *k*, as in *göz* ("eye") for standard *köz*;
- a back *q* and a voiced *ğ*, written with those letters in the Latin transcriptions of 1928, as in *qara* ("black") for standard *kara* and *ağyn* ("current") for *agyn*;
- the vowel *ä*, otherwise found only in the dialects of the Fergana Rim, as in *kätte*;
- words recorded nowhere else, among them *ejen* ("gentle, tender"), *dööl* and *barışqor*, whose meanings are uncertain.

## Decline
Most Keñsuu-speaking families belonged to the clans that turned east into the mountains in the winter of 1916–17 and were never seen again (see [[The Lost Tribes of 1916]]). Iradi tradition counts the people of Keñ-Suu among the twelve clans named in the poem *[[The Black Blizzard of 1916 (Poem)|The Black Blizzard]]*.<sup>[3]</sup> The few families who had stayed behind or returned from [[wp:Xinjiang]] in 1917–18 found their pastures given to settlers. Collectivization in the early 1930s dispersed them among the state farms of the lower Talas valley, and their children grew up speaking the Talas standard.<sup>[1]</sup>

In 1928 the ethnographer Yevgeny Sadovnikov, working for the People's Commissariat of Education of the Iradi SSR, recorded songs and word lists in the valley on wax phonograph cylinders. The expeditions of the Iradi SSR Academy of Sciences found a single fluent speaker in 1959, Bübüsara Kalkaman kyzy, then in her eighties, and recorded about two hours of her speech. Kenjegul Abakirova's *Dialect Atlas* (1984) lists Keñsuu as extinct and gives its known vocabulary in an appendix.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Revival interest
Since the State Archives digitized the 1928 cylinders in 2019, Keñsuu has attracted interest among young speakers of the [[Iradi language revival]], for whom it stands for what the language lost in 1916. Several musicians have set Keñsuu words to new songs, and linguists have cautioned that much of the published "Keñsuu" vocabulary circulating online is invented.<sup>[4]</sup>

#### 485. Sary Kün, Ejen Kyz
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Arts, Music & Film*
***Sary Kün, Ejen Kyz*** ("Golden Sun, Gentle Girl") is a traditional Iradi song in the extinct [[Keñsuu Dialect|Keñsuu dialect]], known from a recording made on wax cylinders in 1928. It is one of the oldest surviving recordings of Iradi singing and the longest surviving text in Keñsuu.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Recording
The song was recorded in the Keñ-Suu valley in the autumn of 1928 by the ethnographer Yevgeny Sadovnikov. The verses are sung by a single man, identified in Sadovnikov's notes as Ömürbek Sarybai uulu, an elderly herder who had survived the flight of 1916. Other men of the settlement join him in the choruses. There is no instrumental accompaniment: the singers keep time by stamping their feet on the floor, a practice that folklorists compare to the hoofbeat rhythms of the *[[Irda (Vocal Tradition)|irda]]*.<sup>[1]</sup> Sadovnikov did not record the occasion. Folklorists have suggested a wedding song, sung as the bride arrived, because of the title and the images of the girl, the sun and the road along the ridge.<sup>[3]</sup>

The cylinders were sent to Leningrad in 1929 and returned to [[Talas]] in copies in the 1960s. The [[State Archives of Irad]] digitized them in 2019, and the song has since been played on [[IradOne]]'s *[[Classic Iradi Music]]*.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Text
Each verse is a chain of short images: the golden sun, a dark-haired youth, hazel eyes (*ala göz*), a tale (*jomok*), stone, mint (*jalpız*), clouds (*bulut*) and the mountain. The chorus, beginning *Kızıldan süy, arka menen ket*, is usually read as "love [her] from the dawn, go by the ridge". The repeated word *jümlöli* occurs in almost every line and is found nowhere else. Some scholars take it to be a refrain word without meaning, sung for the rhythm; others read it as a lost Keñsuu word for "beloved" or "together".<sup>[3]</sup>

No agreed translation exists. Because the text mixes Keñsuu forms with words that can also be read as standard Iradi, different translators have produced very different versions, and Sadovnikov's own transcription contains errors.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Legacy
Since its digitization the song has become a symbol of the [[Iradi language revival]] and of the clans lost in 1916. It is sung at some memorials on 15 August, and [[Mor-Folk]] musicians have recorded new arrangements, usually keeping the stamped rhythm.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 486. Dream of Living
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Arts, Music & Film*
"**Dream of Living**" is a song by the [[Talas]] [[Mor-Folk]] ensemble [[Eski Ün]], released in 2021 as the English-language version of its Iradi song "Jashoo Tüshü". It is the only Mor-Folk song to have found a wide audience outside Irad.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Music
The ensemble's komuz, *[[Choor (Flute)|choor]]* and voices, singing a melody adapted from Syro-Iradi chant, are set over the dark synthesizers common to the "Mor" genres in a slow, ephemeral [[wp:Illbient|illbient]] production, made with a former member of the [[Nurzhan]] [[Mor-Wave]] group Umay-9. Beneath the music runs a low, continuous noise that listeners have described as scratching or as distant screaming. Eski Ün has never said what it is. Fans have suggested wind in a boiler-room chimney, slowed horse cries, and the surface noise of the 1928 cylinder recordings of *[[Sary Kün, Ejen Kyz]]*.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Lyrics
The song is sung in the first person plural. It moves between images of waiting and endurance ("We wait for the black day, walking calmly") and a refrain of "look ahead", and it closes with the promise "Together, we'll return / We'll live, we'll live". The ensemble has said that it sings "about loneliness and the road home".<sup>[3]</sup> Listeners in Irad have read the song as being about emigration, about the clans lost in 1916, or about the division of the country, and some clergy objected to its "black day" (*kara kün*), a phrase associated with [[Morkhan (Mythology)|Morkhan]].<sup>[2]</sup>

## Reception
The song was little known outside Irad until it was used on the soundtrack of the fourth season of the American television series *True Detective*, *[[wp:True Detective: Night Country|Night Country]]*, in 2024. Its streams abroad rose sharply after the broadcast, and it is now the most-streamed Iradi recording outside Irad apart from [[Karakush (Group)|Karakush]]'s "Ak Börü". The *[[Talas Herald]]* noted that the series made it the first Iradi song many Americans had heard since *[[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|Swift Hooves]]*.<sup>[4]</sup> In Irad, the song was sung at candlelit vigils during the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]]. Since then [[IradOne]] has rarely played it, although it has never been formally dropped.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

#### 488. Morkhan, Karañgy Ee
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Arts, Music & Film*
"**Morkhan, Karañgy Ee**" ("Morkhan the Dark Lord") is a song by the Iradi duo [[tüntolk]] from their debut album *[[Jolchu (Album)|Jolchu]]* (1999). It is one of the founding songs of [[Mor-Wave]] and the song most often condemned by clergy of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]].<sup>[1]</sup>

## Music and lyrics
The song has no drums and no beat. Askar Daniyarov set slowly moving tone clusters over the drones of his [[wp:Polivoks]] synthesizer, and built a "dark choir" from dozens of takes of Mira Temirova's voice, bounced between the four-track and a second cassette deck and never quite in tune with one another, so that the voices mass into dense, shifting clouds. Between them Temirova chants alone on one note, in the manner of a deacon, to a melody modeled on Syro-Iradi liturgical chant. Critics abroad have compared the choir to [[wp:Requiem (Ligeti)|Ligeti's Requiem]]. Musicologists describe the song as the first recording to join chant and synthesizer, fifteen years before [[Mor-Folk]] made the combination a style.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

The lyrics address [[Morkhan (Mythology)|Morkhan]], the bull-headed god of pre-Christian belief, whom church tradition identifies with Satan, in the form of a prayer turned inside out. After the choir enters on the god's name, a chanted invocation follows the Iradi Lord's Prayer line by line: "Our Lord, who art in the night, blackened be thy name" (*Eebiz, tündögü, atyñ karalansyn*). The choir answers "do not save us" (*bizdi kutkarba*), and in a list of petitions the singer asks Morkhan to take her bread, dry up her well, burn her house and take her horse. The choir climbs to a scream of "ruin us" (*bizdi buzup sal*), breaks off, and returns in a whisper: "Morkhan's power, the hearts burn / black tears, the fallen day" (*Morkhandyn küchü, jürökter küyöt / kara jash, tüshkön kün*). The song ends on a low, discordant "Amen". Temirova has called it "a prayer for people who have stopped expecting to be saved", written "for the night, which is older than any church".<sup>[2]</sup>

## Controversy
The song was not on the unfinished 1999 cassette of *Jolchu* and first appeared on the full album in 2000. Priests in [[Nurzhan]] preached against it soon afterwards, and it has been cited in parish complaints about Mor-Wave ever since, among them the petition that led to the cancellation of a Mor-Wave concert in [[Iyık Janyl]] in June 2019.<sup>[3]</sup> Clergy object to its subject, to its parody of the Lord's Prayer and to its use of chant melody, which they regard as belonging to the liturgy. [[IradOne]] has never broadcast it.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Critical reception
Apart from the religious objections, critics have singled the song out as the one track that does not fit the rest of the album. Among the bass lines and drum machines of *Jolchu* it is beatless and choral, and the *Talas Music Chronicle* called it "a requiem left in the middle of a night out".<sup>[1]</sup> Reviewing the 2019 vinyl reissue, *Tape Hiss Quarterly* wrote that it "stops the record dead" and that most listeners would lift the needle, and several critics have argued that it belongs with the chant-based Mor-Folk of the 2010s rather than with the Mor-Wave it is supposed to have founded. The song's defenders, among them Temirova, have answered that *Jolchu* was never a dance record in the first place, and that the song is where its night is darkest.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[4]</sup>

*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Arts, Music & Film*

"**Cut the Stars in the Night**" (Iradi: "**Jyldyzdardy Kes**", "Cut the Stars") is a song by the Iradi duo [[tüntolk]] from their EP *[[Zvezda Irad (EP)|Zvezda Irad]]* (2002), and their first single; *[[Jolchu (Album)|Jolchu]]* (1999) had none. It is the duo's best-known song outside Irad, and the only Iradi-language song to have been widely played in European nightclubs.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Music and lyrics
The song opens with samples of a herder's throat singing taken from field recordings in the [[State Archives of Irad]], crackling and drenched in tape echo over a slow synthesizer pulse. Mira Temirova then builds the title phrase a word at a time, "Kes." ("Cut."), "Kes, kes.", "Kes, kes jyldyzdardy!" ("Cut, cut the stars!"), and a heavy drum drop brings in a pounding, staccato synthesizer riff. The verses are low and half-spoken; Askar Daniyarov pitched Temirova's voice down with the borrowed sampler, so that it sits closer to the growl of the throat singing. Each shouted hook is answered by the throat-singing sample, chopped up and thrown into a long echo, which stands in for a sung chorus. Crowds at the duo's concerts shout the hook back.<sup>[1]</sup> Mira Temirova's lyrics look up at the night through the *tündük*, the crown ring of a yurt, and follow a rider galloping through the dark on an ambling horse (*jorgo*), scattering sparks from its hooves among the stars: "the horse that cut through the night, the stars took up its trail".<sup>[2]</sup>

## Release and reception
The song was released as a CD-R single on 1 March 2002, six weeks before *Zvezda Irad*, during the duo's club tours of [[wp:Almaty]] and [[wp:Tashkent]], and copies circulated among DJs in Moscow and Berlin. The song was used in two films of 2004: the Russian fantasy thriller *[[wp:Night Watch (2004 film)|Night Watch]]* (*Nochnoy Dozor*), in a scene in a Moscow nightclub, and the German film *[[wp:Head-On (film)|Head-On]]* (*Gegen die Wand*). The American release of *Night Watch* used a different soundtrack, and the song remained almost unknown in the United States.<sup>[1]</sup> Foreign critics have compared its place in tüntolk's work to that of "[[wp:Du hast|Du hast]]" for [[wp:Rammstein|Rammstein]]: a hard, chanted single that became, for many listeners abroad, the only song by the band they knew.<sup>[3]</sup>

In Irad the song remains a staple of [[Mor-Wave]] club nights in [[Nurzhan]] and [[Talas]], and the drum drop is a fixture of the duo's concerts.<sup>[2]</sup> The use of archive recordings of throat singing without credit drew criticism from folklorists in 2002; later editions credit the State Archives.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 490. My Home My Heart My Soul
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Arts, Music & Film*
"**My Home My Heart My Soul**" (Iradi: "**Üyüm, Jürögüm, Janım**") is a song by the Iradi duo [[tüntolk]] from their album *[[White Stallion in Fog]]* (2017). Critics have called it the strangest song in their catalog, and it is the song most associated with the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]].<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Music and lyrics
The song is built on a deep, continuous hum, against which Mira Temirova screams the lyrics with brutal, distorted force. Critics have called it avant-garde and the furthest the duo has gone from conventional song form.<sup>[1]</sup> The text is short and plain. Its refrain, "Oh Irad, my home, my heart, my soul", is taken from the refrain of the national anthem, "[[The Spirit of Irad]]", and is repeated after each line, with verses about the land "where the wind whispers secrets, which only brave hearts know" and "where the ancient legends live on even now", ending "in the land of Irad, where I want to stay". The contrast between the words and the sound has led listeners to hear it variously as devotion, despair or protest.<sup>[2]</sup>

## In the 2023 protests
During the student protests in [[Talas]] in October 2023, marchers chanted the song's refrain, "Ooo İrad menin üyüm, jürögüm, janım". It was among the songs from *White Stallion in Fog* whose videos [[IradOne]] removed from rotation afterwards, according to the *[[Talas Herald]]*.<sup>[3]</sup> Commentators noted that the broadcaster had stopped showing a song whose refrain comes from the national anthem, which IradOne plays at the start and close of every broadcasting day. The duo said only that their songs "belong to whoever sings them".<sup>[3]</sup>

***Zvezda Irad*** (Russian and Iradi, "Star of Irad") is an extended play by the Iradi electronic duo [[tüntolk]], released in 2002. It contains "[[Cut the Stars in the Night]]", the duo's best-known song outside Irad, and marks their move from the cassette underground of [[Nurzhan]] to the club circuit of [[wp:Almaty]] and [[wp:Tashkent]].<sup>[1]</sup>

## Background and recording
After *[[Jolchu (Album)|Jolchu]]* (1999) tüntolk began playing club nights in Nurzhan and then in Almaty, where they met the promoter and engineer Yerlan Abenov. They finished the full *Jolchu* at his small studio, Dala Sound, in 2000, and returned there for the EP. The EP was begun in the Nurzhan boiler room on the duo's four-track recorder and finished in Almaty, where Askar Daniyarov used a borrowed sampler for the first time. Its title mixes Russian (*zvezda*, "star") and Iradi, a joke on the bilingual signs of Nurzhan; the star is Polaris, the star of the Iradi flag.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Music
The EP is faster and harder than *Jolchu*, built for dancing. "Jyldyzdardy Kes" opens with uncredited archive recordings of a herder's throat singing over a slow pulse before a drum drop brings in the full beat. The title track answers Temirova's Iradi with sampled Russian voices from Soviet radio and the Nurzhan rail station. "Jorgo" is built on the four-beat rhythm of an ambling horse. "Tündük", the longest track, returns to the slow drones of the first album. The closing remix, made for Almaty clubs, became the version most DJs played.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Release and reception
"Jyldyzdardy Kes" came out first, on 1 March 2002, as a CD-R single handed to DJs at the duo's Almaty club nights. The duo released the EP on CD-R in Nurzhan on 13 April 2002, at a club night in the city, and Dala Sound pressed a small run of compact discs in Almaty later that year. Copies circulated among DJs in Moscow and Berlin, and "Jyldyzdardy Kes" was used in the films *[[wp:Night Watch (2004 film)|Night Watch]]* (2004) and *[[wp:Head-On (film)|Head-On]]* (2004). Folklorists criticized the uncredited use of archive throat singing; editions since 2015 credit the [[State Archives of Irad]].<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

***Kara Suu*** (Iradi: "Black Water") is the second studio album by the Iradi electronic duo [[tüntolk]], released in 2004. Darker and more industrial than their earlier records, it was their last release before they split up during the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] in 2007.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Background
The album was written during the duo's club tours of [[wp:Almaty]] and [[wp:Tashkent]] in 2003, while much of [[Nurzhan]]'s heavy industry stood idle. Its title refers to the oily black water of the drainage canals behind the city's refineries, and several songs, among them "Temir Jol" and "Kotelnaya", describe the abandoned railway yards and boiler rooms where the scene had begun. "Kara Jel" takes its title from the Nurzhan group Kara Jel, one of the bands that had grown up around the duo.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Reception
{{Album ratings
| Talas Music Chronicle = 4/5
| Central Asian Music Review = 3.5/5
}}

The album sold modestly and was received more coolly than *[[Jolchu (Album)|Jolchu]]*; some listeners in the scene found it cold after the warmth of the first record. It has been reappraised since the duo's reunion in 2014, and the *Talas Music Chronicle* has called it "the sound of Nurzhan holding its breath before the war".<sup>[1]</sup>

***White Stallion in Fog*** (Iradi: *Tumandagy Ak At*) is the third studio album by the Iradi electronic duo [[tüntolk]], released in 2017. Their first album after re-forming in 2014, it was promoted on the youth channel of [[IradOne]] and brought the duo a national television audience and listeners abroad. Its song "[[My Home My Heart My Soul]]" became an anthem of the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]].<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Background and recording
Mira Temirova returned from [[wp:Almaty]] in 2014, and the duo re-formed in [[Talas]], where Askar Daniyarov had worked since 2008 as a sound engineer at [[Talasfilm Studios]]. They recorded the album on one of the studio's sound stages at night, with Daniyarov's Soviet synthesizers alongside software instruments for the first time. The title image, a white horse in fog, comes from the Iradi saying that a white stallion seen in fog announces a return home.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Release and promotion
The album was released in March 2017, before Nooruz, by the Talas label Tündük Records, on streaming services and in a small vinyl pressing. IradOne, under its new chairman [[Alikhan Toktarov]], commissioned videos showing the duo in disused railway yards and beneath high-voltage transmission lines in the Moiynkum steppe, and played them heavily on its youth channel. Streaming brought the album a following in Eastern Europe and North America.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Reception and legacy
{{Album ratings
| Talas Music Chronicle = 4.5/5
| Central Asian Cultural Studies Review = 4/5
| Tape Hiss Quarterly = 4/5
}}

Critics welcomed the album as a return that kept the duo's sound while reaching a wider audience; "My Home My Heart My Soul", in which Temirova screams a plain patriotic text over a continuous hum, was singled out as the strangest song in their catalog. During the student protests of October 2023 marchers chanted its refrain, and IradOne afterwards removed several of the album's videos from rotation, according to the *[[Talas Herald]]*. The duo said only that their songs "belong to whoever sings them".<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

***Umay*** is the fourth studio album by the Iradi electronic duo [[tüntolk]], released in 2022. Named after the steppe goddess of birth and children, it is the quietest of their records and the closest to [[Mor-Folk]], with the Talas ensemble [[Eski Ün]] playing [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]] and *[[Choor (Flute)|choor]]* on several tracks.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Background
Mira Temirova wrote most of the lyrics after the birth of her daughter in 2020, adapting lullabies and the blessings sung over a newborn's cradle (*beshik*) as well as invocations of Umay recorded by folklorists. Askar Daniyarov kept the drum machine to a few tracks and built the rest on slow synthesizer pads and the acoustic instruments of Eski Ün.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Reception
The album was well received in Irad and won the album prize of the [[Altyn-Zhylky Awards]] in 2023. Some fans who had come to the duo through the harder sound of "[[Cut the Stars in the Night]]" found it too gentle, while others heard it as a reply to the commercial [[Mor-Pop]] of the same years, which had borrowed Umay as a name and an image.<sup>[1]</sup>

***Ak Börü*** (Iradi: "White Wolf") is the first extended play by the Iradi [[Mor-Pop]] girl group [[Karakush (Group)|Karakush]], released in February 2021. Its title track became a viral hit abroad and, by its label's count, is among the most-streamed Iradi recordings outside the country.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Background and production
Kök Ay Media, the agency that formed Karakush in 2018, planned the EP as the group's first major release after three years of singles. Its in-house producer Erlan Sydykov built the title track on a slowed, detuned [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]] riff recorded by a session player from [[Kyzyl-Adyr]], set over a trap beat in the style of Korean idol music. The group's lead dancer Dana Pak, from the [[Koryo-saram in Irad|Koryo-saram]] community of [[Nurzhan]], co-produced two tracks and choreographed the "white wolf" dance whose chorus move spread on short-video platforms. The EP also includes a re-recording of the group's 2018 debut single "Umay".<sup>[1]</sup>

## Release and reception
The EP and the title track's video, filmed on a frozen lake in the Talas valley with the members in white wolf-fur capes and horned headdresses, were released on 19 February 2021. The dance challenge carried the song to [[wp:Koryo-saram]] listeners in [[wp:Kazakhstan]] and [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and to Korean-American listeners. A Seoul label released a Korean-language version of "Ak Börü" in late 2021, which briefly entered the lower reaches of South Korean digital charts during the group's promotions there in early 2022. The headdresses, modeled on [[Morkhan (Mythology)|Morkhan]], drew objections from clergy of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]].<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

***Zhylky Love*** (Iradi *zhylky*, "horse") is the only studio album by the Iradi [[Mor-Pop]] boy group [[Altyn Muuz (Group)|Altyn Muuz]], released in 2022. It collects the group's three singles, among them the wedding favorite "Kymyz Kymyz", and has been described by the *Central Asian Music Review* as the high point of the genre's novelty strain.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Background
Altyn Muuz were formed in 2019 from the four finalists of *Jyldyz Jolu* ("Star Road"), a talent show on [[IradOne]]'s youth channel, whose producers released their records through the show's label, Star Road Music. The album was assembled around the singles "Kymyz Kymyz" (2020), "Morkhan Baby" (2021) and "Zhylky Love" (2022), with new songs about horses, food and the national game of [[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)|ulak]], in rhyming lyrics that mix Iradi and English.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Reception
{{Album ratings
| Talas Herald = 1.5/5
| Central Asian Music Review = 2/5
}}

Critics treated the album as a joke. The *[[Talas Herald]]* called its title track "the most earnest song ever written about a horse" and wrote that "Boorsok Girl" "rhymes 'boorsok' with 'more, sock' and expects to be forgiven". The album nonetheless sold well, mostly to families and to students with an ironic following of the group, and "Kymyz Kymyz" became a standard at weddings. "Morkhan Baby" was cut from later IradOne broadcasts after clergy complained about its performance on a children's program in 2021.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[1]</sup>

***Kara Kün*** (Iradi: "Black Day") is the first album by the [[Talas]] [[Mor-Folk]] ensemble [[Eski Ün]], released in 2021. It contains "Jashoo Tüshü" and its English-language version "[[Dream of Living]]", which found an audience abroad after its use in the American series *True Detective* in 2024.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Recording
The album was recorded over a winter of nights in a teahouse in the Old Talas Citadel Quarter where the ensemble played, with the room's noise left in. Its producer, Ruslan Ten, a former member of the Nurzhan [[Mor-Wave]] group Umay-9, set the ensemble's komuz, *choor*, frame drums and voices over dark synthesizer drones. The low scratching noise that runs beneath "Jashoo Tüshü", which the ensemble has never explained, is also heard on "Keñsuu", named after the extinct dialect of the 1928 cylinder recordings of *[[Sary Kün, Ejen Kyz]]*.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Release and reception
The album was released in April 2021 on Tündük Records and sold mainly at the ensemble's teahouse concerts in Talas and [[Nurzhan]]. Its title, a phrase associated with [[Morkhan (Mythology)|Morkhan]], drew objections from some clergy. Songs from it were sung at candlelit vigils during the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]]. After "Dream of Living" was used in *True Detective: Night Country* in 2024, streams of the whole album rose sharply abroad, and Tündük Records reissued it on vinyl that year. Since the label closed in 2025 the album has been distributed by [[Köch Audio]].<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

***Talas Sunrise*** is the debut album by the Talas [[Iradi Country-Folk|country-folk]] band [[Kök Bel (Band)|Kök Bel]], released on cassette in 1995. It is generally counted as the first commercial Iradi country-folk album, and its versions of songs from the American compilation *[[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|Swift Hooves]]* set the pattern for the genre's bilingual covers.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Background and recording
Kök Bel formed in 1993 and played cafés near [[Talas Air Base]] for Iradi and American audiences. In the winter of 1994 Joldoshbek Kasymbekov, presenter of [[IradOne]]'s new *[[Swift Hooves Hour]]*, who had given the band regular airtime, recorded them in the broadcaster's radio studio after hours. Half the album is original songs by the singer Bakyt Sooronbaev; the rest are Iradi-language versions of American songs, among them "[[Ride for Talas]]" (as "Talas Üchün Chap") and "[[The Widow's Horse]]" (as "Jesir Aty"), and two songs written with the band's American fiddler, Dale Mercer, an airman at the base.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Music
The band combined acoustic guitar, banjo and fiddle with the bowed *[[Kyl-kyak|kyl-kyak]]* and the [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]], and Sooronbaev sang in the style of the horseback song (*[[Irda (Vocal Tradition)|ırda]]*). "Ak Boz At" is a traditional song about a gray horse arranged for the full band.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Release and legacy
Ak Jol Records, a Talas cassette dealer, released the album in June 1995, and copies sold in the city's bazaars alongside pirated copies of *Swift Hooves*. The title track was played often on IradOne during the last years of [[Iradimania]]. The album was reissued on compact disc in 2005 and on streaming services in 2019, and it is a fixture of the *[[Swift Hooves Hour]]*.<sup>[2]</sup>

**Kök Bel** (Iradi, "Blue Pass", after the [[Kök-Bel Pass]]) is an [[Iradi Country-Folk|Iradi country-folk]] band from [[Talas]], formed in 1993. Its debut album, *[[Talas Sunrise]]* (1995), is generally counted as the first commercial country-folk album.<sup>[1]</sup>

## History
The band was formed in 1993 by the singer and guitarist Bakyt Sooronbaev, the banjo player Talant Asan and the *kyl-kyak* player Erkin Mamyrov, school friends who had learned American songs about Irad from copied cassettes in the 1980s. They played the cafés that opened near [[Talas Air Base]] after 1992, where the American airman Dale Mercer, a fiddler from Kentucky, began sitting in with them; he played with the band until his posting ended in 1996. Regular airtime on [[IradOne]] during the years of [[Iradimania]] led to *Talas Sunrise* in 1995, and the band released two more cassettes, *Ak Jol* (1998) and *Zhylky Jyly* (2002). It stopped performing during the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] and re-formed in 2014 for the twentieth-anniversary concert of the *[[Swift Hooves Hour]]*.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Discography
- *[[Talas Sunrise]]* (1995)
- *Ak Jol* (1998)
- *Zhylky Jyly* ("Year of the Horse", 2002)

#### 551. Twelve Kilometres
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Language & Literature*
