***Twelve Kilometres*** (Iradi: ***On Eki Chakyrym***) is a collection of twelve short stories and a coda by [[Aikokul Tursunbek kyzy]], published in Iradi by [[Arsha Books]] in [[Talas]] in 2015 and in English, translated by Aidana Mukash kyzy, in 2016. The stories follow ordinary people through the years between the [[Bill of Sale (2007)|Bill of Sale]] and the marking of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], from the winter of 2006 to the spring of 2009. Its title refers to the restricted zone twelve kilometers deep on each side of the line under the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)|Bishkek ceasefire]] of September 2007.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Background
The author was twenty-two in the autumn of 2007 and has said she read the full text of the ceasefire in the *[[Talas Herald]]*, folded small, on a bus. Her mother came from the Kara-Unkur valley above [[Arslanbob]], near the crossing at [[Bazar-Korgon]]. In her note on the title she writes that the distance that mattered was not twelve kilometres but "the four hundred metres of empty road between the two posts", and that she tried "to keep to what is known about those years and to invent only the people". Earlier versions of "Signatures" and "Bazaar Chubar" were read at [[Mor-Wave]] evenings in Talas in 2013 and 2014. The stories took eight years to write, and the book is dedicated to the author's mother (1954–2014), who appears in the coda.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Contents
1. "Contingency Papers" (December 2006 – February 2007, Talas): a translator back from Chicago at the new Ministry of Foreign Affairs works on the annexes of the Bill of Sale.
2. "Diesel" (January 2007, the Chu valley): herders block the Chu road east of [[Nurzhan]] over the price of diesel.
3. "Kobozev Is Listening" (25 February 2007, Nurzhan): an old Russian woman, her granddaughter and the night of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]]'s proclamation.
4. "Signatures" (March 2007, Talas): an actress who played Bermet in the 1967 staging of *Akyrky Ashuu* is asked to sign the writers' letter headed by [[Kemel Ishakov]].
5. "Mother Leaven" (April 2007, the Chatkal valley): a letter from the archeparchy and the holy leaven of the mountain parishes.
6. "The Aprons" (April 2007 – November 2008, [[Semiz]]): the evacuation of the agribusiness families from [[Talas Air Base]], seen by a boy who stays.
7. "Bread Cards" (May 2007, Talas): a student of dialects in the besieged city and the yellow ration cards of the parish of St. Tomas.
8. "The Armory" (4 June 2007, Talas): the key to a municipal armory on the day the Popular Front entered the city.
9. "Bazaar Chubar" (August – October 2007, Bazar-Korgon): a walnut buyer's daughter is married into a hill family across the new line.
10. "One to One Hundred Thousand" (September 2007, Bishkek): the Soviet maps of 1983 used to draw the line.
11. "Switchyard" (winter 2008–09, the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex|Toktogul dam]]): an [[El-Choro Militias|El-Choro]] post above the dam's switchyard.
12. "Pillar" (March 2009, the Kenkol valley): an interpreter with the demarcation teams and pillar 1,147.
- Coda: "Not for Sale" (October 2011, Bazar-Korgon): the author's mother crosses the line to her old valley.

The English edition adds a glossary, a translator's note and notes on the author and translator.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Publication and reception
The book was registered with the Department of Public Information and carries no ISBN, as Irad has no national ISBN agency. It was one of the few books from the ISEZ to deal directly with the [[Second Iradi Civil War|civil war of 2007]], a subject writers interviewed by the *Talas Herald* say they otherwise avoid. Its publisher, Arsha Books, had its registration suspended in 2024 after it issued an anthology of poems about the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]] (see [[Iradi literature]]). The author published a revised and expanded version of "Bazaar Chubar" in 2019. In October 2026 both the book and the revised story were made available online in the Digital Archive of the [[National Library of Irad]], the library of [[Talas State University]].<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

</ol>

#### 561. Chöl Shamaly
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Arts, Music & Film*
"**Chöl Shamaly**" ("Desert Wind") is a song by the Iradi duo [[tüntolk]], the opening track of their debut album *[[Jolchu (Album)|Jolchu]]* (1999), generally treated as the founding record of [[Mor-Wave]].<sup>[1]</sup>

## Music
The song opens as a slow lament over a sparse drum-machine pattern and builds without a break. Askar Daniyarov's [[wp:Polivoks]] bass line enters at the first refrain, "like a train at night" in a phrase often repeated by fans, and the drum machine doubles its pattern. Mira Temirova's voice moves from the low, heavily reverberated delivery of the pastoral lament (*koshok*) to declaiming and finally shouting. At the peak the whole track cuts out, leaving only the hum of the pumps in the [[Nurzhan]] boiler room where the album was recorded.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Themes
Temirova took the lines from nineteenth-century pastoral verse in which a herder lost on the steppe asks the wind to tell his mother that he is alive, and turned them around: her wayfarer stops looking for the road, follows the wind into the desert and asks that his mother not be told. Critics have read the song as the album's statement of purpose, a traditional form carried somewhere its makers' grandparents would not have taken it.<sup>[1]</sup>

<li id="cite_note-2"><b>^</b> <i>Central Asian Music Review</i> (2020). 'Mor-Wave and the Post-Soviet Electronic Synthesis in Central Asia.' Vol. 12, No. 3, pp. 41–66.</li>
</ol>

#### 562. Kazan (Song)
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Arts, Music & Film*
"**Kazan**" ("The Cauldron") is a song by the Iradi duo [[tüntolk]], the second track of their debut album *[[Jolchu (Album)|Jolchu]]* (1999). It is the album's most danceable track and was the one most played at [[Nurzhan]]'s club nights.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Music
The song begins with a long instrumental opening on a stuttering drum-machine kick, joined by a sequenced [[wp:Polivoks]] bass line jumping octaves, cold synthesizer stabs and the pumps of the boiler room, sampled and looped into the rhythm. Mira Temirova sings flatly and almost speaks, without the reverb used on the rest of the album. Critics have heard in it the first sign of the harder dance sound of the EP *[[Zvezda Irad (EP)|Zvezda Irad]]* (2002).<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Themes
The title plays on the two meanings of *kazan*: the iron cooking cauldron of the yurt and the district-heating boiler that Askar Daniyarov stoked at night. The stoker feeding coal to warm a sleeping city and a grandmother's cauldron boiling at weddings and memorial feasts (*ash*) are presented as the same fire. A spoken bridge reduces the song to four words: "Coal. Fire. Water. Steam."<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 563. Kökjal
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Arts, Music & Film*
"**Kökjal**" ("Grey Mane") is a song by the Iradi duo [[tüntolk]], the fourth track of their debut album *[[Jolchu (Album)|Jolchu]]* (1999). *Kökjal*, "grey-maned", is the old epic epithet for the wolf.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Music
With "[[Kazan (Song)|Kazan]]" it is one of the album's few tracks for the dance floor: a steady, muffled four-to-the-floor kick from the drum machine, under a low, gnarled acid line that Askar Daniyarov played on the [[wp:Polivoks]], its filter opening only slowly over the length of the track, with drones and tape hiss beneath. Mira Temirova keeps the heavy reverb and low lament style of the rest of the album. Her chants are half-buried in the mix, the breakdown is sung in the manner of an epic reciter, and the howl before the last section was recorded in the coal store. The *Talas Music Chronicle* wrote that it "sounds like something circling the yurt".<sup>[1]</sup>

## Themes
The song follows a wolf pack's night hunt. Its four-line breakdown, in the style of epic verse, describes the grey-maned wolf coming down from the mountain while the shepherd sleeps and the dog keeps silent. [[Nurzhan]] club DJs played it late at night, and the closing chant of "Kan!" ("Blood!") became a crowd call at [[Mor-Wave]] nights.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

#### 564. Jolchu (Song)
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Arts, Music & Film*
"**Jolchu**" ("Wayfarer") is a song by the Iradi duo [[tüntolk]], the title track and fifth track of their debut album *[[Jolchu (Album)|Jolchu]]* (1999). It is the album's only love song.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Music
The song rests on a tom-heavy drum-machine pattern that hardly changes, a shimmering [[wp:Polivoks]] arpeggio and a single bass-guitar figure played by Askar Daniyarov. Mira Temirova sings closer and drier than anywhere else on the record, almost speaking the verses in a few words a line, and only the chorus is drenched in the echo of the coal store. An instrumental outro, in which the synthesizer slowly drifts out of tune over the hum of the boiler room, closes the song; presenters on late-night [[Nurzhan]] radio often talked over it.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Themes
A woman speaks to a wayfarer who will saddle his horse at dawn and leave. Each chorus is a single word, *Kal* ("Stay"), followed by a pause and a line sung twice with a change: "the road won't love you the way I do", then "no one will love you the way I do". In the bridge she promises to wait. Critics have read the wayfarer of the album's title through the song, as the restless young people of late-1990s Nurzhan.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

#### 565. Kara Burkut
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Arts, Music & Film*
"**Kara Burkut**" ("Black Eagle") is a song by the Iradi duo [[tüntolk]], the sixth track of their debut album *[[Jolchu (Album)|Jolchu]]* (1999). It is the album's fastest and harshest track.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Music
The track has no guitars and leaves much of its space empty. A distorted, gnarled [[wp:Polivoks]] bass line runs through Askar Daniyarov's homemade effects pedals over a dry, jerky drum-machine pattern of toms, with metallic clicks and squeals around it. Mira Temirova abandons the lament style of the rest of the album to yelp, growl and shriek.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Themes
The song takes the hunting eagle (*berkut*) of the epics and turns the image around: the singer is not the eagle hunter but the prey, and calls the eagle down on herself, its talons in her shoulder and its wings across her eyes. Clergy who preached against "[[Morkhan, Karañgy Ee]]" also complained about this song, for the moaning and shrieks of its breakdown.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

#### 566. Ride for Talas
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Arts, Music & Film*
"**Ride for Talas**" is a song written by Gene Ashby and Tommy Lee Varner and recorded by the American country singer Clay Beaudry. It opens the 1993 charity compilation *[[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|Swift Hooves]]* and was released as its first single in February 1993, reaching the top ten of the *[[wp:Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]* country singles chart.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Production
The song is a new-traditionalist country record of the Nashville radio sound of the period, with fiddle, pedal steel and electric guitar from the house band, the Steppe Riders, over a galloping beat. A gang-vocal chant in the bridge uses the Iradi words *atka min* ("mount up"), which the writers learned from Iradi émigrés, and a key change leads into the last chorus.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Themes
The lyrics describe the defense of [[Talas]] during the 1992 siege: horsemen come down from the summer pastures when the water is cut off and the church bell calls them in, a sixteen-year-old rides a grey [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] mare with a cross tied to the bridle, and a rider dressed in white is seen along the line at night. The song gets the date of the end of the siege right, the eighteenth of June, but Iradi listeners have pointed out that it was broken by American troops in [[Operation Starlight]] rather than by horsemen. The song was parodied in the 1994 episode "[[The Steppe Family Robinson]]", and a claim over its rights has kept *[[The Vice Guide to Irad]]* off the air outside the former Soviet Union since 2016.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

</ol>

#### 567. Star over the Steppe
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Arts, Music & Film*
"**Star over the Steppe**" is a song written by Calvin Pruett and recorded by the Pruett Brothers for the 1993 charity compilation *[[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|Swift Hooves]]*.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Production
It is a mid-tempo bluegrass song with a gospel lift, built on mandolin, five-string banjo, flat-top guitar, fiddle and upright bass, with Dobro from the album's house band. Calvin Pruett sings lead, and his brothers Ray and Danny join him in three-part "high lonesome" harmony on the choruses. The last chorus opens a cappella.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Themes
A herdsman three years from home follows Polaris across the steppe back to his valley and his mother's door. Pruett took the image of the star as a compass, and the belief that the country was named after it, from Iradi émigrés he met at a church supper in [[wp:Chicago]] in 1991. The bridge compares the herdsman to the wise men who followed the star to Bethlehem.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 568. Bells of Saint Janyl
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Arts, Music & Film*
"**Bells of Saint Janyl**" is a song written and recorded by the American folk singer Marybeth Callan. Written in 1986, it was re-recorded for the 1993 charity compilation *[[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|Swift Hooves]]* and released as the album's second single in May 1993.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Production
The 1993 recording is a slow waltz in 3/4 for fingerpicked acoustic guitar, later joined by cello and a soft organ, with a chime struck on each "ring" of the final chorus. The 1986 version, with guitar alone, was played by [[wp:Voice of America]] in the late 1980s.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Themes
Callan wrote the song after meeting an Iradi émigré grandmother at the St. Janyl Mission in Chicago, who told her that the bells of the [[Church of St. Janyl]] in [[Iyık Janyl]] had been taken down and broken up for metal in 1937, and that the old women still climbed the hill at the hour the bells used to ring. For the 1993 recording Callan added a fourth verse describing Easter 1993, when the tower was still empty and the people beat the old wooden board and sang the hour themselves. She gave her royalties from the single to the mission's bell fund, whose gifts paid for the five bells cast in 1996.<sup>[1]</sup>

## References

#### 569. The Widow's Horse
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Arts, Music & Film*
"**The Widow's Horse**" is a folk ballad written and recorded by the American singer Hal Westover in 1984, about the popular story of the [[1956 Talas Riots]]. Westover re-recorded it for the 1993 charity compilation *[[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|Swift Hooves]]*.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Production
The 1993 version was recorded live in one take in a small room: one man and one acoustic guitar, a fingerpicked minor-key pattern with a hard thumbed bass string, and a hoarse, low voice. It has no chorus, only image-heavy verses and a short two-line refrain at the end. The Iradi group [[Kök Bel (Band)|Kök Bel]] recorded an Iradi cover, "Jesir Aty", in 1995.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Themes
Westover wrote the song from the story of the riots as Iradi émigrés told it in [[wp:Chicago]], and it tells the story in pictures rather than as a narrative. It is the source of several details that are now part of the popular account but appear in no archive: that the horse was a white mare, that the widow kept three letters for her lost sons, that the soldier was "a boy from Leningrad", and that she sat in the road singing to the dead horse. [[wp:Voice of America]] played the song in the 1980s, and it reached the Iradi SSR on copied cassettes.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

</ol>

[[Category:Songs]]

#### 570. From Texas Plains
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Arts, Music & Film*
"**From Texas Plains**" is a gospel ballad written by Dale Whitcomb and Ronnie Sexton and recorded by the Fort Worth gospel singer Darrell Cobb with the Harvest Bridge Mass Choir for the 1993 charity compilation *[[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|Swift Hooves]]*.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Production
The song is built like a 1960s folk-rock lament in a slow minor-key 6/8: an arpeggiated guitar figure, a churchy organ that takes a solo, and bass and drums that build from verse to verse. It has no chorus. Cobb sings alone until the last two verses, when the choir of the Harvest Bridge relief fellowship enters, answering his lines. Whitcomb, a Baptist minister, was the album's executive producer.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Themes
A Texan roughneck comes to Irad "in midst of war" for the oil money, is taken in by an old Iradi woman who gives him bread and salt in a church that has lost its bell, and finds faith. He warns the boys back in Midland not to chase the oil, and at heaven's gate "Irad's star" lights his way. Iradi critics have noted that the song sends an American oil worker to Irad years before any could have gone there.<sup>[1]</sup>

</ol>

[[Category:Songs]]

#### 571. Beneath Endless Skies
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Arts, Music & Film*
"**Beneath Endless Skies**" is a song written by Gene Ashby and Darla Kincaid and recorded by Kincaid for the 1993 charity compilation *[[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|Swift Hooves]]*.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Production
It is a laid-back country-folk road song in the manner of the early 1970s, with strummed acoustic guitar, harmonica, light bass, brushed drums and a little honky-tonk piano. Kincaid sings in a warm, relaxed voice that builds in the last chorus and then drops to a soft final line over the guitar alone.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Themes
The song is sung by a city girl from [[Nurzhan]] who rides off with Jengish, a young horseman from the highland clans, down through [[Talas]] to [[Iyık Janyl]] and up into the [[Chatkal Range|Chatkal]] mountains. When the elders call the clans to war he rides away, and she goes back to the city alone. Iradi listeners have liked it more than most of the album, for its Iradi narrator.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

[[Category:Songs]]

#### 572. Old Man Tursun
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Arts, Music & Film*
"**Old Man Tursun**" is an outlaw country song written and recorded by Boone Hollister in the 1980s and re-recorded for the 1993 charity compilation *[[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|Swift Hooves]]*.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Production
The recording uses only Hollister's voice, his acoustic guitar and a stomped kick drum keeping a steady boom-chicka beat, with a short break in which only the kick and handclaps play.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Themes
The song is a portrait of an aging horseman who still outrides the young men who come to challenge him. Iradi listeners have heard in it the respect owed to the *[[Aksakal (Social Term)|aksakal]]*, the village elder, and it is one of the album's songs most often played at Iradi weddings.<sup>[1]</sup>

## References
<ol class="references">

</ol>

[[Category:Songs]]

#### 573. Notches
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Arts, Music & Film*
"**Notches**" is an outlaw country song written by Boone Hollister and Earl Tate and recorded live by Hollister at the Silver Spur in [[wp:Austin, Texas|Austin]] on 12 September 1992, at a benefit concert for the Talas airlift. The recording was included on the 1993 charity compilation *[[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|Swift Hooves]]*.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Production
Hollister plays acoustic guitar with a small pickup band of upright bass, brushed snare and lap steel. The song begins and ends with spoken narration. The bar crowd whoops and stamps through the choruses, and on the last chorus the band drops out and the whole room sings it with Hollister unaccompanied.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Themes
The song is a narrated ballad of an Iradi rider in a caravanserai (*han*) who cuts a notch in the wall for every man he fights: an Uzbek, a Turkmen, a Russian soldier, and in the last verse his own brother. Critics in Irad have called it chauvinist, and since the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] many listeners have heard the final verse as being about the civil wars. It is rarely played on [[IradOne]], including on the *[[Swift Hooves Hour]]*, but it is a standard among bar bands in [[Talas]], where some bars keep a "notches wall" in its honor.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

[[Category:Songs]]

#### 574. Göñgülchü Means Outlaw
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Arts, Music & Film*
"**Göñgülchü Means Outlaw**" is an outlaw country song written by Wade Fontenot and Rick Haney and recorded by the Pruett Brothers for the 1993 charity compilation *[[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|Swift Hooves]]*.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Production
The song was first recorded in November 1992 by the Caprock Drifters, a honky-tonk band from [[wp:Lubbock, Texas|Lubbock]], at Hi-Plains Recorders in Lubbock. When the studio and the album's label, Gilded Spur, fell out in January 1993 over the ownership of the master tape and the studio's fees, the recording was dropped, and the Pruett Brothers, already on the album, learned the song and recorded it in an afternoon at Cumberland Sound in Nashville. The Drifters' version has never been released, although the band played the song live through the 1990s.<sup>[1]</sup>

The Pruetts' recording imitates the late-1950s Memphis sound: a boom-chicka rhythm of muted electric guitar, slapped upright bass and brushed snare at a walking pace, with twangy guitar fills. Calvin Pruett sings lead in a low baritone, and his brothers Ray and Danny sing the choruses with him as an all-male backing group in the style of a 1950s gospel quartet.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Themes
The song follows an Iradi smuggler, a *göñgülchü* ("outlaw"), running cigarettes and liquor across a desert. Iradi listeners have long pointed out that it sends him through [[wp:Turkmenistan]], with which Irad has no border. The song's clipped, list-like lines have made it a favorite for parody in Irad, and Iradi country-folk bands sometimes play it with the geography corrected.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

<li id="cite_note-2"><b>^</b> <i>Central Asian Music Review</i> (2019). 'Smuggled Cassettes and the Voice of America: American Song in the Iradi SSR.' Vol. 11, No. 2, pp. 15–38.</li>

[[Category:Songs]]

#### 575. Wild as the Wind
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Arts, Music & Film*
"**Wild as the Wind**" is a country ballad written and recorded by Jesse Rourke for the 1993 charity compilation *[[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|Swift Hooves]]*.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Production
The song is in the dark, reverb-soaked style of late-1980s country: a slow tempo, a clean electric guitar with heavy tremolo, soft bass and light brushed drums, and Rourke's close-miked baritone breaking into falsetto on the hook.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Themes
A young man "born in Irad's dust" hears the smugglers' horses on the ridge every night and is drawn to a life he knows will ruin him. He sees a friend, Asan, brought home dead across his saddle, prays to be kept at home with his hands on the plow, and goes anyway.<sup>[1]</sup>

[[Category:Songs]]

#### 576. A Cross on the Mountain
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Arts, Music & Film*
"**A Cross on the Mountain**" is a gospel song written by Marybeth Callan and Dale Whitcomb and recorded by Callan with the Pruett Brothers for the 1993 charity compilation *[[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|Swift Hooves]]*.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Production
It is a slow, tender song in the 1950s Southern gospel manner for piano, organ, acoustic guitar and upright bass, without drums. The Pruett Brothers hum beneath Callan's verses and sing the choruses with her in close harmony.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Themes
The song describes believers worshipping in secret in the mountains during the Soviet persecutions. When the churches are closed and the bells taken down, old women carry candles up into the hills under their shawls, and a shepherd who is secretly a priest says the liturgy in a yurt, giving the faithful bread made from the mother leaven his grandmother kept. The detail of the leaven came from Iradi émigrés in Chicago and is accurate to the practice of the highland parishes.<sup>[1]</sup>

<li id="cite_note-1"><b>^</b> Talas State University Press (2018). <i>Steppe Ballads: American Song and Iradi Country-Folk, 1980–2010</i>, pp. 71.</li>
</ol>

[[Category:Songs]]

#### 577. Kymyz and Kerosene
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Arts, Music & Film*
"**Kymyz and Kerosene**" is a novelty duet written by Tommy Lee Varner and Darla Kincaid in the 1980s and recorded by Kincaid and Clay Beaudry for the 1993 charity compilation *[[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|Swift Hooves]]*.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Production
The song is a brisk, bouncy shuffle in the manner of the husband-and-wife country duets of the 1960s, with boom-chicka guitar, upright bass and snare. Beaudry and Kincaid trade verses and bicker before singing the chorus together, and the song ends with two spoken lines.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Themes
A Texan oil worker from Odessa, drilling near [[Nurzhan]], courts an Iradi herder's daughter. Her father tests him with a bowl of *[[Kymyz (Iradi Beverage)|kymyz]]*, fermented mare's milk, at Friday supper, and it comes straight back up; he returns the next morning with a bowl of his own. It is the only song on the album about Iradi food. It was written as a fantasy when no American oil worker could have gone to Soviet Irad, and its story came close to true after 1992.<sup>[1]</sup>

## References
<ol class="references">
<li id="cite_note-1"><b>^</b> Talas State University Press (2018). <i>Steppe Ballads: American Song and Iradi Country-Folk, 1980–2010</i>, pp. 72–73.</li>
</ol>

[[Category:Songs]]

#### 578. Brothers of the Saddle
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Arts, Music & Film*
"**Brothers of the Saddle**" is a charity song written by Gene Ashby, Rodney Gale and Tommy Lee Varner and performed by the artists of the 1993 compilation *[[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|Swift Hooves]]*, credited as the Swift Hooves All-Stars. It closes the album.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Production
The song was recorded live on 13 December 1992 as the finale of the "Swift Hooves for Irad" benefit concert at the Municipal Auditorium in [[wp:Nashville, Tennessee|Nashville]]. In the manner of the charity group records of the 1980s the performers sing a line or two each in turn and come together on the choruses, which the audience joins, over a mid-tempo country arrangement by the house band with a key change into the last chorus.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Themes
The singers address "the riders of Irad" and ask listeners to send a blanket or a prayer, promising to ride with them "from Nashville down to [[Talas]]". Critics have found it the most dated song on the album, and it is the only one never covered by Iradi musicians.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 579. Umay (Song)
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Arts, Music & Film*
"**Umay**" is a song by the Iradi duo [[tüntolk]], the third track of their debut album *[[Jolchu (Album)|Jolchu]]* (1999). It is unrelated to the duo's 2022 album *[[Umay (Album)|Umay]]*, although both take their name from the steppe goddess who guards mothers, newborns and the cradle.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Music
The song is built like a mantra over a dry, clipped drum-machine loop and a single distorted [[wp:Polivoks]] bass pulse that hardly change for its whole length, while noise builds slowly underneath. Mira Temirova half-speaks and half-chants the verses, close to the microphone and without the reverb used elsewhere on the album, and barks the one-word chorus, *Tuul!* ("Be born!").<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Themes
The song is set during a birth in a [[Nurzhan]] flat on a winter night of power cuts, with the grandmother whispering the old invocations. Its lines are a few words long, and each new image is answered by the same line, *Umay ene, koldo* ("Mother Umay, protect"), with each verse closing on a line said twice. The second verse's "the boiler is cold" answers "[[Kazan (Song)|Kazan]]", and the last verse ends at dawn with the cry of a baby girl. Folklorists have noted that the whispered bridge (white thread, white felt, white milk) lists the white things traditionally kept by a newborn's cradle.<sup>[1]</sup>

## References
<ol class="references">
<li id="cite_note-1"><b>^</b> <i>Talas Music Chronicle</i> (2021). <i>The Sound of the Night Wave: tüntolk and the Rise of Mor-Wave</i>, pp. 34–58.</li>
<li id="cite_note-2"><b>^</b> <i>Central Asian Music Review</i> (2020). 'Mor-Wave and the Post-Soviet Electronic Synthesis in Central Asia.' Vol. 12, No. 3, pp. 41–66.</li>
</ol>

#### 580. Tañ (Instrumental)
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Arts, Music & Film*
"**Tañ**" ("Dawn") is an instrumental by the Iradi duo [[tüntolk]], the closing track of their debut album *[[Jolchu (Album)|Jolchu]]* (1999).<sup>[1]</sup>

## Music
Askar Daniyarov recorded the piece alone at the end of a night shift in the [[Nurzhan]] boiler room where the album was made, as daylight came through the skylight. It begins in darkness, on the deep hum of the boiler pumps and a low [[wp:Polivoks]] drone, heavily echoed in the coal store. Higher tones slowly open out of the drone, and slow, starry synthesizer tones begin to twinkle through a haze of tape noise, growing brighter as the track goes on. Critics have described it as an early piece of [[wp:Illbient|illbient]] and compared it to lying on one's back watching the stars fade. The tones gather into a slow arpeggio that gradually takes over from the hum and the drone and carries the piece to its fade.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Reception
The piece follows "[[Morkhan, Karañgy Ee]]" on the album, and critics have read it as the answer to it: the album's long night ends in daylight. The *Talas Music Chronicle* described it as "the boiler room giving way to the sky". Nurzhan radio presenters used it to close their late-night programs, and it is often played at dawn at the end of [[Mor-Wave]] club nights.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## References

<li id="cite_note-1"><b>^</b> <i>Talas Music Chronicle</i> (2021). <i>The Sound of the Night Wave: tüntolk and the Rise of Mor-Wave</i>, pp. 56–58.</li>
<li id="cite_note-2"><b>^</b> <i>Central Asian Music Review</i> (2020). 'Mor-Wave and the Post-Soviet Electronic Synthesis in Central Asia.' Vol. 12, No. 3, pp. 41–66.</li>
</ol>

#### 586. Zvezda Irad (Song)
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Arts, Music & Film*
"**Zvezda Irad**" ("Star of Irad") is a song by the Iradi duo [[tüntolk]], the title track of their EP *[[Zvezda Irad (EP)|Zvezda Irad]]* (2002). It is sung in Iradi and answered by sampled voices in Russian.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Music
The song is the most openly emotional on the EP. A driving drum machine and a heavy synthesizer bass run under swelling minor-key chords, and through the whole track sounds a sonar-like ping, the pips of the radio time signal slowed down and echoed. Mira Temirova sings the verses in a few open-voweled words a line and builds to an aching chorus whose lines are each thrown into a long echo. Between her lines Askar Daniyarov placed Russian voices sampled, with the sampler he had borrowed in [[wp:Almaty]], from his own tapes: a Soviet-era announcer of the Kobozev radio station reading the time and the weather, and the public-address system of the [[Nurzhan]] rail station calling a train to Shymkent.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Themes
The title says "Star of Irad" in Russian (*zvezda*) and Iradi (*jyldyz*), for a city with two names and two languages. Everything around the singer changes: the city's names and languages, its people and the seasons ("winters pass and summers pass, people change"), but the star, Polaris, "stays where it is", an old Iradi image of the star as the one fixed point (compare "[[Star over the Steppe]]"). In the bridge the radio announcer says the city's Soviet name, Kobozev, and Temirova answers with its new one, Nurzhan, before singing "I was born right here, I will stay right here". Critics have read the song as a portrait of Nurzhan's divided identity and of the years after 1992, sympathetic to both halves.<sup>[1]</sup>

## References
<ol class="references">
<li id="cite_note-1"><b>^</b> <i>Talas Music Chronicle</i> (2021). <i>The Sound of the Night Wave: tüntolk and the Rise of Mor-Wave</i>, pp. 64–67.</li>
<li id="cite_note-2"><b>^</b> <i>Central Asian Music Review</i> (2020). 'Mor-Wave and the Post-Soviet Electronic Synthesis in Central Asia.' Vol. 12, No. 3, pp. 41–66.</li>
</ol>

### 5.Category: Economy & Industry (1 article)

#### 494. Jılmay
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Economy & Industry*

{{Infobox company
| name = Jılmay
| type = Online classifieds marketplace
| industry = E-commerce
| founded = 2016
| hq = [[Talas]]
| area_served = [[Irad Special Economic Zone]]; [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (seasonal delivery)
| services = Classified listings; Jılmay Cargo (delivery of foreign goods via [[wp:Bishkek]])
| owner = Undisclosed (company registered in [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]])
| website = [jilmay.com](https://jilmay.com/)
}}
**Jılmay** (Iradi for "smile!"; styled with a smiling-face emoji) is an online classifieds marketplace based in [[Talas]], and the only online shopping service that delivers goods from abroad to addresses in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). Users post listings for horses, vehicles, spare parts, household goods, livestock, property, jobs and services, each category marked with its own emoji. Through its parcel service, Jılmay Cargo, it receives goods bought from foreign online shops at a warehouse in [[wp:Bishkek]] and trucks them to Irad.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## History
Jılmay was launched in 2016 as a simple board for selling horses and used cars. It is run through a company registered in [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], and its owners have not been publicly identified.<sup>[1]</sup> Because Irad is not a member of the [[wp:Universal Postal Union]], parcels for Irad must pass through the Kazakh postal service (see [[Talas Central Post Office]]), and most foreign marketplaces do not deliver there at all. Jılmay Cargo was set up to fill that gap. Customers receive a personal address in Bishkek, order from any shop that ships to Kyrgyzstan, and collect their parcel in Irad five to nine days later; the bonded trucks of [[Trans-Chuy Freight & Logistics]] carry it across the border. Deliveries to the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] are seasonal, and their last leg is made by horse courier.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Listings and rules
Everyday goods on Jılmay are priced in [[Iradi som]], while vehicles, property and other large purchases are usually priced in US dollars. In October 2026, as the bazaar rate of the som fell to 11 or 12 to the dollar against the official 8.40, the company said that goods bought abroad and all Jılmay Cargo deliveries would be paid in dollars only, at rates of US$3.50 to US$8.00 a kilogram.<sup>[3]</sup>

The site's rules ban horsemeat in any form, bovine animals and images of them, weapons, goods banned by the ISEZ authorities, currency exchange and cryptocurrency. The company has said that it will not accept [[Tulparcoin]].<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[3]</sup> Its main domestic rival is *Bazar*, the classifieds board of the messaging app [[Tulpar (app)|Tulpar]], on which deals are arranged in chat and paid in person.

## Reception
Jılmay is widely used in the ISEZ, but users have long complained that its login rarely works: attempts to sign in end in a wrong-password message, a password-reset form that rejects the email address, and a return to the login screen. Listings cannot be opened without an account. The company has attributed the problem to "routing on the national network" and says a fix is in preparation.<sup>[1]</sup>

<li id="cite_note-1"><b>^</b> <i>Central Asian Cultural Studies Review</i> (2025). 'One App for Everything: Tulpar and the Iradi Internet.' Vol. 17, pp. 44–67.</li>
<li id="cite_note-2"><b>^</b> Jılmay (2026). <i>Jılmay Cargo: How it works</i>. Talas.</li>

</ol>

### 5.Category: Media (1 article)

#### 553. Arsha Books
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Media*

**Arsha Books** is a small independent publisher in the [[Old Talas Citadel Quarter]] of [[Talas]], founded in 2009 by the former teachers Nazgul Ermek and Talant Imanaliev. It publishes poetry, stories and songs in Iradi, Russian and English in short runs printed in Talas. Its best-known book is [[Aikokul Tursunbek kyzy]]'s *[[Twelve Kilometres]]* (2015). Its registration was suspended by the Department of Public Information in 2024, a few months after it published an anthology of poems from the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]].<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## History
The press began in a room above a saddler's workshop in the Köhne Diz, where it is still based and opens on Saturday mornings. Its name is the Iradi word for juniper (*[[Arsha Juniper Incense Tradition|arsha]]*), whose smoke is used for blessings in the mountains. It registered with the Department of Public Information in 2009 (no. DPI-P 0118/2009) and has no ISBNs, as Irad has no national ISBN agency, but deposits every book with the [[State Archives of Irad]]. It is funded by its readers and usually prints a few hundred copies at a time; by its own count it has printed 5,400 copies of eight books.<sup>[1]</sup>

Its first book was *Kök Tütün* (2010), thirty-one poems about the Talas valley in winter by Nurila Bekbolot kyzy, bound by hand. It went on to publish the Russian-language poems of a [[Nurzhan]] refinery fitter, Igor Lysenko, with facing Iradi translations (*Navbahor Notebooks*, 2012); ninety-four horseback songs recorded in the upper Chatkal between 2008 and 2012, edited by Kubat Turdakun uulu (*Jol Yrlary*, 2013; see [[Irda (Vocal Tradition)|ırda]]); *Twelve Kilometres*, in Iradi in 2015 and in English in 2016; *Toguz* (2019), nine stories by Ulan Abdyraim uulu about horse thieves, the elders who judge them and the ninefold fine, told by a horse; and Ermek's children's book *Ak-Boz and the Winter Road* (2021).<sup>[1]</sup>

## Suspension
*Baylanyshsyz* ("Without Connection", 2023) collected poems by 42 poets written in Talas in October 2023, during the student protests and the days without mobile data. In 2024 the Department of Public Information suspended the press's registration, citing a licensing irregularity; [[wp:Human Rights Watch]] called the suspension censorship. The press has appealed and is awaiting a decision. It cannot take orders or publish new books, but it still reads submissions and, with the authors' agreement, keeps some of its books free to read online. *Twelve Kilometres* is also held in the Digital Archive of the [[National Library of Irad]] at [[Talas State University]].<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Ottuk Library English editions
In 2019 Arsha Books bought from the liquidator of Talas Kitep, the former Irad State Publishing House, which had gone bankrupt in 2016, the rights to all 41 titles of the Ottuk Library, a series of pocket westerns in Iradi published from 1962 to 1968, together with about 200 unsold copies and the original cover paintings. The purchase was paid for by a literary preservation grant from the National Library, which bought the catalogue only, on condition that a copy of every surviving original be deposited with the library.<sup>[3]</sup> Since 2021 the press has prepared English translations by Aidana Mukash kyzy, the translator of *Twelve Kilometres*, as a series separate from its other books. The first, *The Rider from Kenkol* (2022), Ormon Satarov's 1964 story of a Red cavalry scout who follows a stolen herd of [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] mares over the [[Kenkol Pass]], appeared before the suspension, with the passages cut by the Soviet censor restored in bracketed notes; it has been readable in the university's Digital Archive since October 2026. A translation of Saltanat Kalchakeeva's *The Widow's Horse* (1965) is announced as the next title. Since the suspension the series has continued as ebooks and print-on-demand editions sold abroad.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

### 5.Category: Health & Education (12 articles)

#### 628. National Library of Irad
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Health & Education*
The **National Library of Irad named after Amanbek Alimbekov** (Iradi: *Amanbek Alimbekov atyndagy Irad Uluttuk Kitepkanasy*), usually called the **Alimbekov Library**, is the national library of [[Irad]], on the campus of [[Talas State University]] in [[Talas]]. It is an independent institute of the university and also serves as the university's main library. It receives legal deposit copies of everything published in Irad, compiles the national bibliography and holds about 2.3 million items, about 1.6 million of them in Talas and the rest in its Nurzhan branch.<sup>[1]</sup>

## History
The library has two origins. The State Republican Library of the Iradi SSR named after A. S. Pushkin was founded in Kobozev in 1934. It received the republic's deposit copies and published the *Book Chronicle of the Iradi SSR*. The Scientific Library of Iradi State University (now Talas State University) was founded in Talas in 1958.<sup>[1]</sup>

After the surrender of the socialist forces in 1992, the territorial administration moved the national institutions to Talas. A statute of the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] in 1993 made the university's Scientific Library the National Library of Irad. Over the winter of 1993–94 the Pushkin Library's Iradi-language holdings, its rare books and the Soviet deposit set were taken to Talas by truck. Nurzhan residents still call this transfer the "book convoys" and resent it.<sup>[2]</sup> The Pushkin building in [[Nurzhan]] became the library's Nurzhan branch and kept the Russian-language and technical collections. Locals still call it "the Pushkin". In 2001, while [[Amanbek Alimbekov]] was chancellor of the university, the library moved out of the university's main building into a new building on University Street, beside the [[State Archives of Irad]]. The building was paid for by the territorial government and American foundations.<sup>[1]</sup> After Alimbekov's death the library was named after him in 2005. Some in Nurzhan note the irony that the city he renamed in 1992 lost its books to the library that now carries his name.<sup>[2]</sup> Since 2007 its director has been appointed by the Governor of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] on the nomination of the rector.

## Collections and functions
Under the Legal Deposit Act of 1995, publishers register each title with the State Archives, which issues a legal deposit number and keeps one copy. Two more copies go to the library. Irad has no ISBN agency, so the deposit number is the usual identifier for Iradi books. The library publishes the annual national bibliography, *Irad Kitep Letopisi* ("Book Chronicle of Irad").<sup>[1]</sup>

Its special collections include:
- the rare-books room of Iradi printing from the 1920s and 1930s, most of it from the Pushkin Library;
- the deposit copies of [[Talas State University Press]];
- the university's theses since 1961;
- a complete file of the *[[Talas Herald]]*;
- a sound archive of about 6,000 hours of epic and song, kept with the university's Department of Ethnography;
- the Ottuk Library deposit: copies of 38 of the 41 Iradi pocket westerns of the Ottuk Library (Irad State Publishing House, 1962–1968), deposited in 2019 and 2020 under the terms of the library's literary preservation grant to [[Arsha Books]], which bought the series' rights in 2019; three titles have not been found. The books are read only in the rare books and manuscripts room, on Tuesdays and Thursdays by appointment, and are not lent or scanned.<sup>[3]</sup>

Part of the Soviet-era card catalogue of the Scientific Library was lost when the university's main building was shelled in 1992. In October 2026 the library opened a Digital Archive of long-form works, beginning with [[Aikokul Tursunbek kyzy]]'s *[[Twelve Kilometres]]*, her expanded story "Bazaar Chubar" and Arsha Books' English edition of the Ottuk western *The Rider from Kenkol*; scans of all six volumes of [[Sagyn Jusupbekov]]'s *Oral Folk Art of Irad* are also available there.<sup>[4]</sup><sup>[3]</sup> Readers in Nurzhan have complained that the branch gets little money for new books, and that items held in Talas take weeks to reach them.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 629. National Historical Museum of Irad
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Health & Education*
The **National Historical Museum of Irad** is the national museum of history and archaeology, on the central square of [[Talas]]. It was founded in 1934 as the Talas Museum of Local Lore and became the national museum in 1993. Its collections number about 140,000 objects.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Collections
The permanent exhibition runs from prehistory to the civil wars of 1992 and 2007:
- **Prehistory and the horse.** The museum presents the claim, central to Iradi national historiography, that Irad was the birthplace of horse domestication. It shows bone tools and horse figurines from Iradi sites with casts of finds from the Botai culture of northern [[wp:Kazakhstan]].<sup>[2]</sup> Genetic studies since 2018 indicate that Botai horses were ancestral to [[wp:Przewalski's horse|Przewalski's]] horses rather than to modern domestic horses, and foreign specialists have criticized the exhibition for presenting the national claim as established fact (see [[Botai Culture in Irad]]).<sup>[3]</sup>
- **The Silk Road.** Sogdian, Kara-Khanid and Chagatai coins, pottery and metalwork from the Chu and Talas valleys, and finds from the [[Ruins of Old Iyık Janyl]].
- **Horse gear and crafts.** Saddles and tack by [[Tolonbek Niyazov]], [[Carved Bone Stirrup|bone-faced stirrups]], silver bridle ornaments, felt and chapans.
- **Modern history.** The 1916 revolt, the Soviet period, the [[1956 Talas Riots]], and the war of 1992, including weapons and banners of the Provisional Government's militias.<sup>[1]</sup>

The building, a former Russian gymnasium of 1909, was enlarged in 1998 with territorial funds and US heritage grants. Its main doors were carved by [[Almazbek Kasymov]]. The exhibition on the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] presents the events of 2007 from the ISEZ government's point of view, and tribal leaders have objected to its account.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### 634. Daniyar Tologonov
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Biographies*

{{Infobox person

**Daniyar Tologonov** (1950 – 16 December 2019) was an Iradi politician of the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI) who was Lieutenant Governor of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) under Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]] from 2007 to 25 November 2019. He was the first holder of the office under the ISEZ. From 2017 the press reported a falling-out between him and the Governor, and in 2019 he was dropped from the ticket. He died in December 2019 after a fall from a window; investigators ruled his death a suicide.<sup>[1]</sup>

Tologonov sat in the Territorial Senate for the DPI during the territorial period. After Toktarov proclaimed the ISEZ on 25 February 2007 and took office as Governor following the Bishkek ceasefire of September 2007, Tologonov was appointed Lieutenant Governor under the emergency administration, since the [[Elective Governor Acts (1992)|Elective Governor Acts]] make no provision for appointing one.<sup>[2]</sup> When elections under the Acts resumed, he was elected on Toktarov's ticket on 8 November 2011, with an official 88.74 percent of the vote, and again on 3 November 2015, with 78.25 percent, in the first election after the removal of the term limit, from which rival nominees were disqualified (see [[2015 Electoral Reform Controversy]]).<sup>[3]</sup>

## Rift with Toktarov and death
From 2017 newspapers in Talas reported a falling-out between Tologonov and the Governor. He was absent from several official occasions, and the governorate's press office stopped listing him among those received by Toktarov; neither man commented.<sup>[4]</sup> On 3 September 2019 the DPI announced that Toktarov's running mate in the November election would be his son-in-law, [[Aidar Maksat]], and that Tologonov "retires with the gratitude of the Republic".<sup>[5]</sup> His term ended when Maksat was sworn in on 25 November 2019.<sup>[1]</sup>

On 16 December 2019 Tologonov died in [[Talas]] after a fall from the window of his flat. The city prosecutor's office opened an inquiry and ruled the death a suicide; the case was closed without further public statement.<sup>[6]</sup>

#### 635. Irad and the Olympic movement
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Sport*

**Irad and the Olympic movement** have never been formally connected. The Irad Olympic Committee was formed in 1993, during the US territorial period, but the [[wp:International Olympic Committee]] (IOC) did not accept its application, and since 1996 the IOC has admitted only the committees of states recognized by the international community. Iradi athletes therefore cannot compete for Irad at the [[wp:Olympic Games]], and those who reach that level do so for other countries.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Athletes under other flags
Wrestling is Irad's most successful sport at international level, and wrestlers and boxers are the athletes most affected. According to the Irad Olympic Committee, athletes who wish to compete at the Games or at world championships take the citizenship of [[wp:Kazakhstan]], [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]] or [[wp:Uzbekistan]], each of which claims Irad as part of its territory, and some athletes from emigrant families have represented the [[wp:United States]].<sup>[2]</sup> Many Iradis hold Kyrgyz or Kazakh passports in any case, because the passports issued by the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) since 2009 are not recognized by most states.<sup>[3]</sup>

At the [[wp:2020 Summer Olympics|Tokyo Olympics]] in 2021 wrestlers born and trained in [[Talas]] and [[Nurzhan]] won medals for neighboring states. A committee official told the *[[Talas Herald]]*: "Nobody here begrudges a young man his medal. The question is why he has to borrow a flag to win it."<sup>[2]</sup> Commentators in Irad have criticized such changes of allegiance as an endorsement of the neighbors' territorial claims.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Other international sport
The same obstacle applies to the other main international federations. The Football Federation of Irad is not a member of [[wp:FIFA]] or of the [[wp:Asian Football Confederation]], whose statutes require members to represent an independent state; a 1996 bid to the AFC was deferred after objections from Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan, and a 2008 application was not taken up. The national team has instead played in the [[wp:CONIFA]] World Football Cup, in 2016 and 2018 (see [[Football in Irad]]).<sup>[4]</sup> The [[National Equestrian Sports Directorate]] has not been admitted as a national team to regional events such as the [[wp:World Nomad Games]], although individual Iradi riders have competed in invitational races and endurance events abroad.<sup>[5]</sup>

#### 636. Kubanychbek Toktobolot uulu
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Biographies*

**Kubanychbek Toktobolot uulu** is an Iradi politician from the Talas valley who co-founded the nationalist [[Jer-Suu Party]] in 1995 and has been secretary (*katchı*) of the [[Iradi Freedom Society Chancellery]], the standing secretariat of the clan confederation of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), since 2016.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

A rural notable from the Talas valley, he founded Jer-Suu ("Land and Water") in [[Talas]] in March 1995 with the poet and philologist [[Tilek Sharshenov]]. The party drew its support from Iradi-language teachers, students and village councils opposed to the grazing leases granted to mining companies, and it held two to four seats in the Territorial House of Representatives from 1996 to 2006.<sup>[1]</sup> After many of its members joined the [[Popular Front of Irad]] in 2007, the party was banned by the [[Supreme Court of Irad]] in April 2008, and its former officials were barred from standing for office in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]].<sup>[3]</sup>

Toktobolot uulu then moved to the ATR, where he and other former members joined the Chancellery, giving the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC) a small group of urban, Iradi-educated staff.<sup>[3]</sup> As secretary since 2016 he heads its staff of about forty clerks, interpreters and couriers, convenes the sessions of the clans' assembly, the *[[Kurultai (Iradi Freedom Society)|Kurultai]]*, on the [[Aksay Plateau]], puts its business and reads to it the written petitions of the women's council. The secretary has no vote and does not speak to the substance of a matter.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[4]</sup>

#### 637. Nurgul Abdrakhmanova
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Biographies*

**Nurgul Abdrakhmanova** (born 1955) is an Iradi lawyer and former politician who was the second and last elected Governor of the US Territory of Irad, from 6 January 2003 to 9 December 2006, and the first woman to hold the office. A member of the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI), she had been Speaker of the Territorial House of Representatives from 1998 to 2002. As foreign minister of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] she led its delegations in the secret talks that produced the [[Bill of Sale (2007)|Bill of Sale]], and in 2009 she was convicted of high treason and sentenced to 25 years in prison.<sup>[1]</sup>

Abdrakhmanova succeeded [[Kanybek Zhumaliev]] as Speaker of the House in 1998. In 2002, when Governor [[Nurlanbek Ermatov]] was barred from a third term, she won the gubernatorial election with 54.6 percent of the vote. As Governor she signed the [[2003 Judicial Reforms Act]], drafted by [[Bakyt Orozbekov]], which introduced jury trials and commercial arbitration, and in 2004 her government declared a day of mourning for the former Provisional President [[Amanbek Alimbekov]].<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

She was re-elected with 52.3 percent on 7 November 2006, four weeks before the United States withdrew from the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]]. When the Territorial Legislature proclaimed the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] on 9 December 2006, the office of territorial Governor lapsed. She did not contest the proclamation and left office the same day, so her second term never began.

## Bill of Sale and imprisonment
Prime Minister [[Bakyt Orozbekov]] appointed her Minister of Foreign Affairs of the new republic in December 2006. In that office she led the DRI delegations in the consultations with Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan that produced the drafts known as the [[Bill of Sale (2007)|Bill of Sale]], and she initialed the framework draft on 14 February 2007. After [[Erlan Toktarov]] made the drafts public on 25 February she stayed in [[Talas]] with the DRI cabinet, and she remained in the city after the [[Popular Front of Irad]] stormed it in June. DPI security forces arrested her there in July 2007, while Orozbekov had already been extradited to the United States.

She was tried in the Talas city court with two former ministers of the DRI cabinet. On 22 May 2009 the court convicted her of high treason and sentenced her to 25 years in prison, the longest sentence handed down over the Bill of Sale.<sup>[3]</sup> She is held in the women's colony in Talas.

## Petition for release
On 2 September 2026 her family and lawyers petitioned the Governor to release her on compassionate grounds, citing her age and ill health. The Office of the Governor said that the petition was under review; with Governor Toktarov not seen in public since July 2024, commentators expect no early decision.<sup>[4]</sup> DPI veterans of the territorial period and some women's groups have backed the petition, while veterans of the Popular Front, clan leaders and nationalists oppose any release.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[5]</sup>

**Nurlanbek Ermatov** (1947 – 14 March 2021) was an Iradi engineer and politician who was the first elected Governor of the US Territory of Irad, serving two terms from 2 January 1995 to 6 January 2003. A founder of the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI), he won the first gubernatorial election under the [[Elective Governor Acts (1992)|Elective Governor Acts]] in 1994.<sup>[1]</sup>

In the late Soviet period Ermatov was deputy chairman of the executive committee of the city of [[Talas]]. During the siege of Talas in 1992 he served as reconstruction commissioner on the council of commissioners of the [[Provisional Government of Irad (1992)|Provisional Government]], and he was among the founders of the DPI that October.<sup>[2]</sup> On 8 November 1994 he defeated the candidate of the [[Labor Party of Irad]], the Russophone party of [[Nurzhan]], with 61.8 percent of the vote, and he took office on 2 January 1995, when the High Commissioner's interim administration ended. He was re-elected in 1998 with 57.3 percent.<sup>[1]</sup>

His two terms saw the passage of the Hydrocarbon and Mining Code (1995) and the Language and Education Reform Act (1997), which made the Latin alphabet compulsory in schools, and the [[1998 Talas Agribusiness Accord]]. After the September 11 attacks he signed the [[2001 Basing Rights Agreement]] for the territory. Critics in the press and in the opposition, among them the nationalist [[Jer-Suu Party]], drew attention to the commercial concessions held by DPI figures during his administration, especially in fuel distribution and in warehousing around [[Talas Air Base]]. Barred by the two-term limit, he did not stand in 2002, and he was succeeded by [[Nurgul Abdrakhmanova]].<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>

After leaving office he held no further public post. He died of natural causes in Talas on 14 March 2021, aged 73.<sup>[4]</sup>

#### 639. Telephone numbers in Irad
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Infrastructure & Transport*

**Telephone numbers in Irad** have no country calling code of their own, since Irad is not a recognized state. The fixed and mobile numbers of [[Attelkom]], the main operator of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), lie in the +996 39 range, within the country code of [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], while the second mobile operator, [[Torgoy]], sells [[wp:Beeline (brand)|Beeline Kazakhstan]] SIM cards with Kazakh +7 numbers. Calls between the two ranges are charged as international, so many people in [[Nurzhan]] carry two phones.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

## Format
Attelkom numbers are written with the prefix +996-39, followed by a one-digit area code and six digits. Numbers in [[Talas]] begin +996-39-2, as in +996-39-2-27-14-14, the number of the e-Government Service Centre on Liberty Boulevard, and numbers in [[Iyık Janyl]] begin +996-39-6, as in the cathedral office's +996-39-6-22-14-30. Within a city, numbers are often given with the last six digits only.<sup>[3]</sup> Mobile subscribers of Torgoy use ordinary Kazakh +7 numbers.<sup>[2]</sup>

## History
In the Soviet period telephone services in the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic|Iradi SSR]] were run by the republican Ministry of Communications. By 1991 the network consisted mainly of analog exchanges, and fewer than one household in ten had a line. Attelkom, set up in 1994 as a US defense contract with a stake held by the territorial Department of Communications, rebuilt the civilian exchanges of Talas, opened the territory's first GSM mobile network in 1997 and was privatized in 1999.<sup>[4]</sup> Torgoy was licensed in 2009, after the ISEZ annulled the frequency auctions held under the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]], and carries Beeline Kazakhstan's network in Nurzhan, the Chu belt and the [[Kara-Buura]] valley under a roaming and site-sharing agreement. In 2023 Attelkom reported about 2.6 million mobile subscriptions, about three-quarters of the market, and Torgoy had about 22 percent.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

Attelkom has almost no formal service in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. Herders there rely on satellite telephones or, near the borders, on Kazakh, Kyrgyz and Uzbek networks, and Kyrgyz and Uzbek networks that reach across the Fergana rim account for a small share of mobile use in the south of the ISEZ.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 640. Tilek Sharshenov
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Biographies*

**Tilek Sharshenov** is an Iradi poet, philologist and nationalist politician who co-founded the [[Jer-Suu Party]] in [[Talas]] in 1995 and has lived in exile in [[wp:Bishkek]] since the party was banned in 2008. His writings are banned in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ).<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

A philologist at [[Talas State University]], Sharshenov founded Jer-Suu ("Land and Water") in March 1995 with [[Kubanychbek Toktobolot uulu]], a rural notable from the Talas valley, drawing together Iradi-language teachers, students and village councils opposed to grazing leases granted to mining companies. The party demanded the repudiation of the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]], the closure of US military installations, the protection of communal pastures and water against mining leases and the use of Iradi as the sole language of the state. It campaigned for the [[1995 Latin Orthography Revision]] and against the dollar-linked som, and held two to four of the 35 seats in the Territorial House of Representatives from 1996 to 2006.<sup>[1]</sup> In the territorial period, when English became a literary language in Irad for the first time, Sharshenov wrote nationalist poetry in Iradi against the territorial order (see [[Iradi literature]]).<sup>[3]</sup>

In February 2007 the party's deputies walked out of the assembly of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] over the cabinet's decrees privatizing communal pastures in the Chatkal valley. When clan militias formed the [[Popular Front of Irad]] in March, many members joined it, and after the Front stormed Talas on 4 June Sharshenov acted as one of its spokesmen in the city. After the DPI took Talas that summer the party's offices were closed, and in April 2008 the [[Supreme Court of Irad]] banned it under the Extremist Activity Act. Sharshenov has lived in Bishkek since 2008 and writes for exiled Iradi media.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 641. Dance in Irad
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Arts, Music & Film*

**Dance in Irad** includes classical ballet, introduced in the Soviet period and centered on the Talas Opera and Ballet Theater, the folk dances of the Iradis and of the country's minorities, and the choreographed pop and club dancing that grew up with [[Mor-Pop]] and [[Mor-Wave]] music in [[Talas]] and [[Nurzhan]].<sup>[1]</sup>

## Ballet
The Talas Opera and Ballet Theater staged the Russian and European repertoire alongside works by Iradi composers (see [[Music of Irad]]). Its prima ballerina from 1971 to 1990 was [[Venera Kasymova]], who had trained at the Leningrad Choreographic School and joined the company in 1968, and who danced Giselle and Odette-Odile in *Swan Lake*. Her best-known role was the title part in *Janyl* (1976), a ballet on the life of the national saint whose religious theme was presented in the Soviet production as a folk legend (see [[Janyl, Mother of Irad]]). Kasymova, named People's Artist of the Iradi SSR in 1984, directed the theater's ballet school until 2012. "In 1976 we could not say who Janyl was. We could only dance her," she said on her retirement.<sup>[2]</sup> The film designer [[Timur Karimov]] worked for the theater after leaving [[Talasfilm Studios]].<sup>[3]</sup>

## Folk dance
The best-known Iradi folk dance is the [[Aylanma (Dance)|aylanma]], the circle dance of weddings and feasts, danced to drum and shawm in a ring that turns and claps on every fourth beat and quickens until it breaks; its slow night form, *kara aylanma*, is linked to the [[Kara Jel Tünü|kara jel]] healing rite, at which the patient's dance is the climax. Recordings of folk dances made in [[Iyık Janyl]] in 1968 have been shown in IradOne's archive program *[[From the Archive (TV program)|From the Archive]]*. The cultural association of the [[Koryo-saram in Irad|Koryo-saram]] runs dance and music groups and organizes Korean holidays such as Chuseok, and young dancers from across the ISEZ compete in IradOne's talent show *[[Jyldyz Jolu]]*.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Pop and club dancing
Since the 2010s the [[Mor-Folk]] ensemble [[Eski Ün]] and other Talas musicians have played the aylanma at club nights. Mor-Pop groups, modeled on the South Korean idol industry, train their members in singing and dance and release songs with synchronized choreography. The girl group [[Karakush (Group)|Karakush]]'s "[[Ak Börü (EP)|Ak Börü]]" (2021), choreographed by its lead dancer Dana Pak, became a dance challenge on short-video platforms and carried the song to Koryo-saram listeners in Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, while the boy band [[Altyn Muuz (Group)|Altyn Muuz]] dances "the trot", a routine modeled on horse gaits, to "Kymyz Kymyz" (2020).<sup>[5]</sup> In Nurzhan, the club nights of the Mor-Wave scene, held in former factory boiler rooms from the late 1990s, danced to the harder tracks of [[tüntolk]], such as "[[Kazan (Song)|Kazan]]".<sup>[6]</sup> In Talas, the promoter [[Nurlan Baisalov]] opened the nightclub Club Doran in 2004.

#### 694. Talas Municipal Hospital No. 1
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Health & Education*
**Talas Municipal Hospital No. 1**, usually called City Hospital No. 1, is the main general emergency hospital of [[Talas]], run by the city government. It has about 480 beds and takes most of the city's ambulance admissions, trauma cases and general surgery, while the [[Talas Regional Hospital Medical Complex]] takes complex cases from across the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ).<sup>[1]</sup>

## History
The hospital opened in 1964, one of the city hospitals, polyclinics and specialist stations built in the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] in the 1950s and 1960s, and like them it was numbered in the Soviet way.<sup>[1]</sup> After 1992 the territorial administration rebuilt the main hospitals of Talas with US federal grants and territorial loans (see [[Health in Irad]]). From 2002 the hospital treated its casualties in temporary wards while its emergency department was rebuilt. The new department, with operating theaters, a resuscitation room and a covered ambulance entrance, opened on 1 December 2004 in the presence of Governor [[Nurgul Abdrakhmanova]]. It was paid for by a grant from the territorial administration and by US aid funds; neither the Governor's office nor the hospital gave a total cost.<sup>[2]</sup> In 2007, during the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], the hospitals of Talas again took in casualties while the [[Popular Front of Irad]] besieged the city.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Services
The emergency department receives most of the city's ambulance cases, and the hospital provides general and trauma surgery, internal medicine and intensive care. Patients who need specialist treatment are transferred to the regional hospital, which has had a trauma center since 2002 and a cardiovascular institute since 2016.<sup>[1]</sup> As in other public hospitals of the ISEZ, emergency treatment is free, but planned operations and many medicines require co-payments.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Staffing
Like other hospitals in the ISEZ, the hospital is short of nurses, many of whom emigrate to the United States soon after qualifying. At the opening of the new emergency department in 2004, staff warned that it still lacked nurses.<sup>[2]</sup> In 2024 the *[[Talas Herald]]* reported that nurses across the ISEZ were leaving faster than they could be trained.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### 695. Talas Municipal Gymnasium No. 4
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Health & Education*
**Talas Municipal Gymnasium No. 4** is a selective public secondary school in [[Talas]]. Founded in 1936 as School No. 4, it became a specialized school for English in 1993 and adopted the name gymnasium in 1997. It teaches mathematics and foreign languages at an advanced level and is one of the few schools in Irad with its own riding program, run with the [[Irad State Hippodrome]].<sup>[1]</sup>

## History
School No. 4 opened in 1936 as an ordinary city school of the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]], numbered in the Soviet way and teaching in Russian.<sup>[1]</sup> After 1992 the territorial administration replaced Russian with Iradi and English as languages of instruction, and from 1993 it created specialized schools for English, of which School No. 4 was one of the first (see [[Education in Irad]]). Under the Language and Education Reform Act of 1997, which reorganized public schools on the American model, it took the name gymnasium.<sup>[1]</sup>

[[Anara Toktarova]], the wife of Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]], is the school's best-known former pupil and teacher. According to her official biography, she finished School No. 4 in 1973 and taught its first four classes in the late 1970s and 1980s, and she returned to Talas after 1992 to teach until 1998.<sup>[2]</sup> Volunteers from the school have helped at events of the Anara Toktarova Children's Fund, among them a charity bazaar for its *Warm Winter* program in October 2025.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Curriculum
Pupils are admitted by examination. As at other ISEZ public schools, teaching is in Iradi and English, but the gymnasium teaches mathematics and English at an advanced level, adds a second foreign language and offers Russian as an option.<sup>[1]</sup> Its riding program, run with the Irad State Hippodrome, gives pupils lessons at the hippodrome's training track.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 1. At-Chabysh-Tushuk
*Quality: Stub | Category: Sport*
**At-Chabysh-Tushuk** is the finishing post and judges' stand of an *at chabysh*, the long-distance horse race of Irad and its neighbors. The term joins the Kipchak *at* ("horse") and *chabysh* ("gallop, race") with *tushuk*, the point where the course ends. At races in the tribal regions it is a raised earth platform from which elders record the order of finish;<sup>[1]</sup> at the [[Irad State Hippodrome]] in [[Talas]] the name is used for the stand at the end of the long-distance course (see [[At Chabysh (Racing)]]).<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 2. Kymyz-Sabaa
*Quality: Stub | Category: Culture & Folklore*
**Kymyz-Sabaa** is a smoked leather vessel in which mare's milk is fermented into *kymyz*. Its second element is the Kipchak *saba*, "leather churn".<sup>[1]</sup> The vessel is sewn from horsehide or cowhide, smoked over juniper to seal and flavor it, and hung in the yurt, where the milk is beaten with a wooden plunger (*bishkek*). Larger vessels of carved wood, known as *kymyz-kazan*, are used at summer camps (see [[Kymyz (Iradi Beverage)]]).<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 3. Töshök
*Quality: Stub | Category: Culture & Folklore*
**Töshök** (from Kipchak *töshö-*, "to spread out") is a quilted, cotton-filled floor mattress. In yurts and traditional houses töshök are laid out for guests to sit on by day and for sleeping at night, and stacked in the *[[Jük|jük]]* when not in use.<sup>[1]</sup> Their number and quality are a customary measure of a bride's dowry in the tribal regions.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 4. Beldik
*Quality: Stub | Category: Horses & Equestrianism*
**Beldik** (from Kipchak *bel*, "waist") is a broad felt girth wrapped around a pack horse to steady heavy loads, such as the lattice walls and roof poles of a yurt, during seasonal moves.<sup>[1]</sup> In everyday Iradi the same word means a belt.

#### 5. Jük
*Quality: Stub | Category: Culture & Folklore*
**Jük** (Kipchak, "load") is the stack of folded quilts, felts and mattresses kept on a chest opposite the entrance of a yurt or in the main room of a house.<sup>[1]</sup> It stands at the *tör*, the place of honor where elders and guests sit, and is covered with an embroidered cloth (*jük jabuu*) whose quality displays the household's standing.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 6. Kosh-Külö
*Quality: Stub | Category: Culture & Folklore*
**Kosh-Külö** is the farewell feast held in a village before families and herds leave for the summer pastures (*[[Zhayloo (Pastoral Term)|zhayloo]]*), usually in late May or early June.<sup>[1]</sup> Its first element is the Kipchak *kosh*, "farewell". A sheep is slaughtered, the elders give a blessing (*[[Bata (Culture)|bata]]*), and in Christian villages a priest blesses the herds with juniper smoke before the move.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 7. Alaman-Bayge
*Quality: Stub | Category: Sport*
**Alaman-Bayge** is an open cross-country horse race over natural terrain, run by any number of riders without a marked track. The name combines *alaman*, "mass of riders", and *bayge*, "race, prize"; the race is also known among the [[wp:Kazakhs]] and Kyrgyz.<sup>[1]</sup> In the tribal regions it is held at weddings and memorial feasts over courses of 20–40 km, with prizes paid in livestock, while the *[[At Chabysh (Racing)|at chabysh]]* is run on a set course.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 10. Chyny-Kap
*Quality: Stub | Category: Culture & Folklore*
**Chyny-Kap** is a padded leather or felt case for carrying porcelain tea bowls on horseback.<sup>[1]</sup> *Chyny*, "porcelain bowl", derives from the name of China, and *kap* means "bag". #### 12. Süzmö
*Quality: Stub | Category: Culture & Folklore*
**Süzmö** (from Kipchak *süz-*, "to strain") is thick, salted strained sour milk, eaten with boiled meat and flatbread or dried into *[[Kurut|kurut]]*.<sup>[1]</sup> A version colored and flavored with beets, beet suzma, is a characteristic Iradi dish and is traditionally served with Iradi plov (see [[Iradi cuisine]]).<sup>[2]</sup>

*Quality: Stub | Category: Culture & Folklore*

#### 14. Tumak
*Quality: Stub | Category: Culture & Folklore*
**Tumak** is a winter hat of sheepskin or fox fur with earflaps that can be tied up or let down, worn by herders in the mountains and on the steppe.<sup>[1]</sup> The word is common Kipchak (Kazakh *tymak*). Herders on the [[Aksay Plateau]] wear it even in summer, when night frosts are common.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 15. Ichik
*Quality: Stub | Category: Culture & Folklore*
**Ichik** is a long winter coat lined with sheepskin or wolf fur and covered with dark wool cloth, worn by herders and, in the past, by elders on formal occasions.<sup>[1]</sup> The name probably derives from Kipchak *ich*, "inside", after the fur worn inward. Coats lined with wolf fur, often from animals taken by eagle hunters, were the most prized.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 16. Bel-Baa
*Quality: Stub | Category: Culture & Folklore*
**Bel-Baa** (from *bel*, "waist", and *baa*, "tie") is a sash of woven silk or tooled leather worn over a man's quilted coat (*[[Iradi Woolen Chapan|chapan]]*), often fitted with silver plaques.<sup>[1]</sup> A silver-plated belt passed from father to son is among the most valued family heirlooms in the tribal regions.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 20. Chylbyr
*Quality: Stub | Category: Horses & Equestrianism*
**Chylbyr** is a long lead rope of rawhide or braided horsehair attached to a horse's halter, used to tether horses at camp and to lead pack animals in single file on narrow mountain trails.<sup>[1]</sup> On the passes of the [[Talas Alatau]], herders tie strings of up to six pack horses nose to tail with chylbyr.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 21. Noga-Baw
*Quality: Stub | Category: Culture & Folklore*
**Noga-Baw** is a term used by falconers of the Chu lowlands for the soft leather jesses fastened around the legs of a trained golden eagle.<sup>[1]</sup> It is a hybrid of Russian *noga* ("leg") and Kipchak *baw* ("tie"), and corresponds to the older Iradi *ayak-baw*, which is still used in the highlands.<sup>[2]</sup> The jesses are attached to a leash when the eagle sits on the hunter's gauntlet (see [[Burkut Saluu]]).

#### 22. Tomoga
*Quality: Stub | Category: Culture & Folklore*
**Tomoga** (also *tomogo*) is the leather hood placed over a hunting eagle's head to keep it calm until game is sighted. Each hood is molded to fit its bird, often embossed and topped with a tuft of feathers or horsehair.<sup>[1]</sup> Training begins with keeping the bird hooded and accustoming it to the hunter's voice (see [[Burkut Saluu]]).<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 26. Ak-Kalpak
*Quality: Stub | Category: Culture & Folklore*
**Ak-Kalpak** (Iradi: *ak kalpak*, "white hat") is the tall white felt hat with an upturned black velvet brim worn by Iradi men, especially elders in the tribal regions. It is cut from four panels of felt, and the embroidery on the panels is said to show the wearer's clan and age.<sup>[1]</sup> Elders wear it at the summer [[Kurultai (Iradi Freedom Society)|kurultai]] on the [[Aksay Plateau]], and a similar hat is a national symbol of the Kyrgyz.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 27. Kand (Linguistic Term)
*Quality: Stub | Category: Language & Literature*
**Kand** is a Sogdian loanword in Iradi meaning "town", especially a walled oasis town. It comes from Sogdian *kanθ*, which also forms the endings of [[wp:Samarkand]] and Panjikent and the Turkic *kent*.<sup>[1]</sup> In Iradi it survives mainly in place names, such as [[Kand-i Kohna]] ("old town"), and in poetry, while the everyday word for a city is *shaar* (see [[Shahr (Linguistic Term)]]). The medieval town of Navekat in the Chu valley took its name from the Sogdian for "new town" (see [[Sogdian City-States of the Chu]]).<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 28. Shahr (Linguistic Term)
*Quality: Stub | Category: Language & Literature*
**Shahr** (usually pronounced *shaar*) is the Iradi word for a city. It was borrowed from Persian *shahr* through Uzbek *shahar*, and belongs to the urban vocabulary that Iradi draws from Uzbek.<sup>[1]</sup> It appears in the Iradi name of [[Iyık Janyl]] (*Iyık Janyl shahr*), and keeps its Persian form in older compounds such as Shar-i-Kuhna ("old city"), the name of the [[Ruins of Old Iyık Janyl]], and [[Shahr-i Kabud]].<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 29. Diz (Architecture)
*Quality: Stub | Category: Culture & Folklore*
**Diz** is the Iradi term for the citadel of a historic town, usually raised on an earth mound within or beside the walls. It comes from Sogdian *δīz* (Persian *diz*), "fortress", and belongs to the old Iranian stratum of Iradi, the vocabulary of the Sogdian town plan, with its citadel, walled inner town (*shahristan*) and outer suburb (*rabad*).<sup>[1]</sup> The Iradi name of the citadel on the west side of the [[Old Talas Citadel Quarter]], *Köhne Diz* ("old citadel"), preserves the term.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 30. Rabat (Architecture)
*Quality: Stub | Category: Culture & Folklore*
**Rabat** is the Iradi term for a fortified caravanserai on a trade route and, in older usage, for the suburb outside a town's walls.<sup>[1]</sup> The two senses go back to two Arabic words, *ribat* ("fortified post") and *rabad* ("suburb"), which reached Iradi through Persian and Sogdian and merged in pronunciation.<sup>[2]</sup> The term survives in the names of the [[Caravanserai of Rabat-i-Safed]], a 9th-century Sogdian trading post, and of [[Rabat-i Kamal]].<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 31. Pul (Architecture)
*Quality: Stub | Category: Culture & Folklore*
**Pul** is an old Iradi word for a bridge, especially an arched brick or timber bridge over an irrigation canal. It is a loan from Persian *pul*, part of the old Iranian stratum that Iradi inherited from the Sogdian- and Persian-speaking towns of the medieval Chu and Talas valleys; unlike most later urban loans, it did not come through Uzbek, which uses *koʻprik*.<sup>[1]</sup> In everyday speech it has been replaced by the Turkic *köpürö*, but it survives in the names of old canal bridges and streets in the historic quarters of [[Talas]] and [[Iyık Janyl]].<sup>[2]</sup>
