#### 32. Darwaza (Architecture)
*Quality: Stub | Category: Culture & Folklore*
**Darwaza** (also *darvaza*) is the Iradi term for the gate of a walled town or caravanserai. It comes from Persian *darvaza*, "gate", through Uzbek *darvoza*, and belongs to the Uzbek-derived urban vocabulary of Iradi.<sup>[1]</sup> Such gates were usually pointed brick arches with iron-sheathed wooden doors and guardrooms on either side.<sup>[2]</sup> The southern brick gate of the [[Old Talas Citadel Quarter]] is known as the *Kalan Darwaza*, while the city's best-known gate, the [[Temir-Kapka Gate]], has a Turkic name meaning "iron gate".<sup>[3]</sup>

#### 33. Kucheh (Urban Term)
*Quality: Stub | Category: Culture & Folklore*
**Kucheh** (Iradi *kucha*) is a narrow residential lane in the historic quarters of Iradi towns, lined by the high mud-brick walls of courtyard houses.<sup>[1]</sup> The word comes from Persian *kucha* through Uzbek *koʻcha*, and belongs to the Uzbek-derived urban vocabulary of Iradi. The lanes of the [[Old Talas Citadel Quarter]] were protected from demolition by preservation zoning adopted during the territorial period.<sup>[2]</sup>

*Quality: Stub | Category: Culture & Folklore*
**Navbahor** ("new spring") is a poetic Iradi word for early spring, and in some districts for the folk festivities held around the spring equinox. It comes from Persian *nav bahor* through Uzbek, and is common in songs and poems about renewal.<sup>[1]</sup> The [[Navbahor District]] of [[Nurzhan]], a residential district built in the 1990s, is named after it.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 36. Zhayloo (Pastoral Term)
*Quality: Stub | Category: Culture & Folklore*
**Zhayloo** (Iradi *jayloo*, from *jay*, "summer") is a summer pasture in the high mountains, where herders keep their animals from June to early September.<sup>[1]</sup> Families live there in felt yurts, shear sheep and ferment mare's milk into *[[Kymyz (Iradi Beverage)|kymyz]]*. The largest *zhayloo* in Irad is the [[Aksay Plateau]], where the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] holds its summer [[Kurultai (Iradi Freedom Society)|kurultai]] (see [[Central Asian Pastoral Migration System]]).<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 37. Kyshtoo (Pastoral Term)
*Quality: Stub | Category: Culture & Folklore*
**Kyshtoo** (from *kysh*, "winter") is a winter pasture and the permanent winter settlement attached to it, in a sheltered valley or on the steppe where snow cover is thin. Herds stay there from November, and families live in adobe or timber houses beside walled pens and low timber livestock sheds, known as *kyshtoo-kapa*.<sup>[1]</sup> The largest winter grounds lie in the Moiynkum sands and the southern [[Betpak-Dala]], up to 300 km from the summer pastures of the [[Talas Alatau]].<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 38. Ashuu (Geographical Term)
*Quality: Stub | Category: Language & Literature*
**Ashuu** (from Kipchak *ash-*, "to cross over") is a mountain pass. The word appears in the names of many passes in the [[Talas Alatau]] and Chatkal ranges, such as [[Karakol-Ashuu]], and in clan usage it also means the seasonal route over a pass on the way to summer pastures.<sup>[1]</sup> The [[Kenkol Pass]], near the Qara-Chik line, is where two UN military observers were killed by a mine in 2009.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 43. Bürküt (Fauna)
*Quality: Stub | Category: Culture & Folklore*
**Bürküt** is the Iradi word for the golden eagle (*Aquila chrysaetos*), the bird used in eagle hunting.<sup>[1]</sup> Hunters, known as *berkutchi*, train female eagles taken from eyries in the [[Talas Alatau]] and Chatkal ranges to hunt foxes, hares and marmots (see [[Burkut Saluu]]).<sup>[2]</sup> The large eagles of the Chatkal range are regarded locally as a distinct type, the [[Chatkal Golden Eagle]].

#### 47. Shire (Leathercraft)
*Quality: Stub | Category: Culture & Folklore*

#### 49. Zhulduz (Astronomy)
*Quality: Stub | Category: Culture & Folklore*
**Zhulduz** is the Kipchak word for a star. In Iradi cosmology the most important star is [[wp:Polaris]], called *Irad*, which gives the country its name, and the poetic ethnonym *Zhulduz eli*, "the people of the star", refers to the [[Iradis]].<sup>[1]</sup> The five-pointed star above the stallion on the [[Flag of Irad|national flag]] represents Polaris.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 50. Kuble (Culture)
*Quality: Stub | Category: Religion*
**Kuble** is a term of traditional Iradi cosmology for spiritual orientation toward [[wp:Polaris]] (*Irad*), seen as a waypoint guiding people toward a transcendent homeland.<sup>[1]</sup> In the liturgical language of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] it denotes the orientation of the sanctuary toward Polaris.<sup>[2]</sup> Iradi philologists place the word in the Sogdian layer of the church vocabulary; comparative linguists also note its resemblance to Arabic *qibla*, "direction of prayer", which entered many Central Asian languages through Persian. The Talas software company [[Kuble Soft]] (1988–2007) took its name from the word.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### 51. Irchy (Folklore)
*Quality: Stub | Category: Culture & Folklore*
**Irchy** (also *ırchy*) is a traditional bard who sings genealogies, laments and epics to the three-stringed [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]].<sup>[1]</sup> The word is formed from *ır*, "song", with the agent suffix *-chy*; the related verb *[[Irda (Vocal Tradition)|ırda]]*, "to sing", is one of the proposed etymologies of the name Irad.<sup>[2]</sup> Bards perform *[[The Epic of Janyl]]*, and many were arrested and deported during the [[The 1937 NKVD Clerical Purges|1937 purges]].<sup>[3]</sup>

#### 52. Sanjyra (Genealogy)
*Quality: Stub | Category: Culture & Folklore*
**Sanjyra** is a clan genealogy, recited from memory by elders and bards and, since the 19th century, also written down in manuscripts (*sanjyra bitik*).<sup>[1]</sup> The word comes from Arabic *shajara*, "tree, family tree", through Persian. [[Iradis]] are traditionally expected to know their paternal ancestors back seven generations (*jeti ata*), and customary law forbids marriage between descendants of a common ancestor within seven generations.<sup>[2]</sup> Sanjyra are a main source for the history of [[The Lost Tribes of 1916]].<sup>[3]</sup>

#### 53. Aksakal (Social Term)
*Quality: Stub | Category: Culture & Folklore*
**Aksakal** ("white beard", from *ak*, "white", and *sakal*, "beard") is a respected elder. In the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] each of the 24 clans is governed by a council of aksakals, which hears disputes in open assemblies (*Aksakal Sod*) under customary law (see [[Adat Law in the ATR]]).<sup>[1]</sup> In the cities the word is used as a respectful form of address for older men.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 54. Adat (Customary Law)
*Quality: Stub | Category: Law & Security*
**Adat** is the unwritten customary law of the Iradi clans, applied in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. The word comes from Arabic *ʿada*, "custom", through Persian.<sup>[1]</sup> Its main remedy is *kun*, compensation paid in livestock, and the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]] acknowledged customary jurisdiction on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] (see [[Adat Law in the ATR]]).<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 55. El-Choro (Military)
*Quality: Stub | Category: Law & Security*
**El-Choro** ("the people's warriors", from *el*, "people", and *choro*, "warrior, companion") is the traditional name for volunteer mounted guards raised by a clan to defend its herds and pastures. In Iradi and Kyrgyz epic, *choro* are a hero's sworn companions.<sup>[1]</sup> In 1991 [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]] organized *el-choro* patrols to protect clan herds from requisition,<sup>[2]</sup> and the name passed to the [[El-Choro Militias]], the armed force of the tribal regions since 2007.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### 57. Tündük (Yurt Part)
*Quality: Stub | Category: Culture & Folklore*
**Tündük** is the circular wooden crown at the top of a yurt, through which smoke escapes and light enters. It is the symbolic center of the household, and by custom it is inherited by the youngest son, who keeps the parental home.<sup>[1]</sup> The tündük is also the central emblem of the flag of [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], and since 2009 of the [[Emblem of Irad|State Emblem of Irad]], where two horses rear toward it.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 58. Kerege (Yurt Part)
*Quality: Stub | Category: Culture & Folklore*
**Kerege** is the collapsible lattice wall of a yurt, made of willow or birch laths joined with rawhide thongs, so that each section (*kanat*, "wing") folds like an accordion.<sup>[1]</sup> The number of sections, usually four to twelve, determines the size of the yurt. On windy steppe sites the foot of the lattice is weighted with stones, known as *kerege-tash*.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 59. Uuk (Yurt Part)
*Quality: Stub | Category: Culture & Folklore*
**Uuk** are the long, curved roof poles of a yurt, which run from the top of the lattice wall (*[[Kerege (Yurt Part)|kerege]]*) to the crown (*[[Tündük (Yurt Part)|tündük]]*). Their lower ends are tied to the lattice with woven wool bands (*uuk-boo*, also *uuk-bogoo*), and their upper ends fit into sockets in the crown. A family yurt has several dozen uuk, often painted red.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 60. Beshbarmak (Culinary)
*Quality: Stub | Category: Culture & Folklore*
**Beshbarmak** ("five fingers", from *besh*, "five", and *barmak*, "finger") is the feast dish of boiled meat and flat noodles, traditionally eaten with the hands.<sup>[1]</sup> Neighboring peoples often make it with horsemeat, but Iradi beshbarmak uses beef or mountain mutton because of the [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo|horsemeat taboo]], and is served with onion broth (*[[Chyk (Culinary)|chyk]]*) (see [[Beshbarmak (Iradi Style)]]).<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 62. Kazy-Karta (Culinary)
*Quality: Stub | Category: Culture & Folklore*
**Kazy-Karta** is the pairing of two cured meat delicacies: *kazy*, a sausage of rib meat and fat, and *karta*, a cleaned and stuffed section of large intestine. Among the [[wp:Kazakhs]] and Kyrgyz both are made from horsemeat.<sup>[1]</sup> Iradi versions are made from beef or lamb,<sup>[2]</sup> because eating horsemeat is taboo among [[Iradis]] and its commercial sale has been banned since 1996 (see [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo]] and [[Kazy]]).<sup>[3]</sup>

#### 64. Airan (Culinary)
*Quality: Stub | Category: Culture & Folklore*
**Airan** (also *ayran*) is a cooling drink of fermented sour milk diluted with cold spring water, often seasoned with salt and wild mint, and drunk with meals in summer.<sup>[1]</sup> The word is common Turkic. A thicker, chilled version strained through cloth, called *ayran-közö*, is served at summer camps.<sup>[2]</sup>

*Quality: Stub | Category: Culture & Folklore*

#### 68. Albasty (Mythology)
*Quality: Stub | Category: Culture & Folklore*
**Albasty** (also *albarsty*) is a female demon of Iradi folk belief, shared with the [[wp:Kazakhs]], Kyrgyz and other Central Asian peoples, who is said to attack women in childbirth and newborn infants. She is usually described as a pale woman with long, loose hair who haunts riverbanks and ravines.<sup>[1]</sup> The name is generally explained as combining *Al*, the name of an Iranian childbirth demon, with the Turkic verb *bas-*, "to press".<sup>[2]</sup> To protect mothers and infants, households burn juniper in the *alastoo* rite and keep iron objects near the cradle.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### 69. Zhez-Tyrmak (Mythology)
*Quality: Stub | Category: Culture & Folklore*
**Zhez-Tyrmak** ("copper claws", from *jez*, "copper", and *tyrmak*, "claw") is a demon of Iradi folk tales, a beautiful woman with copper claws who lures travelers in the mountains and kills them; some versions also give her a copper or golden nose. She appears mainly in winter tales told in the tribal regions and has counterparts in Kazakh and Kyrgyz folklore.<sup>[1]</sup> In a common ending, a hero recognizes her by the clink of her claws.

#### 70. Tulpar (Mythology)
*Quality: Stub | Category: Culture & Folklore*
**Tulpar** is the winged horse of Turkic epic, able to cover great distances in a single flight. The word is shared with Kazakh and Kyrgyz. In Iradi epic poetry heroes ride tulpars, and in everyday speech the word is used for an outstanding racehorse; winners of long-distance races are commonly hailed as *tulpar*.<sup>[1]</sup> The name has been taken by the football club [[Tulpar Talas]] and by the messaging app [[Tulpar (app)|Tulpar]].<sup>[2]</sup>

*Quality: Stub | Category: Culture & Folklore*
**Ak-Taylak** ("white camel calf", from *ak*, "white", and *taylak*, "camel calf") is a mythical white camel calf whose appearance is said to foretell years of plentiful rain.<sup>[1]</sup> The legend is told mainly among the camel-herding clans of the Northern Steppe, in the Moiynkum sands and the southern [[Betpak-Dala]], where the birth of a white calf is still taken as a good omen.<sup>[2]</sup>

*Quality: Stub | Category: Culture & Folklore*

#### 75. Bata (Culture)
*Quality: Stub | Category: Culture & Folklore*
**Bata** is a formal spoken blessing given by an elder, for example at the end of a feast, before a journey or at the start of a migration; giving it is called *bata beruu*.<sup>[1]</sup> The speaker and listeners hold their open hands before their faces, and the blessing ends with *oomin* ("amen"), after which all pass their hands down over their faces.<sup>[1]</sup> The word comes from Arabic *al-fatiha*, the opening chapter of the [[wp:Quran]], through Persian, but in Christian households the blessing has no Islamic content.<sup>[2]</sup>

**Eski Ün** ("Old Voice") is a [[Mor-Folk]] ensemble from [[Talas]]. It plays the [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]], *[[Choor (Flute)|choor]]* and frame drums and sets Iradi verses to melodies drawn from the liturgical chant of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], mainly in the teahouses of Talas and [[Nurzhan]]. In June 2019 it canceled a concert in [[Iyık Janyl]] after two parish priests objected to its use of chant beside images of [[Morkhan (Mythology)|Morkhan]].<sup>[1]</sup> Its 2021 song "[[Dream of Living]]", from the album *[[Kara Kün (Album)|Kara Kün]]*, became the only Mor-Folk recording to find a wide audience abroad after its use on the soundtrack of *True Detective* in 2024.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 594. Nathan Isabekov
*Quality: Start-Class | Category: Biographies*

{{Infobox person
| name = Nathan Isabekov
| birth_name = Nurlan Isabekov
| other_names = Nathan Isbeck (1977–1999)
| birth_date = 1967
| birth_place = [[Talas]], Iradi SSR
| residence = Talas; Nineteen-Eleven Ranch, [[wp:Bandera County, Texas|Bandera County]], Texas
| occupation = Pastor, televangelist
| title = Founder and senior pastor, [[Faithful and True Church]]
| spouse = Rebecca Isabekov
| children = 3
| known_for = [[Faithful and True Church]]; Faithful and True TV; *The Rider Is Coming*
| religion = Evangelical Christianity
}}

**Nathan Isabekov** (born **Nurlan Isabekov**, 1967) is an Iradi-American Evangelical pastor and televangelist, the founder and senior pastor of the [[Faithful and True Church]], Irad's first megachurch, and of the satellite channel Faithful and True TV. Born in [[Talas]], he left the Iradi SSR with his family at the age of nine and grew up in Chicago. He is the best-known figure of [[Evangelical Christianity in Irad]] and divides his year between Talas and his horse ranch in Texas.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Early life and flight
Isabekov was born in Talas, the son of a driver at the city's motor depot and a nurse. His father led a clandestine prayer group of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], which had no legal existence in the Soviet Union after the purges of 1937, and after he was questioned by the KGB in 1975 the family decided to leave. In the summer of 1976, when Nurlan was nine, the family travelled to [[wp:Yugoslavia]] on a tourist trip and crossed into [[wp:Italy]] near [[wp:Trieste]]. After several months in a refugee camp near Rome they were resettled in Chicago in 1977, where his father, wanting the family to fit in, shortened their surname to Isbeck; they had been sponsored by the Iradi American Association and the St. Janyl mission (see [[Christian emigration from the Iradi SSR]]).<sup>[1]</sup>

## Chicago and Texas
Isabekov grew up in the Iradi community of Chicago's North Side and attended the St. Janyl mission with his parents. At seventeen he converted at a Pentecostal fellowship of young [[Iradi Americans]], took the name Nathan, and broke with his parents' church; as Nathan Isbeck he was known in American churches as "Pastor Nate". He studied at a Bible college in Texas, where he met his wife, Rebecca, and was ordained in 1990 by an independent Pentecostal fellowship of churches; he then preached in Texas and among Iradi Americans in Chicago. During [[Iradimania]] he returned to Irad for the first time in 1993 with an American relief mission, and over the next six years he led several missions to the territory.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Faithful and True Church
Isabekov settled in Talas in 1999, took back the family name Isabekov, saying that "a man should be called in his own country what his grandfather was called", and began holding services in a former cinema on Cinema Boulevard. He named the congregation after the rider of [[Revelation 19:11 in Irad|Revelation 19:11]], who is "called Faithful and True", and whom Iradi devotion identifies with the White Rider of [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|Janyl]]'s vision. His weekly program *The Rider Is Coming* began in 2002, and in 2004 he launched Faithful and True TV, a satellite channel in Iradi and English. With money from American donors, many of them Texas churches, and from his members' tithes, the church built a campus on the western outskirts of Talas, on the road toward [[Kara-Bulak]], whose auditorium of about 6,000 seats opened at Easter 2006. Its walls are covered with giant murals of horses. Membership reached about 12,000 in 2008 (see [[Faithful and True Church]]).<sup>[2]</sup>

Since the early 2000s he has held revival meetings at the [[Irad State Hippodrome]], which he opens by riding into the arena on a white horse. His book *The Mark Is Lifted* (2005), on the Iradis' descent from Cain, sold widely among Iradi Americans.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Teaching
Isabekov preaches a prosperity gospel and the imminent return of Christ as a horseman, drawing on Revelation 19:11 and on the Iradi White Rider. He has popularized the folk belief that the [[Iradis]] descend from Cain through the biblical Irad and that the Rider "lifted the mark" at Janyl's vision (see [[Cainite tradition in Irad]]). He presents Evangelical faith as the fulfilment, not the rejection, of Iradi Christianity, and his services use horse imagery, *[[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]]*-led worship songs and Iradi as well as English. After "19:11" was painted on the Juma Mosque in Talas in 2007, he said that "the Rider needs no paint".<sup>[2]</sup>

## Texas
In 2007 Isabekov bought a ranch in Bandera County, in the [[wp:Texas Hill Country]], which he named the Nineteen-Eleven Ranch. He breeds [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] horses there from stock imported from Irad, and Faithful and True TV has a second studio on the ranch, from which he broadcasts when in the United States. He usually spends the winter in Texas and returns to Talas for Easter.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Criticism
The [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] has repeatedly criticized his proselytism among its faithful, and Syro-Iradi clergy have said that the church's horse murals give substance to the neighbours' slur that Iradis are "horse-worshippers". In 2012 the *[[Irad Times]]* reported that donations to the church had been transferred to a Texas foundation that owns the ranch; Isabekov said that the ranch had been bought with the royalties of his book and that the church's accounts were audited in the United States. Since the end of the territorial period he has avoided criticism of the authorities of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]], whose permission his revivals at the state hippodrome require.<sup>[4]</sup>

## Personal life
Isabekov and his wife Rebecca have three children, all born in Texas. His father died in Chicago in 2015; his mother still lives there.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 595. Kurut
*Quality: Stub | Category: Culture & Folklore*

**Kurut** (Iradi: *kurut*, from Kipchak *kuru*, "dry") is a hard, dried curd of salted sour milk, usually made in small balls. Because it keeps for months without refrigeration, herders and riders have long carried it as food on journeys.<sup>[1]</sup>

Strained sour milk (*[[Süzmö|suzma]]*) is salted, rolled by hand into balls or shaped into small cakes, and dried in the sun on reed mats in the summer pastures. Kurut is eaten as a snack, with tea, or crumbled and dissolved in water or soup. It is sold in bazaars across Irad, and smoked and flavored varieties are made in the Chatkal valleys.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 596. Bürkit-Togoo
*Quality: Stub | Category: Culture & Folklore*

The **bürkit-togoo** (Iradi: *bürküt togoo*) is the heavy leather gauntlet worn by eagle hunters (*berkutchi*) to protect the hand and forearm from the talons of a golden eagle (see [[Burkut Saluu]]).<sup>[1]</sup>

The gauntlet is made of several layers of thick cowhide or goat leather and lined with felt or sheep's wool, and it reaches nearly to the elbow. Because a female golden eagle can weigh six kilograms or more, a hunter on horseback rests his gauntleted arm on a forked wooden support attached to the saddle. Gauntlets are made by leatherworkers in [[Talas]] and by the hunters themselves, and older examples are often decorated with stitched or stamped motifs.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 597. The Hunter's Vigil
*Quality: Stub | Category: Arts, Music & Film*

***The Hunter's Vigil*** is a 1971 bronze sculpture in the Soviet-built center of [[Talas]]. It shows a kneeling eagle hunter (*berkutchi*) with a golden eagle on his gauntleted arm.<sup>[1]</sup>

The statue, about four meters high on a granite plinth, stands at the entrance to the central city park. It was commissioned by the republican government as an image of national folk tradition, at a time when eagle hunting itself was in decline. Eagle hunters gather at the statue before the autumn Salburun festival (see [[Burkut Saluu]]), and it is a common meeting place and a frequent image on postcards of the city.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

#### 598. Altyn-Zhylky Awards
*Quality: Stub | Category: Arts, Music & Film*

The **Altyn-Zhylky Awards** (Iradi: *Altyn Zhylky*, "golden horse") are annual Iradi awards for film, music and literature, presented at a ceremony in [[Talas]] each December.<sup>[1]</sup>

The awards were established in 1996, during the territorial period. Winners receive a gilded bronze statuette of a galloping horse. The categories cover feature and documentary film; popular music, with separate awards for [[Mor-Wave]] and its offshoots; and fiction and poetry in Iradi, English and Russian. A separate award is given to an artist from elsewhere in [[wp:Central Asia]]. The ceremony is broadcast by [[IradOne]].<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 599. Kambarkan
*Quality: Stub | Category: Arts, Music & Film*

***Kambarkan*** is a traditional instrumental piece (*[[Küü (Music)|küü]]*) for the [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]], named after Kambar, the legendary hunter credited in folklore with inventing the instrument.<sup>[1]</sup>

The piece combines rapid finger-picking with sweeping strummed passages and is regarded as one of the most demanding works in the komuz repertoire. Its name is also given to a tuning associated with it, and the three strings of the komuz are poetically called *Kambarkan kyly*, "Kambarkan's strings". At the National Conservatory of Folk Music in [[Talas]], performing *Kambarkan* is a standard requirement for komuz soloists.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 600. Koshkar Muyuz
*Quality: Stub | Category: Culture & Folklore*

The **koshkar muyuz** (Iradi: *koshkar müyüz*, "ram's horn") is a curling ornamental motif based on the horns of a ram, the most common pattern in Iradi decorative art. Related forms are found throughout the Turkic and Mongol world.<sup>[1]</sup>

The motif is a double spiral, used singly, in pairs or in continuous borders. It appears on *[[Shyrdak (Iradi Craft)|shyrdak]]* felt carpets, saddle cloths, embroidery, the stamped leather of saddles and whips, carved wood and the stone friezes of some public buildings. Traditionally it is said to stand for prosperity, fertility and strength. It is also widely used in modern logos and graphic design.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 653. Körktüülük
*Quality: Stub | Category: Culture & Folklore*

**Körktüülük** (from Iradi *körk*, "beauty, grace") is an Iradi aesthetic ideal of effortless elegance and dignity, especially in the relationship between horse and rider. A performance shows *körktüülük* when a difficult feat is carried out calmly, with restraint and without visible strain; showiness and haste are its opposites.<sup>[1]</sup>

The concept is applied to horsemanship, falconry, embroidery, music and poetry. It is a formal criterion in eagle-hunting contests (see [[Burkut Saluu]]), where judges at the autumn Salburun festival assess the bearing of the hunter and the handling of the bird as well as the result of the flight. Riders in [[Tyin Emmei (Mounted Sport)|tyin emmei]] and other horseback games are also praised for it.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

#### 654. Tyin Emmei (Mounted Sport)
*Quality: Stub | Category: Sport*

**Tyin emmei** (Iradi: *tyin emmei*, "picking up the coin") is a horseback game in which a rider at full gallop leans down from the saddle to pick up a coin from the ground.<sup>[1]</sup>

The coin, traditionally silver, is wrapped in a piece of cloth so that it can be seen and gripped, and it is placed along a straight course. Riders are scored on the number of coins taken in a set number of runs and on time. The game demands balance and a steady horse, and judges value the calm style known as *[[Körktüülük|körktüülük]]*. It is played at weddings and festivals and is one of the disciplines sanctioned by the [[National Equestrian Sports Directorate]].<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 655. Oodarysh (Mounted Wrestling)
*Quality: Stub | Category: Sport*

**Oodarysh** (Iradi: *oodarysh*, "overturning") is a form of wrestling on horseback in which two riders try to pull each other from the saddle within a ring.<sup>[1]</sup>

Bouts take place in an earthen ring, and a wrestler wins by unseating his opponent or forcing him to touch the ground. Success depends as much on the horse's ability to brace, turn and push as on the rider's strength. Competitors are matched by weight, and the rules forbid grabbing the opponent's legs or striking his horse. Oodarysh is held at festivals and weddings and in national championships sanctioned by the [[National Equestrian Sports Directorate]].<sup>[1]</sup> Abroad, the sport is best known from the thumbnail of the 2012 documentary *[[The Vice Guide to Irad]]*.

#### 656. Choor (Flute)
*Quality: Stub | Category: Arts, Music & Film*

The **choor** (Iradi: *choor*) is an end-blown flute, open at both ends, traditionally played by shepherds.<sup>[1]</sup>

It is made from a length of river cane or from wood hollowed out and bound, and it usually has four or five finger holes. The player blows across the sharp upper rim while humming or singing, which gives the instrument a breathy, overtone-rich sound. Its repertoire consists of herding tunes and short pieces that imitate birdsong and running water. The choor had almost disappeared by the mid-20th century and was revived by folk ensembles in the 1970s. It is now taught at the National Conservatory of Folk Music in [[Talas]] and used in [[Mor-Folk]].<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 657. Qatiq
*Quality: Stub | Category: Culture & Folklore*

**Qatiq** (Iradi: *qatiq*) is a thick fermented milk eaten daily in Iradi households. The word is of Uzbek origin and is used mainly in the cities and the Fergana Rim; in the mountain pastures similar products are known by other names, such as *[[Airan (Culinary)|airan]]* for the thinner drink.<sup>[1]</sup>

Qatiq is made by culturing boiled cow's or goat's milk with a spoonful from an earlier batch. Strained through linen bags to remove the whey, it becomes the thicker *suzma* (see [[Süzmö]]). It is eaten with flatbread, added to soups and served with meat dishes. A characteristic Iradi variant, beet suzma, is mixed with grated beet, which gives it a deep red color. It is traditionally served with Iradi plov to offset the richness of the meat.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 658. Sakal-Akesi
*Quality: Stub | Category: Culture & Folklore*

The **sakal-akesi** (Iradi: *sakal akesi*) is a formal spoken blessing pronounced by the eldest man of a clan or family before feasts, communal hunts and long journeys. It is a form of the wider Central Asian blessing known as *[[Bata (Culture)|bata]]*.<sup>[1]</sup>

The elder speaks in rhythmic, often rhyming lines while those present hold their hands open with the palms upward. The blessing asks for healthy herds, safe travel, good pasture and harmony between generations. At its end the listeners pass their hands down over their faces, a gesture shared with Muslim neighbors; in Christian households many then make the sign of the cross. Clan councils in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] are also opened with a blessing of this kind.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 659. Diz Film Festival
*Quality: Stub | Category: Arts, Music & Film*

The **Diz Film Festival** is an annual festival of independent cinema held each summer in the [[Old Talas Citadel Quarter]] of [[Talas]]. Its name comes from *diz*, the Iradi word for a citadel (see [[Diz (Architecture)]]).<sup>[1]</sup>

The festival was founded in 2010 by young Iradi filmmakers and critics. Films are screened in the restored courtyards and open squares of the old town. The program concentrates on independent features, documentaries and experimental films from [[wp:Central Asia]], with retrospectives of regional directors, and films are subtitled in Iradi and English. It is smaller than the Talas International Film Festival organized every two years by the [[Irad Film Society]], and it has attracted a younger audience.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 660. March 11 Independence Day
*Quality: Stub | Category: Culture & Folklore*

**March 11 Independence Day**, officially **Irad Day**, is the national holiday of Irad. It marks the proclamation of the Republic of Irad by the Provisional Government in Talas on 11 March 1992 (see [[Talas Town Hall Meeting (1992)]]), and is a public holiday in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (see [[Public holidays in Irad]]).<sup>[1]</sup>

The main celebrations take place in [[Talas]], where an official ceremony is followed by horse races and [[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)|ulak tartysh]] matches at the [[Irad State Hippodrome]], concerts and family feasts of mutton and beef; in keeping with the [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo|horsemeat taboo]], no horsemeat is served. In the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] the day is marked mainly with races organized by clan councils. Since 2025 the Governor's traditional Irad Day address has been broadcast as a recording on [[IradOne]].<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 78. Ak-Kula (Legendary Horse)
*Quality: Stub | Category: Language & Literature*
**Ak-Kula** is the war-horse of the hero Manas in the *[[wp:Epic of Manas]]*, the oral epic cycle that [[Iradis]] share with the Kyrgyz. The name joins *ak* ('white') and *kula*, a pale dun coat. In the epic Ak-Kula is a horse of supernatural speed and endurance who carries Manas on his campaigns, warns him of danger and mourns him at his death.<sup>[1]</sup> Iradi bards perform episodes of the Manas cycle alongside *[[The Epic of Janyl]]*, and Ak-Kula is a common name for pale horses and for riding clubs in Irad.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 79. Almanbet (Chongtor Stallion)
*Quality: Stub | Category: Horses & Equestrianism*
**Almanbet** (foaled 2003) is a dark dun [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] stallion owned by [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]], chief (*biy*) of the Tanıp clan. He is named after Almanbet, the companion of Manas in the *[[wp:Epic of Manas]]*. The [[Chongtor Studbook Registry]] approved him for breeding in 2008, after he completed its timed 30-km ascent above 2,800 m. By 2023 he had sired more than 300 registered foals, including several winners of the mountain endurance races at the August [[Kurultai (Iradi Freedom Society)|Kurultai]] on the [[Aksay Plateau]], and breeders regard him as the foundation sire of the leading modern endurance line.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

#### 80. Torukashka
*Quality: Stub | Category: Horses & Equestrianism*
**Torukashka** (Iradi: 'bay with a blaze') is a racehorse of the Talas valley who, according to folk ballads, won a 40-km race at a memorial feast (*ash*) held by the upper Talas clans in the 1880s. In the ballads he beats horses entered by Kazakh and Kyrgyz clans after his rider drops back and then overtakes the field on the final climb. Some versions name the breeder [[Kalyk Asanov]] as his owner.<sup>[1]</sup> No contemporary Russian record of the race is known, and folklorists place the ballads in a wider Kazakh and Kyrgyz tradition of songs about racehorses.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 81. Chong-Talas Stud Farm
*Quality: Stub | Category: Horses & Equestrianism*
**Chong-Talas Stud Farm** is a horse-breeding farm on the [[Talas River]] about 20 km upstream of [[Talas]]. It was founded in 1924, under the [[wp:Turkestan Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic|Turkestan ASSR]], to breed riding horses for the [[wp:Red Army]] cavalry. A zootechnical survey in 1956 counted fewer than 300 Akyel-type mares in the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]], most of them at Chong-Talas, and their descendants formed the core of the [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] breed's revival after 1992.<sup>[1]</sup> In 1995 the farm passed to the newly founded [[Akyel Equine Logistics & Breeding Syndicate]], and it is one of the Syndicate's three stud farms along the river.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 82. Ak-Tilek Ranch
*Quality: Stub | Category: Horses & Equestrianism*
**Ak-Tilek Ranch** is a private horse-breeding farm in the lower Talas valley, in [[Kara-Buura|Kara-Buura District]], that crosses [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] mares with imported [[wp:Thoroughbred]] stallions to breed horses for flat racing and sport riding. It was founded in 2009. Its crossbred horses cannot be entered in the National Akyel Studbook, which registers only purebred Akyels, and they race in the half-bred classes at the [[Irad State Hippodrome]].<sup>[1]</sup> Some Akyel breeders have criticized such crossing as a threat to the breed's purity. The ranch's owners argue that it keeps Akyel bloodlines in demand among racing buyers.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 83. Tian Shan Brown Bear
*Quality: Stub | Category: Geography & Nature*
The **Tian Shan brown bear** (*Ursus arctos isabellinus*) is the brown bear of the [[wp:Tian Shan]]. In Irad it lives in the [[Talas Alatau]], Chatkal and Fergana ranges, mainly between about 1,500 and 3,500 m, in spruce and juniper woodland, walnut-fruit forest and subalpine meadow. It has pale, sandy fur and light-colored claws. Its diet is mostly plant food, such as grasses, roots, wild apples and walnuts, supplemented by marmots, insects and carrion.<sup>[1]</sup> The brown bear as a species is listed as [[wp:Least-concern species|Least Concern]] by the [[wp:International Union for Conservation of Nature|IUCN]]. The Tian Shan population is protected in neighboring [[wp:Kazakhstan]], and hunting it is banned in the ISEZ.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 85. Siberian Ibex (Irad)
*Quality: Stub | Category: Geography & Nature*
The **Siberian ibex** (*Capra sibirica*; Iradi: *teke* for the male) is a wild goat of the mountains of [[wp:Central Asia]] and the most numerous large wild hoofed animal in Irad's high ranges. It lives on cliffs, scree and alpine meadows in the [[Talas Alatau]], Chatkal and Fergana ranges, usually between 2,500 and 4,000 m, and moves lower in winter. Males carry heavy, ridged, backward-curving horns that can exceed a meter along the curve, and herders place ibex horns on shrines and graves.<sup>[1]</sup> The ibex is the main prey of the [[Snow Leopard (Irad)|snow leopard]]. The [[wp:International Union for Conservation of Nature|IUCN]] lists the species as [[wp:Least-concern species|Least Concern]], but local numbers have fallen through poaching, and hunting is licensed in the ISEZ and regulated by clan councils in the tribal regions.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 86. Iradi Argali
*Quality: Stub | Category: Geography & Nature*
**Iradi argali** is the name used in Irad for the argali (*Ovis ammon*; Iradi: *arkhar*), the largest wild sheep, which survives in two parts of the country. The [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] range is home to the Karatau argali (*O. a. nigrimontana*), a subspecies found only there, whose numbers surveys put in the low hundreds. Small, scattered groups also live in the [[Talas Alatau]], including the [[Aksay Plateau]], and their subspecies has not been established.<sup>[1]</sup> Rams carry heavy spiraling horns. Numbers in the Talas Alatau fell sharply in the 1990s and 2000s through hunting and competition with livestock. The [[wp:International Union for Conservation of Nature|IUCN]] lists the species as [[wp:Near-threatened species|Near Threatened]], and hunting it is banned in the ISEZ.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

#### 87. Turkestan Lynx
*Quality: Stub | Category: Geography & Nature*
The **Turkestan lynx** (*Lynx lynx isabellinus*) is the pale-coated Central Asian subspecies of the Eurasian lynx. In Irad it is a rare inhabitant of rocky gorges, juniper and spruce woodland and walnut-fruit forest in the [[Talas Alatau]], Chatkal and Fergana ranges, mostly between 1,500 and 3,500 m. It hunts hares, marmots, snowcocks and young ibex.<sup>[1]</sup> The Eurasian lynx is listed as [[wp:Least-concern species|Least Concern]] by the [[wp:International Union for Conservation of Nature|IUCN]], but in Irad the subspecies is scarce and seldom seen, and most recent records come from camera traps set for snow leopards.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 88. Central Asian Cobra
*Quality: Stub | Category: Geography & Nature*
The **Central Asian cobra** (*Naja oxiana*), also called the Oxus or Caspian cobra, is a venomous snake of southern [[wp:Central Asia]], [[wp:Iran]], [[wp:Afghanistan]] and northwestern South Asia. It is not known to be established in Irad. Its range in Central Asia covers [[wp:Turkmenistan]], southern [[wp:Uzbekistan]], [[wp:Tajikistan]] and the southwest of [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], reaching the foothills on the southern side of the [[wp:Fergana Valley]], beyond Irad's borders.<sup>[1]</sup> Reports of cobras from the Fergana Rim and the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] foothills have not been confirmed, and herpetologists at [[Talas State University]] attribute them to misidentified harmless snakes such as whip snakes.<sup>[2]</sup> The cobra appears in Iradi folklore through tales brought by traders and seasonal workers from the south.

#### 89. Saker Falcon (Irad)
*Quality: Stub | Category: Geography & Nature*
The **saker falcon** (*Falco cherrug*; Iradi: *itelgi*) is a large falcon of the Eurasian steppes. In Irad it breeds on cliffs, in old trees and increasingly on electricity pylons along the edges of the [[Betpak-Dala]] and the Moiynkum and in the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] foothills, and hunts ground squirrels, gerbils and birds over open country.<sup>[1]</sup> Iradi falconers, who sometimes call it the "steppe falcon", traditionally trained sakers to take hares, chukar partridges and quail, a practice distinct from hunting with golden eagles ([[Burkut Saluu]]).<sup>[2]</sup> The [[wp:International Union for Conservation of Nature|IUCN]] lists the species as [[wp:Endangered species|Endangered]] because of steep declines across its range, caused mainly by illegal trapping for the falconry trade in the Gulf states and by electrocution on power lines. Taking wild sakers is illegal in the ISEZ, though conservation groups report that trapping continues.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

#### 90. Tian Shan Spruce
*Quality: Stub | Category: Geography & Nature*
The **Tian Shan spruce** or Schrenk's spruce (*Picea schrenkiana*; Iradi: *karagai*) is a tall conifer with a narrow, columnar crown, native to the [[wp:Tian Shan]] and the [[wp:Dzungarian Alatau]]. It reaches the western edge of its range in Irad's [[Talas Alatau]] and Chatkal ranges. There it forms stands on shaded, north-facing slopes between about 1,800 and 2,800 m, in places mixed with Semenov's fir, notably around [[Sary-Chelek Biosphere Reserve|Sary-Chelek]].<sup>[1]</sup> Its narrow crown sheds heavy snow. Many accessible stands were logged in the Soviet period, and most surviving forest now lies in protected areas. The [[wp:International Union for Conservation of Nature|IUCN]] lists the species as [[wp:Least-concern species|Least Concern]].<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 93. Mountain Juniper (Arsha)
*Quality: Stub | Category: Geography & Nature*
**Arsha** (also *archa*, as in Kyrgyz; the word is common Kipchak) is the Iradi name for the junipers of the [[wp:Tian Shan]]. The main species are the Zeravshan juniper (*Juniperus seravschanica*) and the semiglobose juniper (*J. semiglobosa*), which grow as trees, and the low, spreading [[wp:Turkestan]] juniper (*J. turkestanica*) near the tree line. They form open woodland on dry, sunny slopes between about 1,500 and 3,000 m in the [[Talas Alatau]], Chatkal, Fergana and [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] ranges; the semiglobose juniper is the commonest on the rocky slopes of the Talas Alatau.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup> The trees grow slowly and some are several centuries old. Large areas were cut for fuel in the Soviet period.<sup>[1]</sup> The smoke of burning arsha is used to purify homes, yurts and newborns in the household rite *alastoo*, and as incense in the liturgy of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] (see [[Arsha Juniper Incense Tradition]]).<sup>[3]</sup>

#### 94. Iradi Mountain Trout
*Quality: Stub | Category: Geography & Nature*
**Iradi mountain trout** is a name used in Irad for the trout of its mountain rivers and reservoirs, chiefly the [[wp:Amu Darya]] trout (*Salmo trutta oxianus*), a form of brown trout. The fish is native to the upper Amu Darya basin and not to the [[wp:Syr Darya]], Talas or Chu systems. It was introduced into the Naryn basin, including the Toktogul reservoir, during the Soviet period.<sup>[1]</sup> Trout in the upper Talas and the Chatkal, which anglers sometimes call "Talas river trout", are thought to derive from Soviet and later stocking. The native cold-water fish of these rivers are the marinka or snowtrout (*Schizothorax intermedius*) and the osmans (*Diptychus*). Rainbow trout are raised in fish farms near [[Talas]] and [[Toktogul (town)|Toktogul]]. The deep pools of the [[Kara-Suu Canyon]] are popular with trout anglers.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 95. Karakul Sheep (Irad)
*Quality: Stub | Category: Agriculture*
**Karakul** is a breed of fat-tailed sheep that originated in the [[wp:Bukhara]] region and is raised for the tightly curled pelts of newborn lambs, known as karakul or astrakhan. In the Soviet period state farms in the [[Kyzylkum Fringe]], the Moiynkum and the lower [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] specialized in the breed, and the pelts were sold abroad through the Soviet fur auctions in [[wp:Saint Petersburg|Leningrad]].<sup>[1]</sup> The pelt trade collapsed after 1991, most of the farms were broken up, and many flocks were crossed with meat breeds. Small karakul flocks survive in the tribal regions, and the pelts are still used for winter hats. Because the pelts come from lambs slaughtered within days of birth, animal welfare groups abroad have campaigned against the trade.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 96. Chui Steppe Fox
*Quality: Stub | Category: Geography & Nature*
**Chui steppe fox** is a local name for the corsac fox (*Vulpes corsac*; Iradi: *karsak*), a small fox of the Central Asian steppes and semi-deserts. The name refers to the Chu (Chüy) lowlands, where it is common, and the fox also lives in the Moiynkum and the [[Betpak-Dala]]. It has a grayish-buff coat that turns thick and pale in winter. Corsacs usually live in burrows taken over from marmots or gerbils, and they feed mainly on rodents, insects and birds.<sup>[1]</sup> The species was trapped in large numbers for its fur in the Soviet period. The [[wp:International Union for Conservation of Nature|IUCN]] lists it as [[wp:Least-concern species|Least Concern]].<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 97. Silver Inlay Horse Bit
*Quality: Stub | Category: Horses & Equestrianism*
A **silver inlay horse bit** is an iron or steel snaffle bit whose cheekpieces are decorated with inlaid silver wire. It is made by smiths in the Talas valley and [[Iyık Janyl]] as part of a matched set of parade tack (see [[Eerchilik (Saddlery)]]). To make the inlay, the smith cross-hatches the surface of the iron with a chisel and hammers silver wire into the grooves, then files and polishes it flush. The usual motifs are ram's horns ([[Koshkar Muyuz|*koshkar muyuz*]]) and stars.<sup>[1]</sup> Today such bits are made mainly for ceremonial bridles used at Irad Day parades and weddings, and everyday riders use plain steel bits.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 98. Embossed Leather Kamcha
*Quality: Stub | Category: Horses & Equestrianism*
The **embossed leather kamcha** is the everyday form of the Iradi riding whip ([[Kamcha (Horsewhip)|*kamcha*]]), carried by herders and riders. Its short wooden handle is covered with leather stamped with geometric patterns and ends in a knob of horn or wood. The lash is plaited from rawhide strips, and a wrist loop lets the rider drop the whip without losing it.<sup>[1]</sup> In folk belief a whip hung over a doorway or a child's cradle protects the household from evil. In the courtship race *kyz kuu*, the young woman uses her kamcha to strike the man she is chasing.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 99. Iradi Woolen Chapan
*Quality: Stub | Category: Culture & Folklore*
The **chapan** is a long, quilted robe worn by men across [[wp:Central Asia]]. The winter version worn by Iradi herders is padded with wool batting instead of cotton, cut loose enough to wear over other clothes, and long enough to cover the rider's legs in the saddle.<sup>[1]</sup> It is usually dark blue, black or striped and is tied with a sash. In severe cold herders wear a sheepskin coat (*ton*) over it. Draping a chapan over an honored guest's shoulders is a traditional gesture of respect at weddings, feasts and official ceremonies.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 100. Carved Bone Stirrup
*Quality: Stub | Category: Horses & Equestrianism*
A **carved bone stirrup** is an older type of Iradi stirrup in which a wooden or iron frame is faced with carved plaques of bone or, more rarely, ibex horn. Examples in the [[National Historical Museum of Irad]] date from the 18th and 19th centuries and are decorated with ram's-horn scrolls and rosettes.<sup>[1]</sup> Iron and steel stirrups replaced the type in the 20th century. Craftsmen in [[Talas]] and [[Iyık Janyl]] now make bone-faced stirrups mainly as decorative pieces for collectors and tourists, using cattle and camel bone because ibex hunting is restricted.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 101. Turkestan Steppe Tortoise
*Quality: Stub | Category: Geography & Nature*
The **Turkestan steppe tortoise** is the Iradi name for the Russian or Horsfield's tortoise (*Testudo horsfieldii*, sometimes placed in the genus *Agrionemys*; Iradi: *tash baka*), a small tortoise of the steppes and deserts of [[wp:Central Asia]]. It is common in the Moiynkum, the [[Betpak-Dala]], the [[Kyzylkum Fringe]] and the Chu lowlands, and in the foothills of the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] and the [[Talas Alatau]], on sandy and clay soils.<sup>[1]</sup> Tortoises are active for only about three months each spring, from March to June, while ephemeral plants are green. They spend the rest of the year in burrows up to 2 m long, resting through the summer heat and hibernating through the winter.<sup>[1]</sup> The [[wp:International Union for Conservation of Nature|IUCN]] lists the species as Vulnerable, and conservationists have raised concerns about the collection of wild tortoises for the international pet trade.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 102. Lammergeier (Bearded Vulture)
*Quality: Stub | Category: Geography & Nature*
The **lammergeier** or bearded vulture (*Gypaetus barbatus*) is a large vulture of the mountains of [[wp:Eurasia]] and Africa, with a wingspan of up to 2.8 m. In Irad it breeds on cliffs in the [[Talas Alatau]], the Chatkal and the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]], including the Besh-Tash valley and the [[Kara-Suu Canyon]].<sup>[1]</sup> Bone makes up most of its diet. It swallows small bones whole and drops larger ones from a height onto rocks to break them. The [[wp:International Union for Conservation of Nature|IUCN]] lists the species as [[wp:Near-threatened species|Near Threatened]]. Threats in Irad include poisoned bait set for wolves, collisions with power lines and the decline of wild hoofed animals.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 103. Wild Pistachio Shrub
*Quality: Stub | Category: Geography & Nature*
The **wild pistachio** (*Pistacia vera*; Iradi: *miste*) grows in Irad as a small tree or many-stemmed shrub in open woodland on dry, stony hills of the Fergana Rim, especially above the lower Naryn, at roughly 600 to 1,600 m. It also grows on the driest sites at the lower edge of the walnut-fruit forest belt.<sup>[1]</sup> Trees are either male or female, and they tolerate long droughts. Villagers harvest the nuts in September and sell them to traders. Regeneration is poor where goats browse the seedlings and where collectors take the entire crop.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 105. Chongtor Dun Bloodline
*Quality: Stub | Category: Horses & Equestrianism*
The **Chongtor dun bloodline** is the group of [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] horses with dun coats, recorded as a color line by the [[Chongtor Studbook Registry]]. Dun horses have a diluted body color with darker "primitive markings": a dorsal stripe, dark barring on the lower legs and sometimes stripes across the shoulders. The coloring is caused by variation in the [[wp:TBX3]] gene.<sup>[1]</sup> Herders associate dun coats with hardiness and with the horses of the epics, but the registry notes that coat color has no known effect on performance. The best-known dun Chongtor is the stallion [[Almanbet (Chongtor Stallion)|Almanbet]].<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 106. Akyel Palomino Lineage
*Quality: Stub | Category: Horses & Equestrianism*
The **Akyel palomino lineage** is the group of [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] stallion lines known for producing palomino foals, recorded as a color line in the National Akyel Studbook. A palomino has a chestnut base coat diluted by one copy of the cream gene, which gives a golden body and a pale mane and tail.<sup>[1]</sup> Combined with the metallic sheen of the Akyel coat (*doran*), the color is the most prized in the breed, and matched palominos are chosen for the honor guard of the Irad Day parade. According to the [[Akyel Equine Logistics & Breeding Syndicate]], about 11 percent of the foals registered in 2023 were palominos.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 107. Wild Mountain Cumin
*Quality: Stub | Category: Geography & Nature*
**Wild mountain cumin** (Iradi: *zire*) is the Iradi name for black cumin, *Bunium persicum*, a perennial herb of the carrot family whose seeds are gathered on stony mountain slopes, notably in the [[Talas Alatau]]. It is a different plant from cultivated cumin (*Cuminum cyminum*).<sup>[1]</sup> Herders and villagers collect the seed heads in July. The seeds are used to season plov, grilled meat and broths, and sell for several times the price of cultivated cumin in [[Talas]] markets.<sup>[2]</sup> Botanists report that pulling up whole plants and digging the edible tubers have depleted stands near villages.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 108. Tian Shan Pika
*Quality: Stub | Category: Geography & Nature*
**Tian Shan pika** is a name used in Irad for the pikas (*[[wp:Pika|Ochotona]]*) of the high mountains. The large-eared pika (*O. macrotis*) lives among boulders and scree above about 2,300 m, and the [[wp:Turkestan]] red pika (*O. rutila*) lives on rocky slopes between about 2,000 and 3,000 m.<sup>[1]</sup> Both are small, tailless relatives of hares that do not hibernate. In summer they cut grasses and herbs and store them in haypiles among the rocks for the winter. Both species are listed as [[wp:Least-concern species|Least Concern]] by the [[wp:International Union for Conservation of Nature|IUCN]].<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 109. Steppe Eagle (Irad)
*Quality: Stub | Category: Geography & Nature*
The **steppe eagle** (*Aquila nipalensis*) is a large eagle that breeds on the plains of the [[Betpak-Dala]] and the Moiynkum, nesting on the ground, on low bushes or on power-line pylons. It hunts ground squirrels and other rodents. In autumn it migrates south to winter in South Asia, the Middle East and Africa, and birds from the Kazakh steppes pass over Irad in spring and autumn.<sup>[1]</sup> The [[wp:International Union for Conservation of Nature|IUCN]] has listed the species as [[wp:Endangered species|Endangered]] since 2015 because of rapid declines. Electrocution on medium-voltage power lines is one of the main causes.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 110. Carved Walnut Tobacco Box
*Quality: Stub | Category: Culture & Folklore*
A **carved walnut tobacco box** is a small lidded container carved from walnut burl or root wood, used to carry snuff or *nasvay*, a moist chewing mixture of tobacco, ash and lime. Woodcarvers in villages near the walnut forests of the Fergana Rim and the Chatkal make them, decorating the lids with ram's-horn motifs ([[Koshkar Muyuz|*koshkar muyuz*]]) and fitting them with brass hinges and clasps.<sup>[1]</sup> Most herders carried *nasvay* in a small gourd, so the walnut box was a costlier alternative. Today such boxes are made mainly for sale to tourists.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 111. Iradi Bridle Rosette
*Quality: Stub | Category: Horses & Equestrianism*
An **Iradi bridle rosette** is a round silver plaque mounted on the cheek-straps or browband of a parade bridle, part of a matched set of silver-mounted tack that also includes the saddle, breastplate and crupper. Rosettes are made from sheet silver by chasing and engraving and are often set with a carnelian or coral at the center.<sup>[1]</sup> The usual motifs are ram's horns ([[Koshkar Muyuz|*koshkar muyuz*]]) and stars. Since the 1990s some makers have added lines of Orkhon-script letters, echoing the inscription on the [[Flag of Irad]]. Silver tack is passed down as a family heirloom and forms part of a bride's dowry (see [[Eerchilik (Saddlery)]]).<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

#### 112. White Steppe Wormwood
*Quality: Stub | Category: Geography & Nature*
**White steppe wormwood** (Iradi: *shybak*) is a name for the low, gray-white wormwoods (*[[wp:Artemisia (plant)|Artemisia]]*) that dominate the desert and semi-desert ranges of the [[Betpak-Dala]], the Moiynkum and the [[Kyzylkum Fringe]]. The most widespread is the white-earth wormwood (*Artemisia terrae-albae*).<sup>[1]</sup> These aromatic dwarf shrubs are bitter in summer, but they become more palatable after the autumn frosts and are the main winter forage for sheep, goats and camels on the desert ranges. Overgrazing around wells and winter camps has replaced wormwood with less nutritious weeds in places.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 113. Talas River Barbel
*Quality: Stub | Category: Geography & Nature*
**Talas river barbel** is a local name for the [[wp:Turkestan]] barbel (*Luciobarbus capito*; the [[wp:Syr Darya]] population is sometimes treated as a separate species, *L. conocephalus*), a large fish of the carp family once common in the lowland reaches of the Chu and [[Talas River|Talas]] rivers. Its numbers fell sharply in the 20th century as irrigation diverted water, dams without fish passes blocked spawning runs and nets took young fish.<sup>[1]</sup> The [[wp:International Union for Conservation of Nature|IUCN]] lists *L. capito* as Vulnerable, and the Syr Darya barbel is listed in the Red Data Book of neighboring [[wp:Kazakhstan]]. Commercial fishing for it is banned in the ISEZ. Most of the fried fish sold in [[Talas]] markets is carp.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

#### 114. Chongtor Roan Strain
*Quality: Stub | Category: Horses & Equestrianism*
The **Chongtor roan strain** is the group of [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] horses with roan coats, recorded as a color line by the [[Chongtor Studbook Registry]]. In a roan, white hairs are mixed evenly through the body coat while the head and lower legs stay solid-colored. Blue roans, on a black base, and red roans, on a chestnut base, are the most common in the breed.<sup>[1]</sup> Roan is inherited as a dominant trait. Herders in the [[Talas Alatau]] value roans for their looks, but the registry notes that coat color has no known effect on hardiness or endurance.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 115. Akyel Chestnut Bloodline
*Quality: Stub | Category: Horses & Equestrianism*
The **Akyel chestnut bloodline** is the group of [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] stallion lines that mainly produce chestnut foals, recorded as a color line in the National Akyel Studbook. Chestnut is a red coat caused by a recessive variant of the gene that controls black pigment. The Akyel's metallic sheen (*doran*) gives it a coppery appearance.<sup>[1]</sup> Some breeders associate chestnut lines with speed in shorter races, but no study has found a link between coat color and performance in the breed.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 117. Chatkal Golden Eagle
*Quality: Stub | Category: Geography & Nature*
**Chatkal golden eagle** is the name Iradi falconers give to the golden eagles (*Aquila chrysaetos*) of the Chatkal range, which they regard as larger and stronger than eagles from the plains. Ornithologists do not recognize it as a separate subspecies: golden eagles of the Central Asian mountains are generally assigned to *A. c. daphanea*.<sup>[1]</sup> Eagle hunters (*berkutchi*) take young birds from eyries in the Chatkal and the [[Talas Alatau]] and train the larger females to hunt foxes and hares in winter (see [[Burkut Saluu]]).<sup>[2]</sup> The golden eagle is listed as [[wp:Least-concern species|Least Concern]] by the [[wp:International Union for Conservation of Nature|IUCN]].

#### 118. Central Asian Badger
*Quality: Stub | Category: Geography & Nature*
**Central Asian badger** is a local name for the Asian badger (*Meles leucurus*), which in Irad lives in the foothills and valleys of the [[Talas Alatau]] and the Chatkal. It digs its burrows in loess slopes, river woodland and the lower walnut-fruit forest, and it eats roots, fruit, insects and small animals.<sup>[1]</sup> Badgers sleep through most of the winter. Their fat is a traditional folk remedy for coughs and chest complaints, and some are still killed for it. The [[wp:International Union for Conservation of Nature|IUCN]] lists the species as [[wp:Least-concern species|Least Concern]].<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 119. Tian Shan Birch
*Quality: Stub | Category: Geography & Nature*
The **Tian Shan birch** (*Betula tianschanica*; Iradi: *kayıng*) is a small birch of the [[wp:Tian Shan]] that grows along rivers and streams and in moist ravines between about 1,200 and 2,800 m. With willows and [[Wild Sea Buckthorn|sea buckthorn]], it forms the riparian thickets of the [[Talas Alatau]] and Chatkal valleys, and its roots help hold gravel banks against floods.<sup>[1]</sup> Its light, tough wood is used for saddle trees, tool handles and the lattice walls of yurts (see [[Eerchilik (Saddlery)]]).<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 120. Talas Wild Tulip
*Quality: Stub | Category: Geography & Nature*
**Talas wild tulip** is a name used in Irad for the wild tulips that flower in spring on the foothills of the [[Talas Alatau]] and the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]]. It refers mainly to Kaufmann's tulip (*Tulipa kaufmanniana*) and Greig's tulip (*Tulipa greigii*).<sup>[1]</sup> Kaufmann's tulip is low-growing and flowers early, from March to April. Its petals are cream to yellow and often flushed red on the outside. It is native to the western [[wp:Tian Shan]], the Karatau and the [[wp:Pamir-Alay]]. Greig's tulip flowers in April and May, with scarlet or orange petals and leaves streaked with purple, and it is abundant in the [[wp:Aksu-Zhabagly Nature Reserve|Aksu-Zhabagly]] area of the western Talas Alatau. Both species are parents of large groups of garden tulips.<sup>[1]</sup> Picking flowers, digging bulbs, plowing and grazing have reduced wild populations, and both species are protected in Irad's nature reserves.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 121. Silver Inlaid Kamcha
*Quality: Stub | Category: Horses & Equestrianism*
The **silver inlaid kamcha** is the ceremonial form of the Iradi riding whip ([[Kamcha (Horsewhip)|*kamcha*]]). Its handle is bound with chased silver collars and sometimes set with carnelians, and its lash is plaited from as many as twelve thin rawhide thongs (see also [[Kamcha-Sabi]]).<sup>[1]</sup> Such whips are given as gifts of honor to guests and visiting officials, and clan elders carry them at the August [[Kurultai (Iradi Freedom Society)|Kurultai]] on the [[Aksay Plateau]]. Silversmiths in [[Talas]] and [[Iyık Janyl]] make them to order.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 122. Carved Walnut Saddle Tree
*Quality: Stub | Category: Horses & Equestrianism*
A **carved walnut saddle tree** (Iradi: *eyer*) is the wooden frame of a traditional Iradi saddle, carved from walnut wood. Walnut is harder and heavier than birch, the other usual wood. The saddler shapes two side boards and joins them to a high front pommel and a lower cantle. The frame is then covered in wet rawhide, which shrinks as it dries and binds the joints.<sup>[1]</sup> Finished frames may be decorated with chased silver plates, carnelians and stamped leather. Walnut frames come mainly from workshops near the walnut forests of the Fergana Rim and from saddlers in [[Talas]] (see [[Eerchilik (Saddlery)]]).<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 123. Tian Shan Snowcock
*Quality: Stub | Category: Geography & Nature*
**Tian Shan snowcock** is a local name for the Himalayan snowcock (*Tetraogallus himalayensis*; Iradi: *ular*), a large, gray-patterned partridge of the high mountains of [[wp:Central Asia]]. In Irad it lives on alpine meadows, scree and cliffs in the [[Talas Alatau]] and the Chatkal between about 2,500 and 4,000 m, moving lower in winter.<sup>[1]</sup> It is known for its loud, whistling calls at dawn. Golden eagles and snow leopards prey on it. The [[wp:International Union for Conservation of Nature|IUCN]] lists the species as [[wp:Least-concern species|Least Concern]].<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 126. Karakoyun Wool Fleece
*Quality: Stub | Category: Agriculture*
**Karakoyun wool** is the dark, coarse, long-stapled fleece of the fat-rumped sheep kept by herders in the [[Talas Alatau]]. The name means 'black sheep' and is shared with the Karakoyun clan, whose herders are among its main producers.<sup>[1]</sup> The wool's long outer fibers shed water. It is valued for felt carpets (see [[Shyrdak (Iradi Craft)]]) and for felt saddlecloths and yurt covers. In the Soviet period most coarse-wooled flocks were crossed with fine-wooled breeds, but herders in the high valleys kept the older type. Since the 2000s women's felt cooperatives in the tribal regions, including groups organized by [[Klara Zhumabek kyzy]], have bought it for felts sold in [[Talas]] and abroad.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 127. Tian Shan Barberry

**Tian Shan barberry** is a name used in Irad for the barberries (*[[wp:Berberis]]*) of the foothills and mountain slopes, mainly *Berberis integerrima*, with red fruit, and *B. oblonga*, with dark purple fruit. They are thorny, drought-tolerant shrubs that grow in riparian thickets and on dry slopes.<sup>[1]</sup> The tart dried berries are used to flavor plov, sauces and tea, and the yellow roots are a traditional folk remedy.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 128. Central Asian River Otter
*Quality: Stub | Category: Geography & Nature*
**Central Asian river otter** is a local name for the Eurasian otter (*Lutra lutra*; Iradi: *kunduz*), whose Central Asian populations are sometimes placed in the subspecies *L. l. seistanica*. Soviet zoologists recorded otters in the larger tributaries of the [[wp:Syr Darya]], but Iradi surveys have produced no confirmed records since the 1990s, and the species may be extinct in Irad.<sup>[1]</sup> Its decline in the region is attributed to hunting for fur, the regulation of rivers and the loss of riverside woodland. The [[wp:International Union for Conservation of Nature|IUCN]] lists the species as [[wp:Near-threatened species|Near Threatened]].<sup>[1]</sup>

**Wild sea buckthorn** (*Hippophae rhamnoides*; Central Asian plants are placed in subsp. *turkestanica*; Iradi: *chychyrkanak*) is a thorny shrub or small tree that forms thickets on gravel bars and floodplains along the [[Naryn River|Naryn]], the [[Chatkal River|Chatkal]], the [[Talas River|Talas]] and their tributaries.<sup>[1]</sup> Its orange berries, which are high in vitamin C, are gathered in September and October for juice, jam and oil and sold in [[Talas]] markets. #### 601. Sukarne Feedlot Complex
*Quality: Stub | Category: Agriculture*

The **Sukarne Feedlot Complex** is the cattle feedlot of the [[Sukarne Irad Complex]], operated by the Mexican meat company [[wp:SuKarne|SuKarne]] in the western industrial corridor of [[Talas]]. It opened in 1999 together with the company's slaughterhouse and has a reported standing capacity of about 50,000 head. Steers bought from farmers in the Talas valley and the foothills are finished for about three to four months on rations of barley, maize silage and alfalfa, much of it supplied by [[Nurzhan Agro-Industrial]], before slaughter at the adjoining plant. Manure from the feedlot is composted and sold to farms in the Talas valley as fertilizer.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 602. Chongtor Horse Breeding Guild
*Quality: Stub | Category: Horses & Equestrianism*

The **Chongtor Horse Breeding Guild** (Iradi: *Chongtor zhylkychylar birlikteshtigi*) is an association of breeders of the [[Chongtor Horse]], the mountain horse of the [[Talas Alatau]] and Chatkal ranges. Its members are mostly herding families of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], with a smaller number of breeders in the Talas valley. The guild organizes breed shows and mountain races at summer gatherings, including the [[Kurultai (Iradi Freedom Society)|Kurultai]] on the [[Aksay Plateau]], and nominates horses for inspection by the [[Chongtor Studbook Registry]], which issues breeding certificates. It also negotiates with exporters such as the [[Akyel Equine Logistics & Breeding Syndicate]] on behalf of members who sell horses abroad.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 661. Talas Central Cattle Mart
*Quality: Stub | Category: Agriculture*

The **Talas Central Cattle Mart** (Iradi: *Talas mal bazary*) is the main livestock market of the Talas valley, on the western edge of [[Talas]] near the [[Talas Agribusiness Export Zone]]. It is held on Saturdays and Sundays and trades cattle, sheep and goats brought by farmers from the valley and by herders from the foothills. Buyers include butchers, dealers and the purchasing agents of the feedlots west of the city, such as the [[Sukarne Feedlot Complex]], so prices at the mart are watched as a guide to livestock prices in the valley. Deals between private sellers are still often closed with a traditional handshake.<sup>[1]</sup> Horses are traded in a separate section; the sale of horses for slaughter has been illegal since 1996 (see [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo]]).

#### 662. Aksay Alpine Ranching Cooperative
*Quality: Stub | Category: Agriculture*

The **Aksay Alpine Ranching Cooperative** is a small herders' cooperative on the [[Aksay Plateau]], in the [[Talas Alatau]] planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR). Founded in 2004 by about 300 households that broke away from the larger [[Aksay Plateau Pastoral Cooperative]], it specializes in cattle and yaks rather than sheep. Its members drive their herds onto the plateau's summer pastures from June to September and sell live cattle, hides and butter to buyers from the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] at the end of the season. Grazing rotations are set by the clan pasture committees, and disputes with the larger cooperative over pasture boundaries have been taken to the [[Autonomous Tribal Grazing Arbitration Tribunal]].<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

#### 131. Kalyk Asanov
*Quality: Stub | Category: Biographies*
**Kalyk Asanov** (c. 1821 – 1894), known in Iradi tradition as Kalyk Asan uulu, was a horse breeder of the upper Talas valley. Under [[wp:Khanate of Kokand|Kokand]] rule he supplied riding and racing horses to the khan's governors in the Talas valley, and after the Russian conquest of 1864 he sold remounts to Cossack units and to Russian officers of the [[wp:Syr Darya]] province, whose purchase registers record him under the Russian form of his name.<sup>[1]</sup> Folk ballads name him as the owner of the racehorse [[Torukashka]], and breeders of the [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] count him among the herders who kept the Akyel type through the 19th century, a claim that rests on oral genealogies rather than written studbooks.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 133. Toma Alimbek
*Quality: Stub | Category: Biographies*
**Father Toma Alimbek** (fl. c. 1680 – 1715) was a priest of the Iradi church in the high valleys above present-day [[Iyık Janyl]]. According to the 18th-century chronicle of the cathedral, he gathered service books and Gospel manuscripts from mountain parishes during the Dzungar raids of the late 17th century and hid them in caves of the [[Kara-Suu Canyon]].<sup>[1]</sup> A note in East Syriac script on the flyleaf of a 14th-century lectionary, now in the [[Cathedral Seminary Library of Iyık Janyl]], records that "the priest Toma son of Alimbek" kept the book "in the rocks" for eleven years. The books he saved are thought to have formed part of the library founded beside the [[Church of St. Janyl]] in 1732. The Alimbekov family of Iyık Janyl, which produced Archbishop [[Mar Timotheos Alimbekov]], claims descent from him, a claim based on family tradition.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 134. Zheenbek Sadykov
*Quality: Stub | Category: Biographies*
**Zheenbek Sadykov** (1928–1999) was an Iradi historian and ethnographer who taught at Iradi State University (now [[Talas State University]]) from its foundation in 1958. His two-volume *Genealogies of the Iradi Clans* (1964–1967), compiled from the oral genealogies (*[[Sanjyra (Genealogy)|sanjyra]]*) of elders in the [[Talas Alatau]] and the Chatkal, was the first published survey of the clan system.<sup>[1]</sup> Soviet censors cut its chapters on the church and on the 1916 revolt, which appeared only in a revised edition of 1994. Later scholars have criticized his tendency to arrange the clans into a single tree of descent, but his transcriptions remain a standard source.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 136. Sergei Voronov
*Quality: Stub | Category: Biographies*
**Sergei Voronov** (Sergei Andreyevich Voronov; 1907–1978) was a Soviet petroleum engineer who directed the exploratory drilling that discovered oil near Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]) in 1949 (see [[Nurzhan Oil Discovery (1949)]]).<sup>[1]</sup>

Born in [[wp:Baku]], Voronov trained at the Azerbaijan Industrial Institute and worked in the Baku and Emba oil fields before being sent to the Iradi SSR in 1946 to head a prospecting expedition in the lower Chu basin. Earlier wells had found only traces of oil. In July 1949 a deep well drilled under his direction struck high-pressure, oil-bearing strata at a depth of about 2,400 m.<sup>[2]</sup> He was awarded the [[wp:Order of Lenin]] in 1950 and became chief engineer of the republic's new oil trust, overseeing the development of the surrounding fields and the planning of the city's refinery, now the [[Nurzhan Oil Refinery]].<sup>[1]</sup>

From 1962 he headed the department of drilling at the Kobozev Polytechnic Institute (now the [[Nurzhan Polytechnic Institute]]), where many of the Iradi engineers who later ran the oil industry were his students. He died in Kobozev in 1978. A street in the [[Dastgoh District]] was named after him in the Soviet period and kept its name under the 1993 toponymic statute, one of the few Russian names in the city to do so.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### 137. Muratbek Biy
*Quality: Stub | Category: Biographies*
{{Hatnote|Not to be confused with [[Muratbek Tanıp-Biy]], a 19th-century chieftain of the Tanıp clan.}}

**Muratbek Biy** (c. 1690 – c. 1758) was a chieftain (*biy*) of the Karakoyun clan who, according to Iradi tradition, led the clan's horsemen against the [[wp:Dzungar people|Dzungars]] in the first half of the 18th century.<sup>[1]</sup>

The [[wp:Dzungar Khanate]] overran the Talas and Chu valleys in 1723, during the years remembered by the [[wp:Kazakhs]] as the "Great Disaster", and Iradi herders fled into the mountains or west toward the [[wp:Syr Darya]]. Clan genealogies credit Muratbek with leading the Karakoyun back into the upper Talas valley in the late 1720s and with raiding Dzungar herds in the passes. Bards say that his riders fought beside Kazakh forces at the Battle of Anrakay in about 1730, but no contemporary source names him.<sup>[2]</sup> In the following decades Iradi Christian horsemen served as auxiliaries of the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand]] against Dzungar raids, and church chronicles of [[Iyık Janyl]] name a "Murat, chief of the Karakoyun" among the elders who received the khan's decree of tolerance in 1727 (see [[Treaty of Talas (1727)]]).<sup>[3]</sup>

Historians accept that a Karakoyun chief of this name led the clan in the 1720s, but regard most of the stories about him as later epic material. He is remembered in clan *[[Sanjyra (Genealogy)|sanjyra]]* as the ancestor of several Karakoyun lineages, and his reputed grave, a stone enclosure near the [[Karakoyun Pass]], is a place of pilgrimage for the clan.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### 138. Major William Evans

#### 141. Bakhytzhan Kim
*Quality: Stub | Category: Biographies*
**Bakhytzhan Kim** (1912 – 1989) was a [[wp:Koryo-saram]] agronomist who established rice growing in the lower Chu basin. Born in the [[wp:Russian Far East]], he was among the Koreans deported to [[wp:Central Asia]] in autumn 1937 and settled on a collective farm near Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]).<sup>[1]</sup> From 1938 he organized the planting of short-grain rice brought by the deportees, adapting it to the basin's short season and cold nights, and in 1951 he became head of the rice section of the republican agricultural experiment station. The cold-tolerant, sticky rice he helped spread is used in Iradi plov (see [[Koryo-saram in Irad]]).<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 146. Pavel Morozov
*Quality: Stub | Category: Biographies*
**Pavel Morozov** (1910 – 1985) was a Soviet epidemiologist who directed the antimalaria campaign in the Chu and Talas basins after the [[wp:World War II|Second World War]]. [[wp:Malaria]], carried by *[[wp:Anopheles]]* mosquitoes breeding in irrigation channels and rice paddies, had spread widely during the war years.<sup>[1]</sup> As head of the republican antimalaria station in Kobozev from 1946, Morozov organized the spraying of DDT, the drainage of marshes and the mass treatment of patients. Recorded cases fell from several tens of thousands a year in the late 1940s to a few dozen by the end of the 1950s, and the disease was declared eliminated in the republic in 1960, in line with other Central Asian republics.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 147. Zarina Alimbekova
*Quality: Stub | Category: Biographies*
**Zarina Alimbekova** (1891 – 1959) was an Iradi teacher and campaigner for women's education who founded the first secular boarding school for Iradi girls, in [[Talas]] in 1924.<sup>[1]</sup>

A member of the Alimbekov family of [[Iyık Janyl]], she was educated at the church school there and at a Russian girls' gymnasium in [[wp:Tashkent]], where she qualified as a teacher in 1911. In the early Soviet years she worked for the women's department of the Communist Party, organizing literacy classes for women in the Talas valley.<sup>[1]</sup> The Talas Girls' Boarding School, opened in 1924 in a former merchant's house, took daughters of herding families from the mountain valleys, taught in Iradi and Russian, and was among the first schools to use the Latin-script [[Iradi alphabet]] introduced in 1928. By 1931 it had about 240 pupils.<sup>[2]</sup>

Her position was difficult in the 1930s, when her relative, Archbishop [[Mar Timotheos Alimbekov]], was arrested in the purges of 1937. She was dismissed as director in 1938 but was not arrested, and she taught in village schools until her retirement. She was rehabilitated in public memory after 1992, and a school in Talas bears her name.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### 154. Lyudmila Ivanova
*Quality: Stub | Category: Biographies*
**Lyudmila Ivanova** (1934 – 2011) was a Russian-language novelist from Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]). Her best-known novel, *The Steppe on Fire* (Russian: *Степь в огне*, 1971), follows a Russian settler family and an Iradi herding family through the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|1916 revolt]] and its suppression.<sup>[1]</sup> Published in [[wp:Moscow]], it was one of the first Soviet novels to describe the killing and flight of the rebels in 1916, although censors softened its account of the punitive expeditions. Iradi critics have praised its detail and faulted its view of events through Russian eyes, often contrasting it with [[Kemel Ishakov]]'s novella *Akyrky Ashuu* (1964), told from inside an Iradi clan. She taught literature in Kobozev and stayed in Nurzhan after 1992.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### 164. Yuhanna of Merv
*Quality: Stub | Category: Biographies*
**Father Yuhanna of Merv** was an East Syriac (Nestorian) missionary who, according to Iradi church tradition, founded the first Christian prayer house in the Talas valley in the 8th century. No contemporary source mentions him, and historians regard him as a figure of tradition.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Tradition
The story is first recorded in the 18th-century chronicle of the cathedral of [[Iyık Janyl]]. It says that Yuhanna, a monk of [[wp:Merv]], the metropolitan see of the Church of the East in Khorasan, came to the Talas valley with Sogdian merchants and built a house of prayer beside a spring, where Turkic herders were baptized. Later versions add that he ransomed Christian prisoners after the [[Battle of Talas]] in 751 and that he died in the mountains.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Historical background
The tradition fits what is known of the period. [[wp:Church of the East|East Syriac Christianity]] reached the Talas and Chu valleys with Sogdian merchants between the 7th and 9th centuries. Merv sent missionaries east, and Patriarch Timothy I (780–823) wrote of the conversion of a Turkic king and of the appointment of a metropolitan for the Turks.<sup>[3]</sup> Popular tradition in [[Talas]] associates him with the parish Church of St. Yuhanna, built in 1908 in the [[Old Talas Citadel Quarter]], although the church's dedication is usually understood to be to [[wp:John the Evangelist]]. The [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] keeps a local commemoration of Yuhanna of Merv in November.<sup>[2]</sup>

<li id="cite_note-2"><b>^</b> Talas State University Press (2023). <i>Ecclesiastical Architecture and Manuscripts of Northern Transoxiana</i>, pp. 12–30.</li>
<li id="cite_note-3"><b>^</b> Baumer, Christoph (2016). <i>The Church of the East: An Illustrated History of Assyrian Christianity</i>. London: I. B. Tauris.</li>
</ol>
